#6453. Scientists Just Found a Key Ingredient for Superconductivity at Room Temperature

Researchers have discovered that a key requirement for superconductivity can persist even at room temperature.

Scientists searching for a superconductor that works at room temperature have identified a potential way forward. New research from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich shows that electrons can form the pairs needed for superconductivity even at room temperature. The findings, published in Science, suggest that a different requirement may be preventing these materials from conducting electricity without resistance.

The key appears to be how paired electrons behave collectively. Although the pairs can survive at much higher temperatures than previously understood, they must also act in a coordinated way for superconductivity to emerge.

Electrical resistance causes energy to be lost as heat whenever current passes through an ordinary conductor. This is useful in a toaster, where resistance heats a metal wire until it glows, but undesirable in power transmission and electronic devices. Superconductors eliminate electrical resistance, potentially enabling more efficient energy storage, levitating trains, and advanced quantum computers.

The obstacle is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C (-436°F), often using expensive liquid helium. Superconductivity was first discovered in 1911, and researchers made major progress in the mid-1980s when they identified materials that could become superconducting at temperatures around -173°C (-279°F). Yet these higher-temperature superconductors presented a mystery: the established theory explaining conventional superconductivity could not account for their behavior.

“We don’t understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all,” says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. “And if you don’t understand it, you can’t systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal.”

Superconductivity requires two essential conditions. First, electrons must form partnerships known as Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated quantum state called phase coherence. Without both conditions, a material cannot sustain superconductivity.

In conventional superconductors, electron pairing and phase coherence emerge together as the material cools below a critical temperature. The new research shows that these processes can occur separately in high-temperature superconductors. Electron pairs can form and remain stable at temperatures far above the point where electrical resistance disappears, including at room temperature.

“This is really good news,” says Swart. “We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren’t possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether.”

The findings indicate that the interaction binding electrons into pairs can remain sufficiently strong at room temperature. This shifts attention toward phase coherence, which may be the limiting factor preventing superconductivity at higher temperatures.

“The ‘glue’ that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature,” says Swart. “This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck.”

The researchers have not demonstrated room-temperature superconductivity, but their results help narrow the search for what is missing. Swart plans to investigate how phase coherence develops and what prevents electron pairs from achieving it at higher temperatures.

“If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures.”

Reference: “Equivalence of pseudogap and pairing energy in a cuprate high-temperature superconductor” by Jiasen Niu, Maialen Ortego Larrazabal, Thomas Gozlinski, Yudai Sato, Koen M. Bastiaans, Tjerk Benschop, Jian-Feng Ge, Yaroslav M. Blanter, Genda Gu, Ingmar Swart and Milan P. Allan, 5 November 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.adt3444

#6452. Our Universe Is Held Together by Invisible Galactic Glue—And We Wouldn’t Exist Without It

Its transformative emergence might have occurred within the very first seconds of time, physicists say.

Dark matter isn’t like other matter. It doesn’t interact with visible light or any other electromagnetic force. And yet, it seems to push around regular matter through its gravitational influence. Dark matter rules the universe, maybe holding galaxies together, but we still don’t know what it is.

A battery of cosmological probes has revealed clues to the presence—and influence—of dark matter in the universe: Stars orbit galactic centers far too quickly. Galaxies zip around clusters with excessive velocities. Massive objects bend the light passing by them with more gravitational force than we can account for with visible observations. And the history of the universe has revealed the incredibly speedy growth of gigantic structures.

The conclusion is that there’s something more to the universe than our traditional electromagnetic measurements can detect. Yet this thing simply doesn’t emit or absorb light. What could it be?

What we know is that it’s cold, heavy, and slow. Yet, new research suggests that it may have once been the complete opposite: hot, light, fast … and insignificant.

How do you turn dark matter from zero to hero? The answer lies in the strange and wonderful physics of superconductivity, which lets electricity flow with zero resistance. In a new paper, theoretical physicists Guanming Liang and Robert Caldwell from Dartmouth College outline a hypothetical scenario for flooding the universe with dark matter when it was mere seconds old.

For decades, cosmologists have been following one particular compelling idea to explain dark matter, known as WIMPs, for weakly interacting massive particles. These are hypothetical particles that only interact with the rest of the universe through gravity and the weak nuclear force (which rules subatomic particles’ behavior). But searches for WIMPs have so far come up empty.

To fill the gaps, theorists have been busy, generating dozens of new theories every year to unravel the mystery of dark matter. The vast majority of these ideas come from the land of high-energy physics, invoking this-or-that exotic process or super-theoretical particle that we might see someday in a collider. These massive machines smash high-energy subatomic particles together in the search for new particles.

But Liang and Caldwell took a different tack, turning instead toward condensed matter physics. This branch of physics makes major breakthroughs all the time, but without as much public fanfare as the high-energy work.

At a fundamental level, condensed matter physics is the study of stuff. It gives us an understanding of how everyday things work on subatomic levels—from why glass is transparent to how heat flows through new materials. And it’s also the study of everyday materials under extreme conditions, which leads to completely counterintuitive behaviors.

For example, take electrical resistance. Electrons flowing down a wire bump into each other, which saps energy out. This is why we can’t, for instance, have solar arrays in the desert that can pipe their electricity all around the country.

But if you cool some materials down to nearly absolute zero, the electrons bind up together in a new state of matter. And when they do that, all the resistance disappears, and electricity can flow uninterrupted. This is known as superconductivity, and it’s through superconductors that we’re able to harness tremendously large currents to drive technologies like MRI machines and maglev (magnetic levitation) trains.

In Liang and Caldwell’s model, dark matter starts out as a hot soup of fast-moving, massless particles in the extremely early universe. But as the universe expands and cools off, the dark matter particles pair together, the way electrons do in a superconductor. When they do that, the dark matter particles undergo a radical transformation, emerging on the other side with a brand-new set of properties. The pairs become slow-moving, heavy—and dark.

However, the model revealed an unusual quirk: that if the dark matter particles start out with even a tiny bit of mass, then not all of them bind up together as pairs. Most of them stay in the background, where they soak up all of spacetime. This behavior might provide an explanation for another mysterious ingredient in the cosmos, dark energy, which is responsible for causing the accelerated expansion of the universe.

So far Liang and Caldwell’s idea is just that: a guess as to how the universe might actually work. But it’s a testable one. The properties of these paired-up dark matter particles may leave behind a subtle signature in the appearance of the cosmic microwave background. That’s the light left over from when the universe cooled from a plasma to a neutral state, when it was around 380,000 years old.

To be fair, the idea is probably wrong. But that’s okay. We have no idea what dark matter is, and we need to flex every analytical and creative muscle we have to solve a puzzle that spans the entire universe. And we need to draw from as many sources of inspiration as possible, whether it’s high-energy physics, condensed matter physics—or even something else.

We never know when we’re going to be right. It’s only by searching in the dark that we’ll find out.

Paul M. Sutter is a science educator and a cosmologist at Johns Hopkins University and the author of How to Die in Space: A Journey Through Dangerous Astrophysical Phenomena and Your Place in the Universe: Understanding Our Big, Messy Existence. #6451. A Natural “Varnish” May Explain How 37,000-Year-Old Cave Art Survived

A new technique uses UV light to reveal a natural mineral varnish that may have helped preserve Chauvet Cave’s 37,000-year-old charcoal drawings.

About 37,000 years ago, Paleolithic people entered a limestone cave in southeastern France and drew the animals around them, including cave bears, cave lions, bison, and horses. An ancient rockfall later sealed away the artwork, leaving it undiscovered until the 1990s. Today, Chauvet Cave holds some of the oldest artwork in existence, along with clues to how the cave itself helped preserve it.

Getting close to those clues requires care. The site is so historically important and fragile that its location is kept secret and access is secured behind a huge steel door. Inside, prehistoric footprints lie in front of the artwork. Researchers examining the walls must also protect these traces of the people who once walked through the cave.

Researcher Philippe Walter describes the purpose of that painstaking work. “We examine every piece of evidence to decode the techniques of prehistoric artists and understand how the paintings have been preserved over time.”

In a study reported in ACS Omega, Walter and his colleagues investigated the charcoal drawings without touching the cave walls. They focused on mineral deposits that had formed over the artwork, looking for evidence of how the drawings were created and how the cave’s geology may have contributed to their preservation.

To work around the fragile footprints, the team placed a portable spectrometer on a protective walkway about 8 feet (2.5 meters) from the wall. This instrument measures light, allowing the researchers to examine materials from a distance.

Their approach used ultraviolet, or UV, fluorescence spectroscopy, a technique researchers have used to reveal fluorescent mineral deposits invisible to the naked eye. Certain materials emit light when exposed to UV illumination. By shining a UV beam onto the wall and analyzing the resulting glow, the team could investigate both the mineral deposits and the pigments in the artwork.

Two different colors offered clues to what had happened on the cave walls:

“Our methodology is much like forensic investigation: We examine every piece of evidence to decode the techniques of prehistoric artists and understand how the paintings have been preserved over time,” says Walter.

The team anticipates applications beyond cave art, from forensic science to monitoring biofilms aboard the International Space Station. Biofilms are communities of microorganisms that grow on surfaces. A project applying the technique to monitoring them aboard the station is already underway.

Reference: “In Situ Ultraviolet Fluorescence Spectroscopy for the Characterization of Translucent Calcite Coatings over Prehistoric Cave Art” by Yohan Boulard, Thiéry Guillou, Carole Fritz, Gilles Tosello, Maguy Jaber and Philippe Walter, 29 September 2026, ACS Omega. DOI: 10.1021/acsomega.6c05061

The authors acknowledge funding from the French Ministry of Culture, the French National Centre for Scientific Research (Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique), and Sorbonne University.

Disclosure: One of the authors is a founder of Lumentis, a company developing imaging instruments for historical artwork analysis.

#6450. ZWO Seestar S30 Plus review

We tested the brand-new ZWO Seestar S30 Plus, an all-in-one smart telescope for beginners and hobbyists that makes astrophotography accessible to everyone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's much to enjoy about the Seestar S30 Plus. The image quality is great, it's easy to use, and it's compact and lightweight enough to take it anywhere. It's not quite as good as the more expensive S30 Pro, but it's a nice middle-ground option between the S30 and the S30 Pro that gives you a lot of features for the money.

Seestar app is reliable and easy to navigate

All-in-one workflow from shooting to sharing

2K image quality is better than we expected

Editing controls could be a little more responsive

Not suitable for smaller planetary nebulas

Why you can trust Live Science Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best ones for you. Find out more about how we test.

ZWO has just released the newest member of its smart telescope range: the Seestar S30 Plus. This all-in-one smart telescope is designed for beginners and hobbyists who want an affordable way into astrophotography that won't leave you scratching your head, and lets you capture, process and share your images in one simple workflow. It sits between the Seestar S30 and S30 Pro, and is priced at $499 for its release.

With 2K image quality, a light pollution filter and a user-friendly interface, it's a smart telescope that anyone can enjoy, regardless of your experience level, and regardless of whether you're shooting from your city balcony or a dark sky site. Like the other models, it uses dual cameras to capture a wide range of subjects, including deep-sky objects with the telephoto camera, and constellations, star trails and the Milky Way with the wide-angle camera. It's lightweight and easy to travel with, and it even comes with a separate solar filter for solar imaging and eclipse time-lapses.

We got our hands on an advance copy to test ahead of its release, so we put it through its paces on several different celestial subjects.

The Seestar S30 Plus is one of the smallest, most compact smart telescopes on the market, weighing just 3.63 pounds (1.65 kg) and measuring 8.3 x 5.5 x 3.2 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm). Its sleek, matte white design looks identical to the other Seestar models (we compared it to our S30 Pro), except for the branding on the unit itself.

It comes in a padded soft carry case and includes a small tripod (although we always prefer to use our own), a solar filter, a 40-inch (1 meter) USB-A to USB-C charging cable, a removable shoulder strap for the carry case, and a quick-start guide. With its accessories and case, the whole setup weighs 4.89 pounds (2.22 kg).

On the unit itself, you'll find just one button, which powers it on, plus the USB-C port on the side. Super simple, although we'd have liked the USB-C port to be covered to prevent moisture or dust from getting in.

It comes with a carry case, strap, USB-C cable and solar filter.

The set-up process couldn't be easier. When you turn the telescope on, you'll hear a double beep and see the power button light up alongside the red dots on the black screen to indicate the battery level. Four dots mean the battery is full. The telescope will tell you when it's ready to connect, at which point you can sync it up to the app on your smartphone or tablet. To turn it off, you just select "Shutdown" in the app, which closes the arm and turns the unit off.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It also features an anti-dew heater, which we've found works quite well in mild to moderate humidity. On a couple of our shoots, we noticed a tiny bit of condensation forming on the unit when the humidity was higher, so we wouldn't feel confident leaving it unsupervised for long periods on a particularly dewy evening. (We used the Clear Outside app to monitor the humidity levels.)

The Seestar App is user-friendly and easy to navigate, with just the right amount of controls: you have plenty of options to choose from but it doesn’t become overwhelming. The main Seestar page is where you'll likely spend most of your time, as this is where you can search for celestial objects to shoot, access your album, plan a shoot and read up on what objects Seestar recommends based on your time and location.

The Stargazing section is where you can select or search for the subject you want to shoot. You can use the search function to find a specific target or browse Tonight's Best, and you can also search through different types of subjects like galaxies, nebulas, clusters and more. From here, you can also select planets, track comets and photograph constellations using the wide camera.

Click on a subject and the app will display information about it, including its current altitude and coordinates, which help determine what time is best to shoot that particular object. It automatically applies the appropriate filters and settings, but you can override these if you want to.

There's very little to complain about when it comes to using the app. It has lots of information for beginners, so you don't need a ton of knowledge about the night sky, and everything is fairly self-explanatory. There were a couple of occasions when it failed to calibrate itself (for example, when we tried to locate the Pleiades, which had just risen above a tree), and other times when we chose a new target and it slewed the long way round instead of only having to move slightly. But otherwise, the app worked well.

The AI Enhance section has some good editing tools to bring out the best from your photos. You can reduce the stars, adjust the brightness, contrast, saturation and RGB curves, apply denoise and eliminate any satellite trails — although we'd love a dehaze slider to bring out some of the fainter nebulosity of certain objects. The sliders could do with being a little more responsive, especially the RGB curves, but overall, it does a pretty good job of editing your pictures to get a pleasing result.

We had about 10 days to test our review unit before its release, so we could only capture as much as the weather permitted in that time. We'll add more images to this review over the coming weeks. All our tests were conducted from our backyard in a Bortle 4 region, and captured before moonrise to eliminate as much light pollution as possible. Due to these time constraints, we aimed to capture our images for a total of 60 minutes each, although we'd have ideally aimed for longer in some cases.

Now for the fun part — the images. The Seestar S30 Plus has a focal length of 160mm, which is advantageous for capturing large subjects like the Andromeda Galaxy, the North America Nebula and the Pleiades. Large emission nebulas are where it really shines; however, the focal length is too short to capture smaller apparent objects.

For this review, we aimed to capture as many different types of objects as possible. All our images were edited in the Seestar app with, in some cases, a few minor tweaks in Lightroom. You also have the option to download the individual files to your computer to process them yourself in dedicated astrophotography software, which is advantageous if you're a more experienced user.

Everyone's favorite star cluster, the Pleiades, was one of the first targets we wanted to capture. We could see the faint blue nebulosity after as little as 15 minutes of integration time, and it only improved over time. After 60 minutes, we had a really nice image and could easily bring out the blue haze via the editing tools in the app. However, we got a much more impressive result after tweaking our image a little further in Lightroom, bringing out even more haze and reflective dust.

The Andromeda Galaxy is a perfect target for the Seestar S30 Plus. It takes up a large portion of the frame, and with long integration times, it can reveal beautiful details in the faint outer arms. We shot for around an hour in our tests due to weather and time constraints, but we still got an impressive image. As we approached 60 minutes, there was a lot of cloud cover, and we noticed it struggling to stack images toward the end of the session, so we stopped the integration at 57 minutes.

Andromeda is certainly going to be the most impressive galaxy for the Seestar visually, as most others will appear smaller in the frame and will need longer integration, so make sure you have a clear, dark night for it.

Large emission nebulas are where the Seestar S30 Plus thrives, and the North America Nebula is a great target. It covers the whole field of view, and the red hydrogen gas easily comes to the forefront of the image.

The Eastern Veil Nebula is another lovely target where you can bring out the beautiful red and turquoise hues in as little as 15 minutes, but longer integration times will yield brighter, more colorful results.

Planetary nebulas are where you will see the limitations of the Seestar's 160mm focal length. Most planetary nebulas have a very small apparent size — we've previously captured the Dumbbell Nebula and Cocoon Nebula with our S30 Pro, and they were a tiny dot in the middle of the screen. We tried the Helix Nebula, and even though it's one of the largest apparent planetary nebulas, it's still fairly small on the Seestar S30 Plus. You can still get a decent image of it, but if you want to focus on imaging planetary nebulas, you'll need a bigger scope. Because it was very low in the sky and there was some interfering cloud, we stopped integration at 27 minutes.

The Seestar S30 Plus is an affordable entry point into deep-sky astrophotography without the confusing settings and expensive setup. It's ideal for beginners, although more experienced users will likely want to upgrade to the superior image quality and extra features of the S30 Pro.

Still, for under $500, we can't complain. Not only is the Seestar S30 Plus easy to navigate and use, but it teaches you about space in a fun and interactive way, and you don't need to spend hours stacking individual frames on your computer to process — although you still can do that if you want more control over your editing.

If you can stretch your budget, the S30 Pro is a worthy upgrade. It produces 4K images and offers more pro-level features.

To see deeper into space, the Seestar S50 Pro has a longer focal length of 260mm and a larger 50mm aperture, making it better for smaller apparent objects.

If the imaging aspect doesn't interest you, the Celestron StarSense Explorer range of telescopes connects to your phone to guide you around the sky, but you observe the cosmos through an eyepiece instead of capturing it on your phone.

Read our full Celestron StarSense Explorer LT 70AZ review

Kimberley Lane, E-commerce writer for Live Science, has tested a wide range of optical equipment, reviewing camera gear from Sony, Canon, OM System and more. With over 6 years of photography experience, her skills span across landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in a number of national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan. She has also contributed to our sister site Space.com and Tech Radar, and she regularly uses binoculars and telescopes to stargaze in the dark skies of South Wales.

#6449. How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hawkmoths can create ultrasonic bursts that thwart the sonar of predatory bats

The pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) is one of many species whose males make ultrasound by scraping specialized genital scales against spines along the abdomen.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.

But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.

Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.

“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

#6446. Why Did Polynesians Suddenly Sail Across the Pacific After 1,700 Years? Scientists May Have Found the Answer

The real history behind Moana may be tied to a devastating drought that pushed Polynesian voyagers toward wetter islands and helped reshape human settlement across the Pacific.

In Disney’s Moana, a young Polynesian girl sails beyond her island’s barrier reef to save her threatened home. Scientists have now uncovered evidence that a real environmental crisis may have helped drive one of history’s greatest ocean migrations, pushing Polynesian voyagers across the Pacific after centuries without expanding farther east.

The findings offer a fascinating connection to the story behind Moana, which recently returned to theaters in a live-action adaptation.

Around 3,000 years ago, the ancestors of modern Polynesians arrived in Samoa and Tonga. For approximately 1,700 years, their eastward expansion appeared to stop. This mysterious period became known as the “Long Pause.”

Then, between AD 900 and 1050, everything changed. Within roughly 250 years, Polynesian voyagers had reached and settled islands across the Pacific, including Tahiti and Hawai’i, with their expansion extending to the continental Americas.

Researchers from the University of Southampton and the University of East Anglia believe a prolonged drought helped trigger this extraordinary movement.

David Sear, Professor of Physical Geography at the University of Southampton and lead author of the study, said, “We have confirmed the theory that the end of the Long Pause coincided with a period of mega drought in the homeland islands of Samoa and Tonga – and also a period of increasing rainfall in the receiving islands. As they headed east, they found wetter islands with nobody on them.”

To uncover what happened, the team examined ancient mud buried beneath swamps and lakes in Samoa, Tonga, French Polynesia, and the Cook Islands.

Dr. Mark Peaple, a paleoclimate research fellow at the University of Southampton, conducted the geochemical analysis. He studied chemical traces left by freshwater algae and leaves, focusing on different forms of hydrogen called isotopes. Their proportions change depending on rainfall, allowing scientists to reconstruct how wet or dry the islands were thousands of years ago.

The evidence revealed a severe drought beginning shortly before the migration and continuing during it. When the Long Pause ended, Samoa and Tonga were experiencing their driest conditions in the last 2,000 years. Meanwhile, islands farther east were becoming wetter.

Climate modeling led by Manoj Joshi, Professor of Climate Dynamics at the University of East Anglia, helped explain why. Changes in Pacific Ocean surface temperatures over several decades had shifted a vast tropical rain belt eastward, leaving Samoa and Tonga with less rainfall.

“The climate changes we identified would have transformed daily life on these islands. Reduced rainfall would have affected freshwater availability, food production and the resilience of communities, creating powerful incentives for people to seek opportunities elsewhere,” Joshi said.

Dan Skinner, a research fellow at the University of East Anglia who conducted climate modeling experiments, identified prolonged drought lasting years or even decades as a definite factor behind the migration.

But worsening conditions were probably not the only influence. Sear explained that growing populations would have placed additional pressure on limited resources. At the same time, Polynesian sailors may have improved their voyaging canoes, moving from U-shaped to V-shaped hulls and developing better rigging. These advances could have helped them sail against the prevailing winds, which generally blow from east to west across the South Pacific.

Together, environmental pressure and improved sailing technology may help explain how Polynesian communities undertook such remarkable journeys.

“There was a huge explosion of migration, and within 250 years they had landed and settled every little dot in the South Pacific, from tiny coral atoll islands to larger lands. It was a very rapid process,” Sear said.

Reference: “How Did changing climate in the tropical South Pacific contribute to the eastward migration and settlement of Polynesia?” by David Sear, Mark Peaple, Peter Langdon, Daniel Skinner, Manoj Joshi, Adrian Matthews, Charlotte Hipkiss, Tim Osborn, Gordon Inglis and Justin Sheffield, 5 May 2026, Journal of Pacific Archaeology. DOI: 10.70460/jpa.v16i2.399

A fresh look at Einstein's equations suggests that gravity can sometimes snap and reconnect, similar to magnetic field lines on the sun. The findings hint at a new way that gravity and matter can trade energy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Magnetic reconnection — the process behind the sun's most violent outbursts — may have a counterpart in gravity.

According to a new theoretical study, sheet-like structures in the gravitational field can break apart and reconnect in new arrangements, much like the magnetic field lines that unleash solar flares.

Built entirely on Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, the study spells out when this "gravitational reconnection" can happen. It also offers a way to measure how fast the theoretical reconnection proceeds, and suggests a change to how gravity and matter trade energy. The process could even play a role in black hole collisions, the researchers suggest.

Magnetic field lines are normally "frozen" into plasma — the hot, electrically charged gas that makes up stars — and carried along wherever it flows. The lines can be stretched and twisted, but not cut. Where this rule breaks down, they can snap and rejoin in a process called magnetic reconnection, releasing pent-up energy in explosive bursts such as solar flares.

"In plasma physics, reconnection has become an essential part of our understanding of how magnetic fields reorganize and exchange energy with matter," Luca Comisso, an astrophysicist at Columbia University and first author of the study, told Live Science via email. "Could something similar be true for gravity?"

"Gravity and magnetism describe very different aspects of nature, so there's no obvious reason to expect them to behave alike," Comisso said. "But when we express Einstein's equations in a particular mathematical form, some of the same principles that govern magnetic fields also emerge in gravity. We wanted to understand whether those similarities extended to reconnection itself."

Comisso and study co-author Felipe Asenjo, a physicist at Adolfo Ibáñez University in Chile, used a mathematical framework known as the tetrad formulation. "Einstein's theory describes gravity through the geometry of space-time," Comisso explained. But in the tetrad formulation, "certain aspects of gravity can be expressed through quantities resembling electric and magnetic fields."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a prior study published in the journal Physical Review Letters earlier this year, the researchers applied this framework to gravity. That study suggested that gravitational fields can form two-dimensional structures called gravitational field sheets. Of the sheets' two dimensions, one stretches through space and the other through time — so each sheet is the trail a line leaves as time passes. A snapshot at any instant therefore catches each sheet as a line, akin to the field lines drawn around a magnet. And, like magnetic field lines frozen into a plasma, "under certain conditions, these sheets evolve without breaking or changing how they are connected," Comisso said.

An illustration depicting the sun’s magnetic field lines over an image taken by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. When magnetic loops get stretched to their limit, they snap and reconnect, triggering solar flares.

In the new study, published Oct. 28 in the journal Physical Review D, the researchers found that this is not always the case. "Gravitational field sheets can break and reconnect in a different arrangement, much like magnetic field lines do in plasmas," Comisso said.

The researchers showed that breaking the frozen-in rule doesn't, by itself, guarantee reconnection. Sometimes, the sheets merely slip relative to the flow that carries them, staying intact because they remain frozen into a different flow. Genuine reconnection happens only when no such alternative flow exists.

"We also derived equations describing how quickly this reconnection can occur and how it can affect the transfer of energy and momentum," Comisso said. In general relativity, gravity and matter can trade energy and momentum, with only their combined total conserved. The study shows that reconnection changes the local rate of that exchange.

Reconnection also alters gravitational helicity, the gravitational counterpart of a quantity that measures how twisted and interlinked magnetic field lines are. Frozen-in sheets keep their helicity fixed, but reconnection can create or destroy it.

The findings don't require new physics. "Everything follows from Einstein's general relativity," Comisso said.

"Einstein developed his theory more than a century ago, and it has passed an extraordinary number of experimental tests," he added. "Yet even after more than a century, there are still new insights to be gained from those same equations."

What could trigger gravitational reconnection in nature remains an open question. Among the candidates the researchers suggested are the singularities thought to lurk at the hearts of black holes and the combined effect of gravitational ripples that are too small to track individually. Quantum effects linked to Hawking radiation ‪—‬ the faint glow that black holes are predicted to emit ‪—‬ could also play a part.

"We're still at the beginning, but one of the most interesting possibilities is that gravitational reconnection could play a role in extreme events, such as the merger of two black holes or the collision of neutron stars," Comisso said. "These are environments where gravity is extremely strong and the geometry of spacetime changes dramatically."

Such collisions send out ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, which detectors such as LIGO (the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) have been recording since 2015. "We'd like to understand whether gravitational reconnection could contribute to transferring energy, and whether it might leave a recognizable signature in gravitational waves," Comisso added. "We don't know the answers yet, but these are questions that we can now begin to investigate."

Comisso, L., & Asenjo, F. A. (2026). Reconnection of gravitational fields. Physical Review. D., 114(8). https://doi.org/10.1103/lmqy-pf9k

#6442. Popular Weight-Loss Drugs May Have a Surprising Effect on Your Brain

Popular weight-loss drugs may offer benefits that extend beyond metabolism, potentially helping preserve memory and other cognitive abilities.

Medications used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes may also influence memory and other cognitive abilities. But whether drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide can actually protect the brain remains uncertain, particularly after major clinical trials failed to demonstrate a benefit in patients with early Alzheimer’s disease.

In Novo Nordisk’s EVOKE and EVOKE+ trials, semaglutide did not slow Alzheimer’s progression, even though it produced changes in several biological markers associated with the disease. Researchers from the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen have now examined the broader evidence in a review published in Science, exploring whether these medications could still help preserve cognitive function in other groups of patients.

GLP-1 medications influence biological processes involved in both metabolism and brain function. Animal experiments suggest they can affect learning and memory, but studies involving humans have produced inconsistent results. Analyses of patient health records have linked GLP-1 treatment to a reduced risk of dementia among people with type 2 diabetes, although these observational findings cannot establish that the drugs directly provide protection.

The potential benefits may differ depending on the cause of cognitive difficulties. People with obesity or type 2 diabetes sometimes experience problems with attention, planning, and mental processing speed. These difficulties are frequently associated with metabolic disturbances and poor vascular health, raising the possibility that treatments targeting these underlying problems could help maintain cognitive abilities.

Stina Börchers, the review’s first author and a researcher affiliated with both universities, believes that identifying the right patients and treatment timing will be essential.

“We need to find out whether these treatments can help people with obesity or diabetes preserve their cognitive abilities, particularly if treatment begins before cognitive problems become established. It is also important to identify which patients might benefit,” says Stina Börchers.

A central unanswered question is whether any cognitive benefits arise from direct effects on the brain, improvements in metabolic health, or both. Better regulation of blood sugar and other metabolic processes could indirectly support brain function, while GLP-1 signaling may also influence neural processes more directly. Separating these mechanisms could help researchers determine which effects are most relevant to preserving cognition.

Christoffer Clemmensen, the review’s senior author and a research group leader at the University of Copenhagen, sees an opportunity to use increasingly advanced obesity medications to investigate these connections.

“Obesity medicines are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering new opportunities to understand how metabolic regulation influences brain function. By disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these drugs on the brain, we may ultimately be able to develop treatments specifically aimed at preserving cognitive function,” says Christoffer Clemmensen.

The researchers are calling for clinical trials that measure memory and other cognitive abilities from the beginning of treatment. Such studies could help establish whether these medications preserve cognitive function, which patients are most likely to benefit, and whether starting treatment before cognitive difficulties appear makes a difference.

They also caution that potential benefits must be weighed against risks in older or frail patients. Rapid weight loss and declining muscle mass can reduce physical functioning, potentially limiting the overall advantages of treatment. Future studies will need to account for these effects when assessing whether obesity medications can support long-term brain health.

Reference: “Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition” by Stina Börchers, Giulia Mazzini, Henrik Zetterberg and Christoffer Clemmensen, 5 November 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aek9987

#6440. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

#6438. Scientists Ranked 20 Protein-Rich Foods on Health, Affordability, and Sustainability. One Surprising Food Came Out on Top

Tofu took the crown in a showdown of 20 protein-rich foods judged on health, affordability, availability, and their toll on the planet.

Protein-rich foods can look very different when cost, access, health, and environmental impact all enter the picture. In a study published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, Dr. Chris Macdonald developed a framework that combines these four considerations to compare commonly consumed protein sources.

Among the 20 foods assessed, tofu took the top spot, while cheddar cheese finished last. The results followed a clear pattern: plant-based foods occupied the entire highest-scoring fifth, and animal-based products made up the lowest-scoring fifth.

Tofu’s lead came from strong results across both parts of the assessment. It earned a perfect 16 points for environmental performance, placing in the best-performing fifth for greenhouse gas emissions, water pollution, land use, and freshwater use. It also scored 20 out of 24 points for health and accessibility, including full marks for providing all nine essential amino acids.

Together, these measures explain why the rankings go beyond protein content alone. They weigh the environmental costs of producing protein alongside nutritional factors and practical considerations such as price and availability.

The paper argues that ratings focused on one feature can leave consumers with an incomplete picture. A product’s performance in one area does not explain its trade-offs elsewhere. Macdonald presents the framework as a way to help people understand those competing considerations and the food systems their purchases support.

As the paper states, “Against deliberate corporate obfuscation and marketing myths, the goal of a holistic score is not to create a new label, but to foster a new literacy, one that empowers us to see the reality of the systems we are funding.

Ultimately, beyond the spreadsheets and scores, lies a fundamental reckoning: our protein choice is a referendum on the compassion we are willing to show to animals, to the planet, and to future generations.”

The research builds on Macdonald’s work at the Better Protein Institute, which examines how much protein people need for optimal health, how to shift consumer behavior effectively, and where investment could support future protein sources. By questioning common assumptions and starting from first principles, that work addresses some of the most frequently Googled questions about dietary protein.

Reference: “What are the best sources of protein? Introducing the BPI Score” by Chris Macdonald, 1 July 2026, Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems. DOI: 10.3389/fsufs.2026.1677796

#6435. Cancer Immunotherapy Has a Dangerous Side Effect. Scientists May Have Found a Way To Stop It

Cancer immunotherapy could become safer by stabilizing the cells that keep immune responses under control, an approach that reversed treatment-related inflammation in mice.

Some cancer patients have to stop immunotherapy when their immune system starts attacking healthy tissue. These reactions can occur with drugs called immune checkpoint inhibitors, which help immune cells known as T cells fight cancer by releasing the brakes that normally restrain them.

Depending on the type of checkpoint inhibitor, 20% to 40% of patients experience these immune-related adverse events. Up to 25% experience severe reactions that result in hospitalization and an end to treatment. There are no U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved treatments for these side effects.

“Immune-related adverse events are a huge problem and can greatly impact quality of life for patients. In many cases, it impacts their ability to stay on immunotherapy or benefit from treatment,” said Abigail Overacre-Delgoffe, Ph.D., assistant professor in the Department of Immunology at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and a member of the Tumor Microenvironment Center at UPMC Hillman Cancer Center.

Overacre-Delgoffe is the senior author of a study published October 22, 2026, in Cell that identifies unstable immune cells as a potential driver of this inflammation. Her team reversed inflammation in mice by blocking a protein in those cells and found that diet and the gut microbiome, the community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract, influenced the severity of the animals’ reactions.

Studying these side effects has been difficult because they vary considerably among patients. Animal models have also struggled to reproduce the complexity of immune-related inflammation in humans.

“Most existing mouse models relied on genetically modified mice or experimental conditions that didn’t really capture the variability we see in patients,” said lead author Dipyaman Patra, Ph.D., a postdoctoral associate in Overacre-Delgoffe’s lab. “This got us thinking about whether common lifestyle factors, particularly diet and the gut microbiome, could influence the host immune system even before immunotherapy begins.”

Overacre-Delgoffe’s earlier work had shown that diet and gut microbes can influence cancer patient outcomes and responses to immunotherapy. To investigate their role in treatment side effects, her team fed mice a diet designed to resemble a Western-style human diet, low in fiber and high in fat and processed carbohydrates. The animals began eating it two weeks before checkpoint inhibitor therapy and continued during treatment.

The mice became susceptible to immune-related adverse events and developed immune and microbiome changes resembling many of those seen in affected patients. This gave the researchers a way to test how gut microbes contributed to the inflammation.

Transferring fecal microbes from mice eating the Western-style diet into mice eating a regular, high-fiber diet caused gut inflammation in the recipients. Transfers could also reduce inflammation. Male mice were less susceptible to severe adverse events, and transferring their fecal microbes into female mice reduced the severity of inflammation in the females.

The team also transferred fecal microbes from patients consuming a Western-style diet into germ-free mice, which are raised without microorganisms. Those recipients developed more severe immune-related adverse events. Together, the transfer experiments provided evidence that the microbiome could influence the severity of these reactions in mice.

Within the immune system, the researchers identified a problem involving regulatory T cells. These cells normally suppress excessive immune responses, but stress can make them unstable, a condition called regulatory T cell fragility. Mice eating the Western-style diet showed signs of this fragility during immunotherapy. The researchers found the same instability in regulatory T cells collected from patients with severe immune-related adverse events, but not in cells from patients without the side effect.

Blocking an immune-signaling protein specifically on regulatory T cells restored their stability in mice and reversed inflammation. Switching the animals to a high-fiber diet or giving them supplements containing metabolites, substances produced through metabolism, also stabilized the cells. Restoring stability significantly reduced the severity of adverse events, supporting the interpretation that regulatory T cell fragility is a major underlying cause in this model.

“We were able to generate the first of its kind preclinical mouse model of adverse events that didn’t require full gene knockouts,” said Overacre-Delgoffe. “By combining this novel preclinical model alongside patient data, we were able to identify a very new mechanism of adverse events that hopefully will result in new targeted therapies, allowing more cancer patients to stay on treatment and out of the hospital.”

The model will give researchers a platform to investigate why some patients develop severe reactions and to identify biological markers that might predict susceptibility. Future work will explore drug targets in specific tissues that could limit or eliminate these side effects without disrupting immunotherapy. Metabolite supplementation is another potential approach to reducing susceptibility without interfering with the microbiome, although its promise here comes from experiments in mice.

“We now have some potential targets that we’re going after that seem to limit immune-related adverse events without negatively impacting immunotherapy, which would be the first of its kind and is quite exciting” Overacre-Delgoffe said.

Reference: “Lifestyle-induced regulatory T cell fragility primes adverse events after immune checkpoint blockade” by Dipyaman Patra, Katelyn Wolfgang, Chenxian Ye, Lora Rigatti, Kelsey Ertwine, Kristin M. Morder, Jessica Jana, Ishita Baral, Drew Hurd, Kaitlin Bossong, Steven Mullett, Yingtong Dou, Stacy Gelhaus, Dario A.A. Vignali, Diwakar Davar, Anthony R. Cillo, Greg M. Delgoffe and Abigail E. Overacre-Delgoffe, 22 October 2026, Cell. DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.055

In this excerpt from "This is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth," author and physicist Christophe Galfard explores the way 19th century scientists were starting to use thermodynamics to understand just how old Earth is.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the 1950s, American geochemist Clair Patterson presented findings that showed Earth is around 4.55 billion years old. His evidence was based on lead isotopic analysis that he used to calculate the age of the Canyon Diablo meteorite, which was discovered in Arizona in 1891. That result is now widely accepted as the age of our planet, but the buildup to this discovery was a long time coming.

Earth's true age was a subject of much debate among scientists in the 19th century. And rather than geologists taking the helm, it was physicists who realized that this giant ball of rock we live on must be far older than the thousands of years that had been assumed in prior centuries. Their main reasoning was heat.

In this excerpt from "This Is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth" (University of Chicago Press/Picador, 2026), author and physicist Christophe Galfard looks at the progression among scientists who were coming to realize that thermodynamics was an essential piece of this long-standing puzzle.

Some two and a half centuries ago, the foremost experts on scientific matters knew a thing or two about heat. They knew, for instance, how heat could be transferred from one place to another. A new science was about to emerge out of this knowledge, a science called thermodynamics, which means "movements of heat" in Greek.

Thermodynamics isn't a force. It is more like a guidebook, a set of rules that apply to large

numbers of particles when they come together. It gives us, humans, a way to understand how particles behave when there is a lot of them without needing to refer to each one of them individually. It shows us how properties that don't exist on their own arise when many particles are together. It deals with these things we call emergent phenomena, such as heat and pressure, and which [Philip] Anderson's "More Is Different" tried to make sense of.

Understanding the dynamics of heat meant a lot to nineteenth-century scientists — so much so that many saw in it the roots of a philosophy so universal and powerful that they thought it should guide us through all our lives. Some even went as far as believing that heat was the source of eternal life. A prominent scientist became so convinced that this was the case that he locked himself up in his house and overheated it, thus shielding himself from all mortal diseases (ageing and death included). The experience was a true torture for the occasional guests who came to visit him, not to mention his wife, who had to endure it day and night.

The scientist held fast to his belief, though, piling on layer after layer of clothing to keep himself ever warmer. Unfortunately, the bulk made it difficult to move, and he eventually missed a step on his own staircase and died from the fall.

As a scientific discipline, thermodynamics was born with a book written in 1824 by a 27-year-old French physicist named Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot, who, as he explained how heat could produce work, told everyone how the steam engine worked.

Lord Kelvin giving a lecture at Glasgow University in 1899.

With Carnot's vision, the way hot objects cool down began to be understood, raising hopes that the resolution of one particular problem might be imminent: the determination of the Earth's age. Were we to somehow guess how hot our planet was at birth, thermodynamics could then be used to tell us how much time had gone by for it to have cooled to its present temperature. Many scientists tried it, keen to be the first one to nail the true age of our world.

Considering our planet in all its complexity to be far too difficult, simplifications were in order, and British physicist William Thomson shot first by picturing our world as a ball. A very simple, rock-solid ball made of pretty much the same stuff throughout, from surface to core. No ocean, no mountain, just a smooth ball the size of the Earth. He then calculated how long it would take it to cool down from being red hot to its present temperature, and declared that the Earth was something between 40 and 400 million years old.

Refining his calculations, he then announced that the world was 100 million years old, before settling for 40 million again.

Thomson's result does not correspond to the true age of the Earth, but it was a start. It was the result of a model, an attempt at figuring out something about our world using still-to-be-refined laws, and mathematical sense. What was more problematic was that no one dared question his results. Even as it shifted from one paper to another, the age of the Earth given by Thomson was always greeted as the right one. A reason for this is that at the end of the nineteenth century Thomson had become Lord Kelvin.

The same Kelvin after whom the Kelvin unit of absolute temperature is named. A scientific superstar who had the power to undo, in a snap of fingers, the career of anyone who disagreed with him.

Lord Kelvin was a physicist, not a geologist, so geologists could have questioned his work, but they didn't. In fact, they weren't bothered. Many of them back then believed that being a geologist was all about intuition and proper English, a language they deemed far more efficient than mathematical gibberish.

That being said, and however wrong the results, Kelvin's calculations were beautiful, giving whoever wanted to think about the problem of the age of the Earth a way forward, which is exactly what one of his former students, Northern Irishman John Perry, did. He thought that Kelvin had overlooked something. As a man of science talking to his former mentor (and job provider), Perry explained his vision to Kelvin but was ignored.

John Perry, a student of Kelvin's, who realized Earth was billions of years old — and that its mantle was a liquid, not a solid.

Still, he published his thoughts in Nature. But again, the article was ignored. Not just by Kelvin, but by the scientific community at large, including geologists.

It would have saved us all quite a bit of time had this not been the case, because Perry not only found a much more correct way to picture the Earth and estimate its age than Kelvin had, but he also found the source of the power that makes our planet's continents drift.

In his model, Perry didn't picture the Earth to be uniformly the same from surface to core as Kelvin had. Instead, he modelled the Earth's interior as being divided into three regions: a metallic core at its centre, a solid crust at its surface, and a mantle that lay in between the two. Rather unexpectedly, Perry didn't envision the mantle as everyone else would have; he believed that it didn't behave like the solid rock it was, but as a liquid.

No wonder his former master didn't take him seriously. However, he pictured the mantle behaving like a liquid only when considered over long periods of time. Sandwiched between a hot core and a colder crust that very much looked like a lid, he believed the mantle had no choice but to behave just like water does in a heated pan, with the hottest parts at the bottom rising and cooling before diving back down and rising up again, in repeated loops, albeit in extremely slow motion. This type of movement is called convection, and it happens in solids, too.

If he was right, there would be two immediate consequences. The first one was that the time it would take for our planet's surface to cool down from red hot to its current temperature could now be far longer than Kelvin had estimated. The lid and the convection patterns prevented our planet from quickly radiating away all its energy into space, so we were now inhabiting an Earth that could be as old as 2 or 3 billion years. Maybe even more. Such timescales were unheard of in the scientific community. Back then, no one knew that the universe itself was 13.8 billion years old. They knew next to nothing.

The second consequence of Perry's model was that the mantle's circular movements underneath the crust could drag the crust itself via friction. The solid surface of our world would then move, and split into pieces that would drift, and collide, and plunge underneath — or slide above — one another. Where they collided, mountain ranges would rise, like the Alps, the Himalayas, the Rockies . . . Where they split apart, rifts would appear, probably in the middle of oceans, along ridges . . . just like [Marie] Tharp had found.

Nowadays, these broken pieces of our planet's surface have all been mapped. They are our world's plates and their movements through time are called plate tectonics. Today, most of us have heard about plate tectonics. Back then, however, no one had, and if very few people remember Perry today, it is because another scientific breakthrough made the estimation of the age of the Earth much easier and precise, showing us that our world isn't 2 or 3 billion years old, as Perry suggested, but precisely 4.567 billion, give or take a few million.

In this immersive and mind-expanding book, acclaimed physicist Christophe Galfard takes you on an adventure like no other to answer the fundamental question: what is life? You’ll travel back in time to witness the cataclysmic asteroid impact that doomed the dinosaurs, experience the tumultuous forces that shaped our planet, and discover how the first stirrings of life emerged from inanimate matter.

Christophe Galfard is a theoretical physicist turned international pop-science bestselling author based in Paris. He co-authored "George's Secret Key to the Universe" with Stephen Hawking and his daughter Lucy Hawking. Galfard's most recent book, "The Universe in Your Hand: A Journey Through Space, Time, and Beyond," has been translated into over 20 languages.

#6432. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

#6430. More Than a Billion Years of Earth’s History Is Missing – Scientists May Finally Know Why

Earth’s rocks are missing more than a billion years of history in some places, and the slow rise and fall of continents may explain how those chapters disappeared.

A study led by University of Wollongong (UOW) PhD candidate Santosh Dhungana suggests that the slow rise and fall of continents helped create the Great Unconformity, a vast gap in Earth’s geological record. Published in Nature, the research links this missing history to currents of hot rock in the mantle that moved continents vertically over hundreds of millions of years.

Normally, rock layers preserve a sequence of events, with younger deposits accumulating above older ones. At the Great Unconformity, that sequence jumps: sedimentary rocks from around the beginning of the Cambrian period, roughly 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite more than a billion years old.

“Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth’s story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren’t lost by chance,” Dhungana said.

The Grand Canyon exposes one of the most striking examples of this geological gap. It lies within what was once the ancient continent Laurentia (modern North America). Similar boundaries appear in Europe, Australia, Africa, and Asia, although the missing intervals vary from about 200 million years to well over a billion.

Explaining the Great Unconformity requires accounting for both the removal of rock and the survival of the eroded surface beneath younger deposits. Dhungana said that although scientists had offered several explanations, those ideas had not been thoroughly tested against Earth’s behavior over time.

To investigate, he and his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, modeled mantle convection across hundreds of millions of years. The mantle consists of hot, solid rock that flows very slowly. Its currents can gently lift enormous stretches of land or allow them to sink.

The models indicated that mantle currents raised the ancient continental cores of Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe), and North China during the Neoproterozoic Era, from about one billion to 540 million years ago. This prolonged uplift would have exposed rock to erosion. The era was followed by the Cambrian period, when animal life diversified dramatically.

The next stage helped preserve what erosion had left behind. During the Phanerozoic eon, which spans the past 540 million years, the continental cores gradually sank. Seas spread across their worn surfaces, and accumulating sediment buried the boundary between the ancient rocks and the younger geological record.

The modeled pattern matched the geography of the evidence. North America, northern Europe, and North China, where the Great Unconformity is especially well preserved and documented, all showed the prolonged rise followed by sinking that the researchers proposed.

“Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface,” Associate Professor Flament said.

“Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed, but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle.”

Reference: “The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity” by Santosh Dhungana, and Nicolas Flament, 4 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11156-5

This study was funded by the Australian Research Council.
