#6394. A tiny remote controlled beetle robot named BeetleBot uses artificial muscles to explore narrow spaces and grab hidden objects

Printed muscles that shrink when heated let this beetle-sized soft robot walk, grip an object and send back what it feels.

Shrink a walking robot and its motors and gears get harder to fit, not easier. Insect-scale machines have mostly solved this problem with tiny, rigid parts. BeetleBot has neither.

Its legs move because strips of printed plastic shrink when an electric current warms them, the way a muscle shortens when it fires.

The robot is about the size of a real beetle, and a person wearing a sensor patch on one finger steers it by bending that finger.

A camera on its head and a pressure sensor in its jaws send back what it sees and what it is touching. The operator can decide the next move without seeing the robot at all.

Inho Kim built it as a postdoctoral researcher at Caltech and is now an assistant professor of chemistry at Sungkyunkwan University. Sang Ouk Kim of KAIST and Wei Gao of Caltech led the work with a group at NTU Singapore.

The artificial muscles are made of a liquid crystal elastomer, a rubbery plastic with molecules that line up in one direction.

Heat it past a certain point and that alignment breaks down so the material contracts along the line of the molecules and pulls. Let it cool and it stretches back.

The team printed each muscle as a stack of layers with a laser-cut metal heating wire sandwiched inside. Running current through the wire warms the plastic.

At 3 volts, a free-standing muscle shortened by about 45 percent but returned to its full length once the power stopped.

Pulling force matters as much as travel. At their strongest these muscles pulled with 0.18 megapascals of stress. This is within the 0.1 to 0.35 range of a mammal’s skeletal muscle.

That’s why a sheet of printed plastic can carry a robot with a camera and a gripper bolted to it.

The placement of those muscles came from the insect. The team dissected and filmed Mecynorrhina torquata, a large flower beetle, and measured how its leg joints swung when its muscles were stimulated.

That relationship set where the artificial muscles went on the beetle robot’s own six legs.

Insects work their legs with muscles arranged in opposing pairs. One pulls a joint one way and the other pulling it back. BeetleBot copies the arrangement.

Its front legs lift and lower the body, bending about 20 degrees, while the back legs swing forward and back, bending about 12 degrees.

Walking consists of those two groups firing in turn. The front muscles lift the front of the body, which tips the rear legs onto the ground. The back muscles then fold and push the beetle robot forward. Heat one side only and the robot turns.

For the head, the researchers copied the mandibles a beetle uses to hold its prey. Two curved flaps close when their muscles contract, a simpler arrangement than the spring-and-air hand built for the same job. A capacitive pressure sensor sits on the gripping surface.

The sensor is two thin, metal-coated sheets with an air gap between them. Squeeze them closer and the electrical charge they hold changes. This is what the beetle robot reports as contact.

It registered a touch in 0.127 seconds, and its reading rose almost in step with pressure up to 50 kilopascals.

The gripper can also tell shapes apart. Gripping a small sphere, a large sphere and a cube produced three different signal traces. This means the operator learns something about the object without ever seeing it close up.

A perching drone reads a branch the same way, by touch, where a camera stops helping.

The control patch is a printed strip of rubbery polymer loaded with carbon nanotubes, tiny conductive threads that form a network through the material.

Bending the finger stretches the strip, breaks some of those connections, and raises its electrical resistance.

Four finger movements produced four clearly separated signals, which the system reads as forward, left, right and grip, then sends to the robot over a short-range, wireless link. The patch held its signal through 1,000 bending cycles.

“A key feature of this work is the bidirectional feedback, which links the information detected by the robot to the user’s next action,” said Inho Kim, the paper’s first author.

Information running both ways is what separates this beetle robot from a remote-control toy. Other soft machines go further still, thinking without electricity by building the logic into the material itself.

The person sends a gesture, the robot sends back a camera frame and a pressure reading, and the next gesture depends on what came back.

To test all of it together, the team set a target object behind an obstacle and had an operator drive the robot there using the camera feed alone.

It took eight separate movements, turns and forward runs in sequence, to get around the obstacle, reach the object, close the gripper on it and carry it.

The pressure signal jumped at the moment of contact, which is how the operator knew to grip. That is the whole loop in one run: a finger moves, legs move, a sensor answers, and the finger moves again.

“This study expands the potential uses of soft robots by connecting the movement of artificial muscles, sensing, and user control in a single system,” said Sang Ouk Kim.

The muscles only work hot. Full contraction needs the plastic above roughly 230°F (110°C), and surfaces on the robot climbed past 212°F (100°C) during walking.

A thermal camera showed that heat staying local to the working muscle rather than spreading through the frame.

Heat is also what sets the pace. Each step waits for the plastic to cool, so the walking cycle runs slower than the muscle’s own limit. Adding payload slowed it further.

Two other limits stand in the way of sending one of these somewhere real. The finger patch’s signals pass through a wired front end before they go wireless, and the course the robot crossed was a small, built setup, not rubble or a pipe.

KAIST said the actuation speed, the energy efficiency and the power supply all need work before soft robots like this one inspect industrial equipment or explore the environment.

Nobody has driven one of these through a space that a person could not enter. Inho Kim said he plans to make the muscles faster and more efficient, and to improve the control methods that use the robot’s own sensing.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6393. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

#6392. Scientists found a hidden ‘aging clock’ in human blood that can predict future diseases and early death

Scientists have figured out a new way to measure how fast your body is actually aging on the inside, rather than just counting the years you have been alive.

Two people born the same year can have bodies that age at different speeds. A routine blood draw may now be enough to tell which is which.

In a study of 18,476 people aged 1 to 96, some had blood chemistry that read older than their birth certificate. Those people went on to develop fatty liver disease, high blood pressure and diabetes more often.

More of them died over the following years, too.

The older readings lined up with everyday habits. Smokers’ blood read about 1.2 years older than nonsmokers’, and people who exercised read about half a year younger.

Linlin Cao, Kun Qian, Jun Pu and Wei Xu of Renji Hospital at Shanghai Jiao Tong University led the study, with participants from six clinical centers in China. It’s observational, so it shows patterns, not causes.

Blood plasma carries thousands of small molecules left over from the body’s chemistry. The field that measures them is called metabolomics.

The team measured 232 of these molecules, in each person, with a laser-based instrument that needs a droplet of plasma and about 30 seconds per sample.

From those, 56 molecules changed most reliably with age. Some rose steadily, such as creatinine, a waste product of muscle.

Others fell early in life and stayed low, such as a building block of collagen that was highest in childhood and dropped fast before age 20.

A set of 12 machine learning models, stacked together, used the 56 molecules to guess each person’s age. The guesses were close.

In 5,252 healthy people used for training, the guess landed within about two years on average. In 5,456 healthy people held back as a test, it landed within about 4.5 years.

The difference between that guess and a person’s real age is the number that matters. The team called it metabolomic age acceleration, and a positive value means the blood reads older than the calendar.

Everyone gave blood in 2019. The healthy participants answered a questionnaire on diet, sleep, smoking, exercise and family history, and 3,745 of them returned for a health check in 2023. Deaths were tracked through January 2025.

The team compared the quarter of healthy people with the most accelerated blood chemistry against the quarter with the slowest.

The accelerated quarter had more new cases of fatty liver disease, high blood pressure and diabetes, and the same held for coronary heart disease and stroke.

The accelerated quarter also died at a higher rate. There were 291 deaths among the 6,169 people with death records, and the accelerated quarter accounted for a larger share of them.

For predicting death, the blood clock edged out two standard yardsticks, a frailty index and the American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 score. It also added information when combined with them.

People of the same age can follow different aging paths, and this is one way to see it.

Several habits lined up with the clock. Current smoking was associated with blood chemistry about 1.2 years older, secondhand smoke with about 0.6 years, shift work with about 0.9 years, and hair dye with about a year.

Sugar, fried food, processed meat and organ meat were also associated with an older reading. Exercise was associated with a reading about half a year younger, and mixed grains with about a third of a year younger.

In 1,500 people who gave blood again in 2023, the clock moved with their habits. Those who became more active or ate less fried food saw their blood chemistry read younger by two to three years.

People newly exposed to secondhand smoke, eating more preserved food, or crossing into overweight saw it read older. The authors wrote that these habit links are observational and shouldn’t be read as causes.

Other studies have tied biological aging to teenage body weight, early menopause and even the time between pregnancies. Air pollution also leaves a chemical trail in the blood.

In 7,768 people who already had a chronic disease, the age guess worked less well, so the team built a different measure.

Using the same 56 molecules, they modeled each person’s risk of death and then asked how far it sat above or below what their age would predict.

They called that age deviation. Eight molecules carried the death signal, and the strongest was 3-methylindole, made by gut microbes from the amino acid tryptophan. The collagen building block, 4-hydroxyproline, pointed the other way, toward lower risk.

Higher age deviation went with worse kidney numbers, more organ systems affected and more conditions at once. Chronic kidney disease had the largest link.

People with high blood pressure who got it under control by 2023 saw their age deviation improve more than those who didn’t.

Nearly everyone in the study was Chinese, so the clock needs testing in other populations before it travels. Most people gave blood only once, and the authors wrote that more frequent sampling and longer follow-up are needed.

The identities of some of the 56 molecules are confident matches rather than certainties.

The open question is whether changing a habit to move the clock changes what happens to a person afterward. The authors wrote that intervention studies would be needed to find this out.

The age-prediction tool, called MetS-Age, is public for researchers to run on their own data.

The full study was published in the journal Science Translational Medicine.

A proposed tabletop quantum sensor could match the precision of the best satellite measurements of frame dragging, a subtle effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have proposed a new tabletop device to detect the subtle way Earth's daily spin on its axis twists the space-time around it ‪—‬ an effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

If built, the sensor could measure the quantum effect known as frame dragging with the same precision as the best satellite experiments, but in minutes instead of years, the researchers proposed in a new study.

The research, published Sept. 17 in the journal Physical Review Letters, aimed to address a classic mismatch in physics. Picture a ring of clocks bolted to a spinning merry-go-round. You synchronize each clock with its neighbor around the ring. Then, you compare the last clock with the first. They don't match.

"It is impossible to synchronize that collection of clocks when you're in a rotating frame," Kai-Isaak Ellers, a physics graduate student at the University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) and first author of the study, told Live Science.

A photo of scientists working on NASA's Gravity Probe B in 2003. This device measured Earth's frame-dragging from space, confirming Einstein's predictions with an 18% margin of error.

Einstein's theory of general relativity predicts that a massive, spinning object drags the fabric of space-time along with it, just like a spoon twirling in honey. The effect is clearly visible around supermassive objects, like the Milky Way's central black hole. But around Earth, the effect is very faint.

So far, scientists have measured Earth's frame dragging only from orbit. They tracked how the twisting of space-time slowly shifts spinning gyroscopes or the paths of satellites. In 2011, NASA's Gravity Probe B satellite, which carried four gyroscopes, confirmed Einstein's prediction with a margin of error of about 18%. Satellites tracked with lasers have since done even better. In July, researchers reported in the journal Nature that the LARES-2 satellite had shrunk that margin of error to just 0.2%.

However, that took about three years of laser tracking. Researchers also had to account for the fact that Earth bulges at the equator and its mass is spread unevenly, which gives the planet’s gravity small irregularities that tug on satellites far more strongly than frame dragging does. To subtract those tugs, the team relied on detailed maps of Earth's gravity made by other satellites.

Measuring frame dragging more precisely is a way to stress-test general relativity. Several alternative theories of gravity predict a slightly different amount of twisting, and a lab-based measurement would also be free of the modeling assumptions that satellite experiments depend on, Ellers said.

The new device is a loop of superfluid helium-4 — helium chilled until it flows without friction and behaves like a single, giant quantum object. The loop is interrupted by a thin barrier riddled with tiny holes, called a Josephson junction. Superfluid helium can slip through the holes, but ordinary liquid helium cannot.

"That's where the quantum behavior comes from," said K. Birgitta Whaley, a quantum physicist at UC Berkeley and a co-author of the study.

As Earth spins and drags space-time, it nudges the quantum state of the helium flowing through the junction. That nudge shifts the frequency at which the helium sloshes back and forth in the loop, which the researchers could detect.

A visualization of Earth's uneven gravity field taken by NASA's Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment in 2009. The lumpiness of our planet's gravitational field makes it harder to precisely measure relativistic effects.

Superfluid devices, many of them built at UC Berkeley, have detected Earth's rotation since the late 1990s. But the helium-4 versions built around a Josephson junction, like the new design, have worked within about a hundredth of a degree of 2.17 K (minus 455.76 Fahrenheit, or minus 270.98 Celsius), the temperature at which helium-4 becomes a superfluid. At that temperature, a lingering fraction of "normal" helium mixed in with the superfluid adds noise.

Instead, the team calculated how the device would behave at a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. Below 0.7 K, the noise changed character, and the team found it drops sharply as the helium gets colder. One key finding in the new paper is the result of the team's thermal noise analysis, which showed how sensitive these devices could be at millikelvin temperatures, Elles said.

The catch is the barrier. Earlier helium-4 devices used holes about 90 nanometers wide. Working at these frigid temperatures demands much smaller holes, about 1 nanometer across ‪—‬ roughly the size of a helium atom. Keith Schwab, a physicist at Caltech and co-author of the study, and his collaborators are developing such materials, but they haven't been built into a working sensor yet.

If they can be, the researchers calculate that the device could measure frame dragging to 0.2% precision in about 35 minutes. If its vibrating membrane were made from the lowest-loss crystals, such as quartz or sapphire, that could drop to about one second, they said.

"This seems to be a very serendipitous discovery that at millikelvin, we can get this high sensitivity," Whaley told Live Science.

The signal corresponds to a time difference of about 10-35 seconds between helium flowing one way around the loop and the other — the same mismatch as the clocks on the metaphorical merry-go-round.

"The interesting thing about it is just how small it is," Whaley said. "It's not so far off from the Planck time," about 10-44 seconds, the shortest slice of time before the known laws of physics are expected to break down. This experiment is still a billion times too large to reach that limit, Whaley said. But future helium experiments could help explore whether time flows smoothly, like a ramp, or ticks forward in tiny, indivisible jumps, like the frames of a movie.

Ellers, K.-I., Christodoulou, M., Schwab, K. C., & Whaley, K. B. (2026). Quantum sensing of gravitational frame dragging with a superfluid ⁴He gyrometer. Physical Review Letters, 137(12), 121404. https://doi.org/10.1103/q3v9-rjm9

#6389. Researchers proved that tiny lab-grown brains can process information and read Braille just like a real computer

Three brain organoids read Braille letters far better than one, and the living tissue held up even when researchers damaged the data.

Could a computer one day run on living brain cells instead of silicon? A small experiment has just given that question a plain, partial answer.

Specks of human brain tissue, known as organoids, were grown in a dish in a lab. They received the shapes of Braille letters as electrical pulses, and a program read the letters back from how the cells fired.

One speck got the letter right about 61 percent of the time. Three specks, with their signals combined, got it right 83 percent of the time.

Tianyi Liu, a doctoral student at the University of Bristol, led the work with Hemma Philamore and Benjamin Ward-Cherrier in the University’s School of Engineering Mathematics and Technology.

The brain organoids are clumps of human neurons and support cells grown in a lab. Each is about a fiftieth of an inch (half a millimeter) across, the width of a mechanical pencil’s lead.

Nothing in this experiment learned anything, and that matters for how far the result reaches.

“We can take information from a real tactile sensor, turn it into a form that a living neural network can receive, and then recover meaningful information from the organoid response,” said Liu.

“That gives us a practical way to connect artificial sensors with biological neural systems, which are a very interesting possible route towards more energy-efficient computing,” she added.

The attraction is power. A human brain runs on roughly 20 watts. Silicon brain-inspired chips scaled up to the size of a cortex would need kilowatts to megawatts, the team wrote.

Other labs have already had lab-grown brain cells tell Japanese vowels apart and play a simple video game.

The brain organoids never touched a Braille dot. A touch sensor did that for them. The team mounted a sensor with a soft silicone pad, a kind of electronic skin, on a small robot arm.

The arm slid the pad across each of the 26 letters on a 3D-printed Braille board about 9 inches by 5.5 inches (23 by 14 centimeters).

A camera inside the pad recorded tiny shifts in a grid of markers as the dots pressed into the gel, the way a robot fingertip gets its sense of touch. Each letter was scanned 10 times at each of five pressing depths, 1,300 recordings in all.

The team split each recording into eight regions, one for each electrode under an organoid. The touch in each region then became a train of electric pulses.

More contact in a region meant more pulses, between four and ten, and a longer contact meant longer pulses.

The organoids live on electrode arrays run by a company called FinalSpark, and the team reached them over the internet. Kept under a steady flow of nutrient liquid, an organoid can stay electrically active for up to about 100 days.

For each letter, the team counted the cells’ firing on each of the eight electrodes for half a second after the pulses arrived. A standard pattern-sorting program then learned which firing patterns went with which letter.

With a single organoid, the program named the right letter about 61 percent of the time, where guessing would get just under 4 percent right.

Three organoids on the same array, each read on its own, scored 59, 62 and 67 percent. Combined into one pattern, the three organoids’ signals lifted the score to 83 percent.

So the gain didn’t come from one unusually good organoid. It came from combining them.

Why that works isn’t settled. The team’s best guess is that the three organoids differ slightly, so each one transforms the same input a little differently. The program then gets three partly different views of one letter.

“Different organoids may have slightly different network connections, developmental states, and ongoing activity, so the same input can produce similar but not identical responses,” Liu said.

“Combining those responses may give us complementary information that we would not get from a single organoid. At the same time, if every organoid behaves differently, it obviously makes it harder to build a predictable and standardized system,” she added.

There was an obvious objection. The pulse patterns were designed to preserve each letter’s shape, so maybe the program was reading the team’s own encoding and the tissue was only passing it along.

The team tested that directly. Given the pulse patterns with no organoid in between, the same program scored 82 percent, almost exactly the three-organoid result. On a clean signal, the organoids made almost no difference.

Then the team corrupted half of the channels in four ways: two kinds of random noise, some entries set to zero, and some values tripled. Reading straight from the pulses, the program fell to between 55 and 67 percent.

Reading from the three organoids, it held at 83 and 82 percent under random noise, and fell to 72 and 68 percent when entries went missing or were tripled.

In every one of the four tests, the organoids came out ahead. That, more than the headline score, is the contribution the team claims for the living tissue. Ward-Cherrier, the senior author, summed up the two results.

“After processing by the organoids, the tactile data still contains enough information to classify Braille letters with good accuracy. Combining outputs from several organoids also showed an improvement in performance.”

The signal in this experiment ran one way. Pulses went in, firing came out, and nothing went back to the tissue to say whether it had been right. No organoid got feedback, so none could get better with practice.

“We showed that tactile information could be encoded, processed through the organoids, and decoded, but we did not demonstrate learning or long-term changes in the organoids,” Liu said.

“We also tested one tactile task using a fixed encoding scheme and a relatively simple measure of neural activity.”

Eight electrodes per organoid is also a coarse view of a clump of cells, too coarse to see fine patterns in the firing.

And the team hasn’t measured how alike the three organoids’ responses are, which would show whether they carry different information or three copies of it. Whether a fourth organoid would help is also untested.

In 2024, a robot with a camera in its fingertip read Braille faster than a person can, and nothing here beats that.

The question this study asks is different: whether living tissue can hold a job inside a machine, and do it on a fraction of the power.

In the next experiments, the team plans to give the organoids textures and edges to feel, and then feedback on what they do with them.

Only then can anyone ask whether this tissue can learn.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence.

#6387. A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Mice that ate lots of fiber had far less particles accumulate in the body

A diet that includes high-fiber foods, like these vegetables, might come with a surprise benefit. Fiber could help carry nanoplastics out of the body, suggests a new study in mice.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

Z. Yu et al. High fiber diet mitigates exposure risk of nanoplastics in male mice. Nature Communications. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41467-026-78675-7

#6386. Jellyfish study shows scientists that evolution may be ‘much more predictable than we expected’

A new study reveals unrelated jellyfish evolved identical genetic mutations, but surprisingly, these matching DNA changes did not result in matching physical traits.

Biologists have always assumed that it is incredibly rare for two different species to independently develop the exact same genetic changes after being separated for millions of years.

However, a new study looking at the DNA of ancient jellyfish shows that evolution repeats itself much more than scientists ever realized.

Across 86 species, lineages that split more than 600 million years ago have repeatedly swapped in the same building block at the same spot in the same protein. It happened far more often than pure chance would allow.

The twist is what those shared changes are not. They mostly have nothing to do with the traits the animals visibly share, such as eyes.

Cory Berger, a postdoctoral researcher in Todd Oakley’s lab at UC Santa Barbara, led the work. Colleagues at the University of Kansas, Texas A&M University and the University of Nebraska took part.

Everything here comes from comparing gene sequences across species; no trait was tested in a lab.

“We’re studying molecular evolution here – to what extent similar genetic changes occur in different organisms,” Berger said. “And that in particular is something we don’t know much about.”

The group the team chose, called Medusozoa, takes in the true jellyfish, box jellyfish and the hydroids, which are small branching animals related to them. The team’s dating, anchored by 17 fossils, puts the origin of the group at about 685 million years ago.

Before anyone could compare genes, the team had to know who was related to whom and when they split.

They built a tree of 621 species, anchored by the full gene sets of 98 of them, 22 sequenced for this study, and then traced three traits across it.

The results show how often evolution repeats at the level of the body, a pattern biologists call convergent evolution. Eyes, for example, arose at least nine separate times.

The free-swimming medusa stage, the bell-shaped adult most people picture, was lost 41 times. Colonies switched from crusts to upright branching forms 32 times.

“Maybe it’s just the case that organisms that have phenotypic convergence who look similar to one another have convergent molecular changes,” Berger said, describing the idea the team set out to test.

The team compared the protein-coding genes of the 86 species, two at a time. This meant 3,570 pairs were compared, across 9,194 gene families.

For each pair, it looked for spots where both lineages had independently changed the same amino acid, one of the building blocks of a protein, to the same new one.

“And then we looked at the patterns of change across those genes. If the same specific change has happened in distantly related species, then we’re calling that convergence,” said Oakley, the senior author.

The team found 426,322 such matches, under a tenth of a percent of all the branch pairs it tested, and they appeared in 8,991 of the 9,194 gene families.

At those spots, the new amino acid also tended to differ more in its chemistry from the old one than at other changed spots in the same proteins. The team reads that pattern as natural selection rather than accident.

Matches did get rarer as the time since two species split grew longer. But the decline was gentle, and even pairs separated by more than 600 million years shared more changes than a model of pure chance predicted.

If evolution reuses genes to build the same trait, species that both evolved eyes, or both lost the medusa stage, should share more genetic changes than other pairs. They didn’t. Pairs with a shared trait were statistically indistinguishable from pairs without one.

Genes known to help build eyes did show up a little more often among eye-bearing pairs. But the same genes had also been under the same kind of selection in species with no eyes at all.

What did set the convergent genes apart was their job.

Genes that deal with the outside world, including energy metabolism, immune defense and breaking down foreign chemicals, carried the most repeated changes. Genes that run the cell’s internal housekeeping, such as cell division, carried the fewest.

“The amount of genetic similarity indicates that at the genetic level, evolution may be more repeatable and maybe therefore more predictable than we expected,” Oakley said.

“But it also means that we still have a huge amount to learn about how the genes function, how that plays out on the whole-organism scale.”

The team counted only one kind of genetic change, a swap of one amino acid for another. Changes in the DNA that switches genes on and off, which may matter more for body shape, were not part of the analysis.

Also, genes facing the environment may simply evolve faster, which would give them more chances to match.

The bigger gap is the cause. For most shared genetic changes, the pressure that drove them in both lineages is unknown.

The team’s own example of a solved case is a pump found in cell membranes. It evolved separately in amphibians, reptiles, mammals and insects to resist the same heart toxins, made by toads and by plants. There, the shared diet explains the shared gene.

The jellyfish data suggest many cases like that are waiting, each with its own explanation. Finding them means measuring the pressures these animals face in the sea as carefully as the team has now measured their genes.

That, the authors wrote, is the next job.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The missing 1.2 billion years of geological history at the Grand Canyon finally has an explanation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than a billion years of geological history is missing from the walls of the Grand Canyon, and now, scientists may know why.

In the canyon's sides, ancient metamorphic and igneous rocks that formed 1.7 billion years ago sit directly under younger sedimentary rocks laid down 500 million years ago. The 1.2 billion-year chunk of history in between wasn't preserved — leaving a geological gap known as the Great Unconformity.

This missing period was a very important time in Earth's history, because it was just before and during the Cambrian explosion, which saw a huge diversification of life on Earth. The Great Unconformity is not only at the Grand Canyon; there are big gaps in the rock layers of that time across North America, the Baltic region of Europe and in northern China. Researchers have long debated why this unconformity exists.

The unconformity is sharply evident in the transition between Cambrian Tapeats Sandstone and Proterozoic Brahma Schist in the Grand Canyon.

Now, a new model of the movement of Earth's middle layer, the mantle, has revealed an explanation: The slow, heat-driven circulation of the mantle pushed these three regions upward during the time when the Great Unconformity was formed, according to new research published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

This uplift would have helped facilitate erosion, meaning sediments formed at that time sloughed off the continents and landed in the ocean. Importantly, the model also shows that in the past 540 million years, these same areas started sinking instead of rising, creating areas for sediments to get caught and then keep piling up in neat layers on the continents — marking the point where the Great Unconformity ends. This matches what geologists can see in North America, the Baltics and northern China.

"We looked at, where are the best places that the mantle would help create a Great Unconformity?" study co-author Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia, told Live Science. "And these three places turned out to be three places where it's known to be quite extensive."

Erosion during Neoproterozoic times, followed by sedimentation during early Phanerozoic times, formed the Great Unconformity. Bottom: Dynamic uplift was followed by subsidence for Laurentia ('LAU'), Baltica ('BAL') and North China ('NCH').

The cause of the Great Unconformity is hotly debated, with some arguing that a global deep freeze known as Snowball Earth could have shoveled sediment off the continents in this period. Glaciation probably played a major role in erosion, Flament said, but the new study suggests that the key driver was deep within the planet. Without the mantle pushing the continents upward, glaciers and other erosive forces would have had no slope to push sediments down, he said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Earth is in a constant state of recycling crust through plate tectonics, said Shanan Peters, a geologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. Oceanic crust sinks back into the mantle through the process of subduction ‪—‬ when one tectonic plate dives beneath another. The chemicals it carries down with it get released back into the atmosphere via volcanic eruptions, linking the mantle with the atmosphere.

And tectonics aren't steady. As continents break up and join back together over eons, different materials get pushed into the crust. For example, the ancient Paleo-Tethys ocean, which lapped off the shores of the supercontinent Pangaea until it closed about 200 million years ago, was rich in carbon-bearing sediments that eroded from the continents, Peters said. When the ocean floor was subducted back into the mantle, this carbon was pushed into the depths of the planet.

It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved.

Today, in contrast, most of Earth's subduction is around the Pacific Rim, and much of the Pacific seafloor is remote from continents, so the seafloor is relatively starved of carbon. What's getting pushed into the mantle now is therefore a different chemical composition than what existed 200 million years ago.

In that sense, referring to the Great Unconformity as "missing information" isn't accurate, Peters told Live Science. Instead, the absence of a rock record in those places at that time reveals something about the processes going on back then — and hints at how geology might have been affecting the atmosphere, and thus life's evolution.

The geological processes occurring during the time of the Great Unconformity may have set the stage for the Cambrian explosion, Peters said. For example, the crystalline rocks exposed on the surface at that time may have released elements like potassium, iron, manganese and carbon into the seas at an increased rate, prompting marine life to invent biomineralization — shells — in response and possibly shifting the composition of Earth's atmosphere to be more oxygen-rich, Peters said.

Flament agreed that the geological changes had significant knock-on effects for life. "It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved," Flament said.

What's particularly interesting about the Great Unconformity is how it reveals not just a period of erosion but also a switch back to the deposition of sediments. The new paper provides an explanation for both, Peters said, and changes in the mantle are just the planetary-scale process to explain this big-picture phenomenon.

"This seems to me to be the only reasonable way to go back and forth between this state over time," he said.

There are still questions about what else the continents were doing in this time period. Peters leads an effort called Macrostrat that is pulling together observations of rock layers around the world, and Flament said he hopes that database will help ground-truth the new models' findings.

"So far in Africa and Russia, we don’t have as comprehensive a database," he said. "Once that is done, we can go and check whether the idea works."

Editor's Note: This story was updated at 10:30 p.m. E.D.T. to note that James Price, not Tia Ghose, edited this story.

Dhungana, S., & Flament, N. (2026). The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity. Nature, 659(8139), 106–112. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11156-5

#6383. Antimatter usually vanishes the exact second it touches regular matter but researchers successfully trapped one piece for months

A trapped positron, cooled almost to absolute zero and held away from every wall, can now be nudged one quantum at a time to test antimatter.

Antimatter has a reputation, mostly from science fiction, for disappearing the instant it touches ordinary matter. Even so, a single particle of it, a positron, has been held in a laboratory in Illinois for months.

Physicists cooled it to about half a degree Fahrenheit (0.3°C) above absolute zero. They hold it in the middle of an empty chamber with magnetic and electric fields, so it never touches a wall.

Held that still, the particle of antimatter behaves like a tiny, artificial atom.

Its energy can only change in fixed steps, and the team can now push it up one step with microwaves and watch it fall back.

Such control is what they need for the next job. This involves measuring the positron’s magnetism so precisely that any difference from an electron’s would show.

Gerald Gabrielse, who directs the Center for Fundamental Physics at Northwestern University, led the work. Thomas Myers, a Ph.D. student in his lab, is the paper’s first author.

“Antimatter gets its popular charm from science fiction,” Gabrielse said.

The positron particle is the electron’s antimatter twin, with the opposite electric charge. Itt disappears the moment it meets an electron, including one in a container wall.

So the Northwestern team suspends the positron in the center of a sealed metal chamber instead.

A superconducting magnet makes it circle in a tight loop, and an electric field from the chamber’s own electrodes keeps it from drifting out along the magnet’s axis. Physicists call the arrangement a Penning trap.

The chamber is chilled so far that its walls freeze out stray gas, leaving almost nothing inside for the antimatter particle to hit.

“If we want to study antimatter, we must handle it carefully,” Gabrielse said. “To be clear, it’s not dangerous. We don’t have enough antimatter to make an explosion.”

The positrons come from a sealed capsule of sodium-22, a radioactive form of sodium. They leave it with up to 546,000 electron volts of energy.

By the time the trapped positron has settled, it has 26 millionths of an electron volt, about 20 billion times less.

The capsule is lowered on a thin, nylon cable down through the refrigerator to the top of the chamber. A positron first passes through a titanium window thinner than a human hair. Then it enters a single crystal of tungsten, where collisions slow it almost to a stop.

On its way out it picks up an electron from the tungsten surface. The positron and the electron, now a neutral pair, drift through a hole in a silver electrode about as wide as a mechanical pencil lead.

Inside the trap the electric field tears the electron away, and the positron is caught.

Loading takes 8 to 11 hours per positron, partly because the source is weak: 18 microcuries, compared with the 500 microcuries used for the best earlier positron measurement.

Cooled this far, the positron’s circling motion drops to its lowest allowed energy and stays there. The chance that a stray bit of heat kicks it up one level is about one in 100 billion. So nothing happens until the team makes it happen.

To make it move, the team feeds in microwaves at about 156 gigahertz, close to the positron’s circling frequency. The positron also wobbles back and forth along the magnet’s axis, about 206 million times a second.

Each quantum of energy it absorbs shifts that rate by about 3.8 hertz, enough to tell the team which energy level the positron is in without disturbing it.

The team’s records show the positron stepping up one level and dropping back, and once stepping up two levels before falling twice.

Left to itself, a positron with one extra quantum releases it again within about 83 thousandths of a second. The trap’s electrodes form a microwave cavity that delays that release to about four seconds, long enough for the faint signal to be read.

A positron also spins, which makes it a tiny magnet. Its spin points either with the field or against it.

A spin in the higher of its two states would take a calculated 2.1 years to flip on its own, but the cavity probably stretches that further.

To flip the spin on purpose, the team applies a second drive for two seconds that changes the spin and the circling energy together. The positron then gives up the extra circling energy on its own, and the spin is left pointing the other way.

The measurement the team wants compares two rates: how fast the positron circles and how fast its spin precesses.

The two differ by about one part in a thousand, and measuring that difference precisely gives the positron’s magnetic moment.

The same lab’s 2023 measurement pinned the electron’s magnetic moment to about one part in 10 trillion, the most precisely determined property of any elementary particle.

The best positron measurement so far, a 1987 experiment, used a positron circling as an ordinary charged particle rather than hopping between quantum levels.

Protons and their antimatter partners, antiprotons, have been compared to about one part in a billion.

The Standard Model of particle physics – the theory of the known particles and forces – says a positron and an electron should be mirror images. It also can’t explain why the universe holds far more matter than antimatter.

“Current theories suggest that there will be no difference in the two measurements. If it turns out they are not equal, that would be the biggest discovery in physics in the last century,” Gabrielse said.

The new paper is the trap and the quantum control, not the measurement.

With more work on the setup and the time it takes to pin down its uncertainties, the measurement now seems feasible, the authors wrote.

At the electron’s precision, it would test that symmetry more than 30 times more precisely than any test so far with electrons and their relatives.

Until then, the Standard Model’s prediction of no difference at all stays a prediction.

The full study was published in the journal Physical Review Letters.

#6382. A new study proves daddy-longlegs spiders are completely harmless to humans, but they are fierce enough to eat live frogs

The famous story about daddy longlegs being secretly deadly to humans is a complete myth. However, they are still amazing hunters.

You have probably heard the old rumor that daddy-longlegs are the most venomous spiders on Earth, but cannot bite you because their fangs are too short.

Spider experts at UC Riverside note this is completely false. However, a new 2026 study shows these bugs are still fierce hunters that can actually catch and eat live frogs.

“Three different unrelated groups are called ‘daddy-longlegs,'” wrote Rod Crawford, an affiliate curator at the Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture in Seattle.

“That is a full-fledged Urban Legend, with no basis in fact whatever,” is Crawford’s verdict on the venom claim. He added that many people believe it who should know better, including some teachers and TV documentary producers.

Harvestmen belong to the order Opiliones. They are arachnids, like spiders, but their body is all in one section.

Cellar spiders, of the family Pholcidae, have the two-section body that all spiders share. They are also known as pholcid or house spiders.

Crane flies are not arachnids at all. They are insects, and like harvestmen, they have no venom.

Harvestmen “do not have venom glands or fangs, so they cannot (and will not) bite you,” the Clemson Cooperative Extension explains.

They also lack spinnerets, the organs spiders use to produce silk. As a result, harvestmen cannot spin webs.

Most adults have an oval body about 1/16 to 1/2 inch (1.6 to 13 millimeters) long. Their second pair of legs is the longest and serves as a sensory structure, somewhat like an insect’s antennae.

Their mouthparts resemble those of crabs or scorpions and hold prey while they eat. Harvestmen are omnivores that eat small insects, including aphids, and scavenge dead insects and other organic matter.

To protect themselves, they release a pungent odor that most predators find distasteful. Their legs break off easily and may keep twitching, which can distract a predator.

In fall, harvestmen sometimes gather in large clusters on trees and homes. They do not damage structures when they cluster.

Like almost all spiders, cellar spiders do have spider venom. Yet pholcid venom “is unusually weak in its effect on insects,” Crawford pointed out, citing a study.

The word “venomous” describes anatomy, not danger to people. An animal qualifies if it has venom glands and ducts that deliver the venom through hardened structures such as fangs or a sting.

“There is no reference to any pholcid spider biting a human and causing any detrimental reaction,” the UC Riverside page states.

Pholcid fangs are short and “uncate,” with a secondary tooth that meets the fang the way the two arms of a pair of tongs come together.

Brown recluse spiders also have uncate fangs, and they can bite humans. The difference may lie in muscle strength, since cellar spiders wrap their prey and do not need as strong a musculature.

The myth is false for harvestmen, while for cellar spiders it is “certainly not based on known facts,” UC Riverside’s spider researchers concluded.

Crane flies are large, long-legged flies that some people call “mosquito hawks” in the belief that they eat mosquitoes.

“Crane flies may look like overgrown mosquitoes, but they do not bite, and they do not eat mosquitoes,” wrote Blake Layton, an extension entomology specialist at Mississippi State University.

The short-lived adults either do not feed or feed only on nectar and other liquids.

Their legs have a special suture that lets them break off easily, which helps the flies escape predators.

There are hundreds of crane fly species, and many of them are aquatic or semi-aquatic.

Mature larvae, known as leatherjackets, are tan, lack true legs and grow to about 2 inches (5 centimeters) long. Some common species feed in the thatch layer of grasses in lawns, fields and roadsides.

Arthropods are usually seen as prey for vertebrates, not as their predators. Several invertebrates are known to eat frogs, but evidence of harvestmen preying on vertebrates had remained largely anecdotal.

First author Esteban Calvache worked with 11 co-authors based in Ecuador, Venezuela, Colombia and Uruguay. The team reported novel field observations of frog predation by multiple harvestman species in the family Cranaidae, at several Neotropical localities.

“These records include the active capture and consumption of live frogs, demonstrating their role as opportunistic mesopredators,” the authors wrote.

Eating vertebrates may also be more taxonomically widespread among arachnids than previously recognized.

The authors argue that harvestmen should be considered potential predators when ecologists map who eats whom in Neotropical food webs.

The study was published in the journal Ecology and Evolution.

#6381. Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Semaglutide helped repair blood vessels and reduce inflammation in the kidneys, a study finds

A patient undergoes hemodialysis, a process that filters waste from blood when the kidneys can’t. A new study shows how the popular weight loss drug semaglutide can help repair damaged kidneys.

Maria Symchych-Navrotska/iStock/Getty Images Plus

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

V. Perkovic et al. Effects of semaglutide on chronic kidney disease in patients with type 2 diabetes. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. doi: 10.1056/NEJMoa2403347

#6379. Lab raised axolotls are surviving in the wild and gaining weight in a huge win for the rare species

Scientists released 18 lab-raised axolotls. Six weeks later, they were all alive and gaining weight, proving captive axolotls can still hunt in the wild.

Axolotls are popular as pets, in video games, and in research labs, but in the wild they are nearly gone. Their only natural home is Lake Xochimilco, a network of canals in southern Mexico City.

When scientists released 18 lab-raised axolotls into two of the city’s wetlands, all of them were still alive about six weeks later.

Two of the axolotls were later caught and weighed again. Both had gained weight. That weight gain suggests axolotls raised in captivity can still find their own food.

Alejandra Ramos of the Autonomous University of Baja California (UABC) led the study. She worked with Luis Zambrano and colleagues at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), where the axolotls were bred.

Animals raised in captivity lose many of their behaviors, Ramos told NPR, including how to recognize a predator and catch prey.

“We were a bit nervous when we released them,” she said, because the team didn’t know whether the axolotls would survive.

The axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) is a salamander that keeps its juvenile features as an adult, including its feathery gills. It spends its whole life in the water.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) lists the species as critically endangered, with an estimated 50 to 1,000 adults left in the wild.

Nine of the axolotls were male and nine were female. Horacio Mena, a veterinarian on the team, surgically implanted a radio transmitter in each one.

Each transmitter weighed about 0.07 ounces (2 grams), a little less than a dime and roughly 3% of an axolotl’s body weight.

In October 2017, the team released eight axolotls into a pond at La Cantera Oriente. The wetland isn’t natural. It formed about 30 years ago, when basalt mining brought underground springs to the surface.

The other 10 axolotls were released in March 2018 into a restored canal in Lake Xochimilco. The canal runs beside a chinampa, a kind of farming island the Aztecs built across the lake.

UNAM scientists set up a refuge there with local farmers, using filters that improve the water and keep out non-native fish.

Volunteers tracked the animals for about six weeks at each site, by rowboat at the pond and on foot at the canal.

All 18 axolotls survived the surgery and the weeks of tracking. The team later recaptured three of them, and two of those were weighed again.

One was a 2.5-year-old female, caught again at the pond three months after her release. She had gained about two-thirds of an ounce (18 grams). That was more than a quarter of her starting weight.

A male recaptured in the Xochimilco canal had gained about a tenth of an ounce (3 grams).

The pond axolotls used far more space than the canal axolotls. A pond axolotl moved around an average area of about 29,600 square feet (2,747 square meters), roughly half a football field.

In the canal, the average area was about 4,100 square feet (382 square meters).

The authors wrote that the pond’s size likely explains the difference. The pond is more than 10 times as big as the canal, and its axolotls also traveled farther each day.

As the weeks went on, the pond axolotls traveled less each day. Ramos’s team suggested they explored at first, then settled once they had found good places to feed and shelter.

At both sites, the axolotls moved the most in cool water, between roughly 60 and 63 degrees Fahrenheit (15.5 to 17 degrees Celsius). In warmer or cooler water, they moved less.

Neither site stayed in that range. Sensors recorded water as warm as 100 degrees Fahrenheit (38 degrees Celsius) in the canal and 87 degrees Fahrenheit (31 degrees Celsius) in the pond.

The authors wrote that the pond may be cooler and more stable than the canal. But they tracked the pond in late fall and the canal in spring, so the two sites weren’t measured at the same time.

Artificial wetlands like La Cantera Oriente could still give axolotls extra places to live, they suggested.

Not every axolotl stayed safe. After the tracking in Xochimilco ended, the researchers saw a great egret, a large wading bird, catch an axolotl in the canal. Local farmers reported seeing a great egret take another axolotl.

So the authors recommended training axolotls before future releases. The animals would be kept in enclosures and exposed to the sight and smell of predators.

Each group was tracked for about six weeks, and not during the warmest months of the year. Just two of the 18 animals were weighed again.

The canal is part of a restoration project that began in 2004, and teams have worked to remove invasive fish from both sites.

Raising axolotls in captivity is the easy part, Ramos said on NPR’s All Things Considered.

“If you do not make this restoration effort, then they’re going to die again,” she said.

The next question is whether released axolotls can survive over the long term and breed in these wetlands. Future research should track both, the authors wrote, and work out the best ways to train axolotls before release.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS One.

Archaeologists have found a 2,200-year-old golden bear in an Iron Age burial in Kazakhstan that may have held seven people.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The gold bear would have been worn on a headdress.

Archaeologists in Kazakhstan have discovered a unique gold bear figurine in a 2,200-year-old burial mound that looters had hit but failed to empty completely.

The sculpted bear stands on its hind limbs and holds a pot-like container between its front paws. The artifact would have been worn as part of a headdress, and holes at its base indicate that it could have been sewn onto the garment, according to a translated statement from the Kazakhstan government.

The 2,200-year-old gold bear is a unique find in Kazakhstan.

The gold bear was unearthed at an Early Iron Age burial mound at the Karagaily burial ground in the southern city of Almaty, along with a surprisingly high number of human bones for a single burial mound.

Although other gold-crafted animals have been found in the region, the newly unearthed bear is the first of its kind.

"The sculpted bear figurine is unique to Kazakhstan. No similar finds have been discovered previously," Lyazzat Sagyndykova, director of the Almaty Museums Association, which conducted the excavation, said in the statement. "This discovery allows us to trace cultural parallels across the whole of Eurasia, from the Black Sea region to Altai."

Archaeologists in Kazakhstan excavated a 2,200-year-old burial mound.

The figurine dates to the Saka period, named for a nomadic horseback-riding people from Iran who lived on the Eurasian Steppe and Tarim Basin of what is now western China. Archaeologists have found comparable gold objects at other excavations in Kazakhstan, according to the statement. For example, a headdress element shaped like a small leopard previously came to light at the Almaty Kok-Kainar burial ground, which dates to the fourth century B.C. Also, the headdress of Kazakhstan's famous "Golden Man," a young Iron Age warrior buried in an extraordinarily lavish grave, also has a gold, sheep-shaped decorative element.

It's unclear which bear species the figurine depicts, but today Kazakhstan is home to two subspecies of brown bear: the Tien Shan or Himalayan brown bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus), which lives in the Tien Shan Mountains in the southeast, and the East Siberian brown bear (Ursus arctos collaris) in the Altai Mountains in the east, according to a study published earlier this year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Preliminary analyses date the recently excavated site to the fourth to third centuries B.C., according to the statement. Based on the number of bones they excavated, experts suspect that the mound, which is around 8 feet (2.4 meters) tall and roughly 85 feet (26 m) wide, may have been the final resting place for four adults and three children.

Archaeologists found a surprising number of human bones in the burial mound.

"Of particular interest is the unusually large number of human remains in a single burial mound, as such burials are atypical for Kazakhstan," Marat Mugalovich Nurpeisov, a senior research fellow at the Almaty Museums Association, said in the statement. "As a rule, burial mounds of a comparable size were intended for the burial of one or two people."

Archaeologists also found pieces of Saka pottery, most of which had been strewn about after the burial had been looted in ancient times, according to the statement. The thieves left behind a 10-foot (3 m) looting pit.

"Research into the Karagaily burial ground is ongoing," Nurpeisov said in the statement. "To clarify the circumstances of the burial and determine the exact number of individuals interred, further analyses are planned, including the involvement of anthropologists."

After all of the investigations are finished, some of the artifacts will be put on display at the Almaty Museum, according to the statement.

#6377. Researchers found hidden layers of ancient earthquake damage inside a single tube of deep ocean mud

Radiocarbon tests on a 16-inch sediment core taken off Japan found seven hidden layers, and several line up with Nankai earthquakes since 1605.

In 2012, scientists aboard the research vessel Tansei-maru pulled a sediment core 16 inches (40 centimeters) long from the Kumano Trough off central Japan, under about 6,820 feet (2,080 meters) of water.

The mud looked the same from top to bottom, and it was logged as homogeneous. Radiocarbon measurements taken less than half an inch apart have now turned up seven disturbed layers inside it.

A University of Tokyo team links most of those layers to underwater slope failures during historical Nankai Trough earthquakes. Every match comes from this one core, and the authors word them cautiously.

The Kumano Trough lies off the Kii Peninsula. It is a forearc basin, a depression that formed as the Philippine Sea Plate slid beneath the Eurasian Plate.

Its floor sits around 6,560 feet (2,000 meters) down, below a steep slope and a shelf less than 6 miles (10 kilometers) wide.

The crew took core KT-12-34-MC01 with a multiple corer in the western part of the basin, far from the mouths of the Shingu and Owase submarine canyons.

The sample is clayey silt. Near 1.6 inches (4 centimeters) down, it shifts from brownish black to olive black, and the naked eye finds nothing else.

X-ray CT scans made with help from Kochi University showed only slight changes in brightness. One brighter band, between about 4 and 6 inches (10 and 16 centimeters), hinted at a past disturbance.

Lead author Akiko Omura, Yusuke Yokoyama and three colleagues at the Atmosphere and Ocean Research Institute measured radiocarbon in the total organic carbon of the mud.

They worked down the core in steps of 0.2 to 0.4 inch (0.5 to 1.0 centimeter), using the single-stage accelerator mass spectrometer at the institute.

Undisturbed seafloor mud gets older with depth. Some horizons in this core broke that rule, and their carbon tested as much as 700 years older than the mud beneath them, well past the average measurement error of about 100 years.

The authors read those reversals as the mark of turbidity currents, fast underwater flows of sediment that can start when a slope fails. Such a flow lifts old seafloor material and drops it on top of younger mud.

“We found several new geological layers that were not visible before,” Yokoyama, a professor at the institute, said in a University of Tokyo statement. He said the redeposited sediments match the material below, which left “the chemical and structural features” indistinguishable.

Organic carbon in this basin tests older than the mud around it, so the team needed a second clock. They picked planktonic foraminifera, tiny shelled ocean organisms, in samples of just 0.75 to 2.35 milligrams, and M. Okitsu of Palynosurvey Co. identified them.

Seven paired depths gave offsets of 700 to 1,109 years between shell dates and carbon dates. Near the top, shells from about an inch down carried a radiocarbon level that, checked against coral records from Ishigaki and Kikai, placed that mud after 1965.

The corrected timeline puts the whole core at roughly 600 years of deposition. The oldest dated part, about 15 inches (37 to 38 centimeters) down, goes back to around 1440 C.E.

Omura’s team then set the layers beside a list of documented earthquakes. According to the paper, layers 1 and 2 may date to the 1944 to 1946 earthquakes and to the Ansei Tokai earthquake of 1854, but it does not say which layer goes with which.

The authors tied layer 3 to the Hoei earthquake of 1707, shown at magnitude 8.6 on the university’s map. That layer overlaps the bright band from the Kochi scan.

A shift in carbon isotopes appears near 6 inches (15 centimeters), where it begins, and the paper says the earthquake might have changed conditions at the site.

The paper offers two options for layers 4 and 5, the Hoei event or a minor submarine earthquake. It says layer 6 could have come from the Keicho earthquake of 1605.

The Kumano River runs directly into this basin, so the team had to consider floods. M. Saito and N. Suzuki at the National Museum of Nature and Science in Tokyo helped run the stable carbon isotope tests that check for land plants.

Carbon-to-nitrogen ratios came back near 8. Carbon isotope values stayed between minus 20 and minus 22 per mil in normal and disturbed layers, which the paper reads as marine organic matter and evidence against a flood origin.

The paper reports data from this one core and gives no estimate of the size or location of any event. Omura’s group presented the work at the 25th International Radiocarbon Conference in Krakow, Poland, in 2025.

Two layers were not fully invisible. Layer 3 lines up with the bright CT band and layer 5 with a pale strip of fine laminae, while scans showed nothing matching the others.

On the paper’s chart, the deepest layer carries a question mark. The authors did not assign it to any earthquake.

The university statement lists severe floods, storms and submarine earthquakes as possible causes of disturbed mud. It also mentions previously unknown earthquakes and written records from the 13th century onward.

The paper connects the layers to historical disasters after the 15th century, and the core stops near 1440. Whether any layer records an earthquake missing from the written history remains open.

On Nov. 9, 2026, the Japan Meteorological Agency posted its regular Nankai Trough assessment and reported no notable change in the odds.

The same notice says a magnitude 8 to 9 earthquake there has a high probability within 30 years, and that about 80 years have passed since the 1944 and 1946 events.

JAMSTEC researchers recently described a buried ridge that may shape where the next Nankai rupture stops. Off North America, deep-sea cores hold about 3,100 years of Cascadia earthquake history in turbidite beds that geologists can see, unlike most layers in the Kumano sample.

Tsunami work has also turned to mud. Patrick Sharrocks of the University of Leeds led a study showing that fine sediment thickened the front of the 2011 tsunami.

According to the university, Yokoyama now wants samples from across the Kumano Sea and beyond. The JSPS and JST CREST funded this round, which began with a 16-inch tube of mud once logged as uniform.

The full study was published in the journal Radiocarbon.
