#6376. The 7 Best Portable Jump Starters to Bring Your Vehicle Back to Life

The days of needing jumper cables and another motorist to revive your vehicle are over.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’ve got a dead car battery, you’ll want the option to revive it without waiting for help. According to AAA’s most recent report, of the 27 million calls received across the country for roadside assistance, 7 million of those vehicles had battery trouble. The causes may include anything from neglecting to turn off your car’s ignition or headlights, residing in an extremely cold climate, or even a slowly deteriorating alternator.

A portable jump starter, which is a compact and powerful battery consisting of lightweight lithium-ion, is a handy device that’s faster, safer, and more convenient than jumper cables because you don’t need to find another car with a willing driver.

Like all batteries, lithium-ion cells have different power ratings and can become depleted from repeated use or by sitting idle over time. That’s why before purchasing a portable jump starter, consider these two specs: peak amperage (amps) which conveys how much power a device can deliver, and capacity (rated in milliampere-hours, mAh), indicating how long a device can hold a charge when stored and still have enough power to provide a jump. It’s also important to monitor the charge level on your portable jump starter from time to time. I do this regularly while waiting to fill my gas tank.

There are other convenience features these devices offer, like USB ports to recharge portable electronics and lights for illumination when it’s dark. Many portable jump starters have what’s called a boost button, which I recommend having, as it supplies extra momentary power for severely drained batteries. After several rounds of testing, research, and evaluation, these are the top portable jump starters to buy now.

I’ve owned close to a dozen vehicles during my 30-year-plus career writing about cars and have had plenty of dead batteries. I keep jumper cables in each of my three current vehicles, and now I also have a portable jump starter on board along with a portable tire inflator, dash cam, and Cobra RAD 700i radar detector, which I move between vehicles depending on which I decide to drive.

In short, each device in this roundup can quickly start a vehicle with a depleted battery. While testing each product, I also evaluated its peak instantaneous power measured in amps, power capacity measured in milliampere-hours, the quantity and variety of output ports to charge portable electronics, and extras such as lights and a boost button.

My recommendations are based on a product’s price, capability, and capacity to fit a wide array of vehicles and budgets. I took into account my own experiences with portable jump starters, each brand’s reputation, and for further background, I spoke with fellow car enthusiasts and auto journalists to get their impressions.

With 6,000-amp peak current to jump-start a vehicle with up to a 12.0-liter diesel engine coupled with 27,000 mAh of power capacity, the Gooloo GT6000 is the most powerful device in our guide. The GT6000 offers up to 24 months of standby time—and with that, you get incredible peace of mind. This device can sit unused for long stretches and still be counted on to crank your car when needed. If its battery is depleted, the GT6000 is ready to jump-start a vehicle after just 7 minutes of recharging and is fully recharged in 1.4 hours via its 100-watt USB-C in/out port.

This device also stands out for its generous quantity and variety of charging ports. In addition to a 100-watt USB-C in/out port, it also has a 12-volt/cigarette-lighter cord to recharge its battery in a pinch. A 15 volt/10-amp DC port can be used to power assorted car accessories like portable air pumps and power inverters. There are two USB-A power ports, one rated at 5-volts/2.4-amps and another rated for 5/9/12-volts

The GT6000 is one of only two devices here with an LCD screen, which makes checking battery level, charging output, temperature, and jump-start status quick and easy. There are 10 safety features, in addition to a built-in LED flashlight with three lighting modes (flashlight, strobe, and SOS) that provides illumination when using the device in low-light situations—important so other motorists can see you if you’re stuck on the side of the road.

While the GT6000 admittedly provides more power than most motorists will likely need, and it’s one of the heaviest of our picks, it is without question the best overall jump starter for maximum instantaneous power, long standby time, quick recharging, and plenty of output ports.

The AstroAI S8 isn’t the most powerful jump-starter recommended but it’s one of the lowest-priced and is user friendly and small enough to fit in your car’s glove box or map pocket. Although it taps out on vehicles with anything larger than a 6.0-liter gas or 3.0-liter diesel engine, it’s fine for most vehicles. I’ve kept this in one of my vehicles for months and used it several times to provide jump-starts to others without an issue.

Protection against reverse polarity, overcurrent, overvoltage, overload, overcharge, over discharge, and short circuiting are built in. The AstroAI S8 has two 5-volt/2.4-amp USB-A output ports to charge portable devices and an LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes. It is supplied with a USB A to USB C charging cable to recharge the device.

The interface is one of the most barebones of all the units tested—just a power button and four blue LEDs to indicate power level. It does have a boost button but is the only unit of our selections without a shut-off switch; instead it automatically powers off after 30 seconds.Full AstroAI S8 Portable Jump Starter Review

This is the smallest device I tested (only slightly larger than most smartphones) and the lightest at 1.2 pounds. With 2,000 amps of peak power, the Gooloo GP2000 can jump-start vehicles with up to 8.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines and its 12,000 mAh of capacity is impressive for its size and price.

It has 10 safety protection features including short circuit and reverse polarity, and a 400-lumen LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes to provide light in dark environments and during emergency roadside stops. It comes with two USB-A outputs—one 5/9/12-volt and one 5-volt/2.4-amp—for charging portable devices, a USB-C charging cable, and a storage case instead of a bag like many portable jump starters at this price.

Like the AstroAI S8, it has only an on-off button. It’s easy to use and has a boost button. I recommend this option for anyone looking for a small, inexpensive, and hassle-free portable jump starter.

With an IP65 water-resistance rating and rubberized casing, the Noco Boost Plus is the portable jump starter I turn to during the rainy season in Oregon—which means anytime other than summer. I go for this one because it has spark-proof and reverse polarity protection for safe use in wet or dry conditions.

Its 1,000-amp peak power rating can start vehicles with up to 6.0-liter gas and 3.0-liter diesel engines. However, its 2,150 mAh capacity is the lowest of any product here, so it may not hold a charge as long as jump starters with a higher capacity. While this is adequate, I don’t recommend a mAh rating any lower.

The Noco GB40’s 100-lumen flashlight is dimmer than that of some of the other units in this roundup but it has the most modes, six total, which include 100-, 50-, and 10 percent; blink, SOS, and strobe. It also comes with a 1-foot USB-C charging cable, but it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A output port for charging your portable electronics.

If you own a large vehicle, the Noco Boost X GBX155 cranks out 4,250 amps to boost batteries instantaneously for vehicles with up to 10.0-liter gas and 8.0-liter diesel engines, and has an impressive 26,750 mAh capacity, just shy of the Gooloo GT6000’s 27,000-mAh spec. A 60-watt USB-C input/output allows recharging from 0-to-100 percent capacity in 2.7 hours to ensure it’s ready to jump-start a vehicle after charging only 5 minutes (slightly faster than the Gooloo GT6000’s 7 minutes.)

I found the Noco Boost X GBX155 more complicated to operate than the other portable jump starters I tested. For example, it doesn’t have a boost button like other units but rather a manual override feature that’s used to jump start severely depleted batteries if the device detects the battery is below 3 volts. Aactivating the feature requires holding the Manual Override button for 3 seconds, which can send the GBX155’s maximum output of 4,250 amps to jump start a vehicle. This Manual Override shuts off the Noco’s automatic spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection so users need to be extra careful to attach the jumper cables correctly (red to positive, black to negative) to avoid damaging the car’s electrical system, and not touch the clamps together, which can create dangerous sparking.

The Noco is heavy, too, at 5.8 pounds. In addition to its 60-watt USB-C input/output, it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A port whereas other lower-priced devices have at least two. But you won’t be working in the dark if you are trying to start your battery at night. This device has a 500-lumen LED flashlight that’s the brightest of the portable jump starters in our roundup. Another perk: it’s got an IP65 waterproof rating (with its input/output ports covered) that only the Gooloo GT6000 and Noco GB40 also have.

For motorheads with multiple vehicles and a garage or shop to keep them, the Clore Automotive Jump-N-Carry JNC660 is a worthy device to have on hand. Its 120-volt male receptacle connects to an extension cord so that it can be powered by a regular wall outlet and is always charged and ready.

This device uses a lead-acid battery instead of a lithium-ion one. This makes the battery replaceable, so this device is not ultimately disposable like portable jump starters with a lithium-ion battery. At 18 pounds, it’s by far the heaviest here, but also has the longest (46 inches) and thickest (2-gauge) jumper cables.

With 1,700 peak amps, it’s not the most powerful portable jump starter included but makes up for that with a 22,000 mAh rating which means its internal battery holds a charge longer. A built-in digital voltmeter shows the battery’s state of charge before and after a jump start and it has a DC outlet to power 12-volt accessories such as a tire inflator or power inverter. A notable drawback: It doesn’t have USB output ports.

For years, I relied on a Battery Tender trickle charger to supply a slow, steady current to keep the battery in my classic Chevy Impala SS charged. If you also have a vehicle that sits idle for months on end, check out the Battery Tender Charge N Start 4120. It does double duty as a trickle charger and a jump starter. However, combining two devices in one comes with compromises such as not having output ports to charge portable devices, or a boost button.

With 1,200 amps of instantaneous current, this device can jump start cars with up to 6.0-liter gas or 4.0-liter diesel engines and proficiently cranked the engine on several large and small vehicles during my testing. Its basic push-button interface makes the Charge N Start a breeze to operate. Safety features include spark-proof connection, reverse-polarity protection, and more.

This portable jump starter sends a small amount of current to traditional lead-acid as well as lithium batteries at 4 amps, and an onboard microprocessor maintains the optimal voltage to keep a battery at 100-percent capacity without overcharging during long-term storage. It also includes temperature compensation to handle a range of climates.

Something you may need to think about is its size. Its larger than other trickle chargers I’ve used, which affects placement. Ideally, a trickle charger should be located close to the battery under a car’s hood. The Charge N Start may be too large to tuck away under the closed hood of certain vehicles, but a supplied 6-foot extension cable that attaches to low-profile battery-charging clamps allows locating the device away from the engine on, say, a shelf next to a wall outlet.

The Noco AX65 is another portable jump starter we’ve tested and recommend, but we moved it out of our guide because it’s not singularly a portable jump starter like the others. This is a combo device with a portable air compressor so you can start dead batteries and inflate flat tires. What I like is that the unit doesn’t skimp on either function. The jump starter has an impressive 16,000 mAh capacity and delivers 2,000 amps of peak power while the tire inflator pumps out 67 liters per minute of airflow, which converts to 2.3 cubic feet per minute (cfm)—well above average for the portable tire inflators I’ve tested.

The portable jump starter can crank a dead battery on vehicles with gas engines as large as 8.0 liters and diesel engines up to 6.0 liters. It can be used for SUVs, boats, and snowmobiles. The not-so-good news: It’s short on output ports compared to the other portable jump starters here, and heavy at more than 9 pounds.

Portable jump starters are essentially heavy-duty batteries that come with jumper cables, controls, and accessories like lights, charging ports, and air pumps. Here’s what to look for when shopping for a portable jump starter that fits your vehicle, needs, and budget.

The two most important specs to look for when comparing portable jump starters are peak amperes (amps) and milliampere-hours (mAh). Peak amps indicate the maximum short-term current a device can deliver, while mAh measures how much electrical charge a battery can store.

Bigger is better for both specs, although mAh isn’t always as prominent or even stated with portable jump starters compared to peak amps. About 400 to 600 peak amps is sufficient to jump-start vehicles like cars and crossovers, although large SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles may require up to 1,500 or 2,000 amps. Some portable jump starters come with a boost button that provides roughly 10 additional amps and is helpful when reviving a very dead battery that needs an extra jolt of juice. At least 10,000 mAh of capacity means the battery in a portable jump starter will hold enough charge for 3 to 6 months to deliver 5 to 10 jump-starts.

Portable jump starters are a much safer alternative to using jumper cables to revive a dead battery because connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that can sometimes ignite gas produced by the battery and cause an explosion. Also, if you connect the cables incorrectly, called reverse polarity, it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, portable jump starters have built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity in addition to other safety features and are much less risky and easier to use.

Most portable jump starters also come in handy for recharging phones, tablets, and other portable devices. USB output ports are the most common, but a few devices also provide a 12-volt outlet. While USB ports typically charge at 2.5 to 5 volts, a 12-volt outlet can not only charge a device faster but can also be used to power devices such as portable air pumps and coolers.

If you need to jump-start a vehicle at night, you’ll be thankful your portable jump starter has an LED flashlight. Typically a portable jump starter’s lighting feature also provides strobe or SOS patterns to warn other motorists on the road of your presence.

Look for a portable jump starter with a boost button to give an extra jolt of juice to a very depleted battery when the device’s standard output can’t crank the engine. This surge of power gives you about 15 to 30 seconds to start the car once the boost button is pressed.

A portable jump starter rated for 400 to 600 amps is sufficient to jump-start most passenger vehicles such as cars, crossovers, and smaller SUVs. But for larger SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles you want to look for a device with at least 1,500 to 2,000 amps. Weather also affects a car battery and engine, so if you live in a very cold climate more power may be needed to jump-start a low or dead battery.

Yes and no since it depends on the wide range of passenger vehicles available. A portable jump starter with a lower amp rating can jump-start smaller vehicles such as most cars, crossovers, and small SUVs. But a large SUV or truck with a large engine will require a portable jump starter with a higher amp rating.

Peak power rating (measured in amps) to ensure a portable jump starter has enough juice to crank your vehicle and capacity (measured in milliamp hours) that indicates how long it can potentially hold a charge are the most two important. Other features to look for include the number and types of output charging ports, whether it has a 12-volt output and charging input, a boost button, and a flashlight.

Definitely. Make sure to first read the owner’s manual to understand how your portable jump starter works before connecting it to a car’s battery. When using it, take off any jewelry and wear safety glasses and gloves anytime you work on a vehicle and especially around a battery. Most portable jump starters come with built-in safety features that will issue a warning if they are connected incorrectly. But it’s up to you to double-check that the jump starter’s red/positive and black/negative clamps are connected to the (typically) red positive and black negative terminals of the car battery.

Yes, a portable jump starter is a much safer alternative to using traditional jumper cables to start a vehicle with a dead battery. Connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that have the potential to ignite gas produced by a battery which in some instances can lead to an explosion. And if you connect the cables incorrectly (in reverse polarity) it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, most portable jump starters come with built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity and are much less risky and easier to use. Plus, with a portable jump starter you don’t have to find another car—and a driver—like you do with jump cables. That said, I carry a set of jumper cables as a backup.

#6375. Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The decrease is probably temporary and a result of high gas prices from the Iran war

The disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Iran has raised oil and gas prices around the world. According to new projections, those higher fuel prices will decrease global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel burning in 2026 by about 0.16 gigatons from 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

#6374. A graduate student’s team found a faint galaxy candidate in Rubin Observatory test data, and hundreds more may still be hiding

A Milky Way companion galaxy named Aquarius IV lies about 355,000 light-years away. A Yale-led team found it in Rubin test data covering about 7 percent of the night sky.

On July 27, 2026, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory on Cerro Pachón in Chile released its second batch of test data. Seven days later, Yale graduate student William Cerny and his colleagues posted a paper about the discovery of a Milky Way companion.

They named it Aquarius IV. It sits roughly 355,000 light-years from Earth, an estimate that rests on a single star, and the data behind the find covered about 7 percent of the night sky.

According to Yale University, it is a galaxy. The authors call that classification tentative and do not rule out a globular cluster, because Rubin has so far picked out only a small number of its stars.

The release is called Early Data Preview 2 and covers about 3,000 square degrees. Rubin took those images between April 2025 and January 2026, before its 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time started in June 2026.

Cerny worked with 18 co-authors at places including the University of Chicago, Fermilab and the University of Washington.

They pulled stars from the release and kept the blue ones in parts of the sky with little dust. Then they ran an algorithm called simple, which looks for small clumps of stars with the colors of a very old population.

The team assumed an age of 13 billion years and scanned distances in steps. They repeated the search with two pairs of color filters and compared the lists to weed out false alarms.

Aquarius IV ranked highest among the new detections, at 8.0 sigma in one filter pair and 7.6 sigma in the other. Sigma measures how far a signal stands above random noise.

The same run also recovered every known ultra-faint satellite in that area, all three known ultra-faint satellites in that area: Aquarius II, Aquarius III and Virgo III.

Peter Ferguson, a postdoctoral scholar in astronomy at the University of Washington and a co-author, credited the data work behind the find. “Finding something as faint as Aquarius IV comes down to how clean your stellar catalog is,” he said.

After the algorithm flagged the spot, the team opened the stacked Rubin images. They also pulled archival pictures from the Dark Energy Camera. Both sets showed an excess of faint blue stars at the same position.

The researchers then checked candidates from an earlier search of Dark Energy Camera data. Aquarius IV was on that list too, at about 6 sigma.

Yale describes the object as only barely detectable by eye in the Rubin image. The automated search found it at high confidence anyway.

The fit gives Aquarius IV an absolute magnitude of about minus 1.9. Half of its light falls within a radius of about 19 parsecs, or roughly 62 light-years.

Its stars match a population about 13 billion years old and very poor in heavy elements. The paper places it among the faintest known Milky Way satellites beyond about 326,000 light-years.

Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies are the dimmest galaxies known, with a total glow of up to around 100,000 suns. Astronomers study these tiny, ancient systems for clues about the early universe. Yale says objects like Aquarius IV consist almost entirely of dark matter.

Size drives the tentative label. The authors note that its radius exceeds that of nearly all Milky Way globular clusters, the dense balls of old stars that also orbit the galaxy. A similar debate surrounded a very faint star system called UMa3/U1, found orbiting the Milky Way.

A second study from the same preview data reported a star cluster named Rubin-GC1. It lies on the far side of the Milky Way, inside a region thick with cosmic dust.

Aashay Pai of the University of Chicago led that work, with Cerny as second author, and it appeared in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. Marla Geha, a professor of astronomy and physics at Yale, co-authored both papers.

“Finding new Milky Way satellites in Rubin Observatory data has been an exciting future prospect for most of my career,” Geha said.

Yale counts about 65 known satellite galaxies of the Milky Way. Some researchers suspect hundreds more remain undetected, and simulations have pointed to dozens of unseen ghost galaxies around our own.

Rubin’s Simonyi Survey Telescope has a 27.6-foot (8.4-meter) mirror and a 3.2-gigapixel camera, which Yale calls the largest digital camera ever built. Ferguson said the test data covered 15 percent of the area the full survey will map.

The paper expects the survey to catch systems like Aquarius IV with better than 85 percent efficiency. Cerny said the full survey “will undoubtedly provide us with many more Milky Way satellite discoveries.”

The 355,000 light-year figure leans heavily on one star. It is a likely blue horizontal branch star, a type of aging star with a predictable brightness, located 0.8 arcminutes from the object’s center.

A footnote in the paper covers the other case. If the star does not belong to Aquarius IV, distances of about 490,000 to 650,000 light-years may fit better. The team already rejected one bright red giant because Gaia data showed it moving too fast across the sky.

The authors call their measurements preliminary. They say deeper imaging and spectroscopy must settle its properties and its classification.

The paper ran as a four-page note in a journal that the American Astronomical Society says is moderated and not peer-reviewed.

Those follow-up observations will go back to the spot in Aquarius that Cerny’s team reported seven days after the test data went public. Rubin’s main survey has more than nine years left to run.

The full study was published in the journal Research Notes of the AAS.

#6373. The true power of humans and AI working together as a team is being heavily underestimated right now

A reanalysis of 74 human-AI studies finds people and AI did best together when AI explanations came with feedback that let humans learn.

A person with a good AI assistant should beat either one working alone. Two years ago a tally of 74 experiments said otherwise: on average, the human-AI pair did worse than whichever partner was better by itself.

A new recount of those same experiments says they left out something that people need in order to get good at anything – finding out whether they were right.

Only 10 of the 74 studies ever told participants the correct answer after a decision. In the few that did, and that also let the AI explain itself, the pair tended to come out ahead.

Julian Berger and Stefan Herzog of the Center for Adaptive Rationality at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin led the reanalysis. Colleagues at the University of Copenhagen and elsewhere in Europe joined them.

They didn’t run new experiments. They went back through every study in the 2024 review and coded what each one had let its participants learn.

“Learning effects in human-machine interaction remain virtually unexplored,” Berger said.

The 2024 review, published in Nature Human Behaviour, pooled studies in which people worked with an AI system on tasks such as sorting images, predicting house prices, or writing code.

Across 370 experimental conditions, the human-AI pair scored below the stronger partner on average.

The pair came out ahead only when the human was already better than the AI. When the AI was the stronger one, the pair did worse than the AI by itself. Neither the AI’s stated confidence nor its explanations changed that.

Berger’s team found that the typical study was a single session, with no practice trials, a median of 30 decisions, and no word on whether any of them was correct.

Only 10 studies, 14 percent of the 74, included a condition with outcome feedback. Just three of those looked at whether people’s use of the AI changed over the trials, and none varied feedback on purpose.

Feedback matters because it is how a person learns when to trust an AI assistant and when to overrule it. Without it, a participant who sees the AI’s answer has no way of telling whether the AI, or they themselves, tend to be right.

The team re-ran the comparison, splitting the 370 conditions by whether people got feedback. With feedback, the pair’s edge over the better partner was slightly positive. Without it, slightly negative.

By the team’s statistics there was an 84 percent probability the gap ran that way, which isn’t enough to be sure of. The team saw a clearer result once it sorted the conditions by AI explanations too.

In the 24 conditions where people got both an explanation of the AI’s reasoning and feedback on the outcome, the pair tended to outperform the better partner alone.

In the 148 conditions with explanations but no feedback, the pair did clearly worse. Without explanations, feedback made no reliable difference either way.

The authors’ reading is that an explanation helps mainly when a person can check it against results and learn how far to trust it.

Because no study varied feedback within an experiment, the team could only compare studies with it against studies without it. Other features of those studies could explain the differences.

In 12 further models that added each of the original review’s other factors, the direction held. Still, they wrote, experiments that switch feedback on and off are needed before anyone can call it a cause.

Most studies also reported only average performance across all trials, which hides any improvement late in a session.

In the three studies with trial-by-trial data, people learned to go along with an AI that was outperforming them when the task gave them something to learn from.

The authors wrote that their estimate may, therefore, understate how much learning helps.

Whether any of this carries over to chatbots is open. Herzog said a conversation with a chatbot could make tailored feedback and explanations easier to deliver.

“But for that to happen, people also need to find out what is actually correct; a chatbot’s answers can be wrong and do not constitute independent feedback,” he said.

He added a second worry. “At the same time, new risks arise from cognitive ‘offloading’ – that is, delegating mental work to AI. In the medium and long term, this could jeopardize learning success or even lead to loss of skills.”

The team called for experiments that vary feedback and the task itself, and for sharing trial-level data so that learning can be measured directly.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Archaeologists have discovered the shoe of the first governor of the Danish West Indies, recovered from a 17th-century ship that was wrecked after one of the most violent mutinies in Denmark’s history.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Maritime archaeologists investigating a 17th-century shipwreck off the coast of Sweden have discovered a fancy shoe and two metal rings used as currency in the transatlantic slave trade. The items were lost during a mutiny on a slave ship in 1683, during which the governor of the Danish West Indies was thrown overboard.

The Danish frigate Havmanden (which translates to "Merman") was en route to St. Thomas, a Caribbean island that is now part of the U.S. Virgin Islands, with convicts and indentured servants aboard destined for work on the island with the Danish West India Company. The plan for the Havmanden, after dropping off the new colonists, was to sail to West Africa to buy enslaved Africans. But due to a shortage of food and water, several crewmembers and convicts aboard seized control of the ship near the Azores in the North Atlantic and began sailing it back to Copenhagen.

The mutineers shot the ship's captain and threw other officers ‪—‬ including Jørgen Iversen Dyppel, the first governor of the Danish West Indies ‪—‬ overboard in the English Channel. After the ship ran aground, the mutineers were tried for their crimes in Copenhagen and sentenced to death.

The story of the Havmanden is one of the most violent mutinies in Denmark's history, according to a Nov. 11 translated statement from the National Museum of Denmark. But now, underwater archaeologists are learning more about the fateful voyage from the wreck, which lies on the seabed just east of Gothenburg, Sweden.

Archaeological divers discovered the rear half of a man's "unusually fine" shoe in the wreckage, according to the statement.

"I see a great many shoes from shipwrecks, but I have never before seen a shoe of such high quality," Vivi Lena Andersen, director of the Rudersdal Museums in Denmark, said in the statement.

The sole has a high level of craftsmanship, Andersen said, which can be seen in the minuscule holes perforating the edge of the shoe. The regularity of the holes would have required tools and expertise that only the most skilled shoemakers had at the time. It was "undoubtedly an expensive and exclusive shoe that only the elite could afford to buy," Andersen said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Because the shoe was likely owned by an upper-class individual, experts think it could have belonged to Iversen, the Danish West Indies governor who was thrown overboard.

"The shoe testifies not only to Jørgen Iversen Dyppel's life and dramatic death, but also provides a personal point of entry into the larger story of the establishment of the Danish colonies in the West Indies and the widespread slave trade Denmark was a part of," Andreas Kallmeyer Bloch, a maritime archaeologist at the National Museum of Denmark's Center for Maritime and Underwater Cultural Heritage, said in the statement.

Additional clues to the Danish slave trade on board the Havmanden included two manillas, ring-shaped pieces of metal that were used as currency in West Africa. European merchants cast manillas from copper, brass or iron and traded them for enslaved people in West Africa, particularly along the coast of modern-day Nigeria. But manillas are rarely found in Scandinavia, according to the statement.

"The manillas add another layer to Havmanden's story and underscore the connection to the slave trade, which was a central part of Denmark's colonial activities in both the West Indies and on the west coast of Africa," Kallmeyer Bloch said.

Denmark continued to engage in the transatlantic slave trade for more than a century after the Havmanden sank. Although King Christian VII of Denmark-Norway banned the trade in 1792, slavery continued in the Danish West Indies until 1848, when hundreds of enslaved people revolted and were finally granted their freedom.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6370. Most of the deep ocean food supply in the Gulf of Mexico suddenly vanished, and most scientists blame the Deepwater Horizon oil spill

Deep-sea fish, krill and squid in the Gulf of Mexico fell 60 to 85 percent after 2011, and the Deepwater Horizon oil spill is the leading suspect.

Marine biologists have always assumed the deep ocean is the safest and most stable ecosystem on the planet. Because it is so vast and isolated from human life, they believed it was practically impossible to destroy.

Unfortunately, a massive die-off in the Gulf of Mexico just proved that assumption is dangerously incorrect.

Between 2011 and 2015, the fish, shrimp, krill and squid living in the dark water below about 650 feet (200 meters) lost 60 to 85 percent of their numbers. Surveys through 2023 have not found them coming back.

The crash shows up in two records. One is the nets that scientists have towed through the same patch of ocean in the Gulf of Mexico for 13 years. The other is ship sonar, whose echoes come back weaker when fewer animals are swimming below.

Nothing in the water itself, not temperature, oxygen or food, changed in step with it. The one event that did line up in time was the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. The authors consider this the most likely explanation.

Tracey Sutton of Nova Southeastern University led the work, with colleagues at Florida International University, the University of South Florida and NOAA.

The paper is careful about what it can show. The spill’s role is inferred from timing and from the absence of any natural driver, not from an experiment.

The record begins in January 2011, three months after the well was sealed. A nine-month campaign towed a net through a grid of 46 stations across the northern Gulf of Mexico. That first campaign is the baseline against which everything since has been measured.

The same net, with six separate bags that open and close on command, was towed again on nine shorter cruises between 2015 and 2023.

Each tow sampled from the surface down to 4,900 feet (1,500 meters) in five depth bands, at noon and again at midnight.

Towing twice a day matters, because most of these animals rise thousands of feet toward the surface every night to feed and sink again at dawn.

Only samples from the Gulf of Mexico’s own water mass were compared, since the Loop Current, which enters from the south, carries fewer animals and would have muddied the count.

Fish numbers per unit of water dropped 63.5 percent between 2011 and the later cruises. Shrimp and krill together dropped 62 percent, and small squid and their relatives dropped 59.7 percent.

The groups that feed almost everything else fell hardest. Krill dropped 72.8 percent and lanternfish 62.9 percent. Bristlemouths, tiny fish that may be the most numerous vertebrates on Earth, dropped 69 percent.

The sonar agreed. Sound bouncing back from the top 650 feet (200 meters) at night, when the migrators are up feeding, was 40 percent weaker after 2011.

A drop that size over three and a half years is bigger than any change recorded over 60 years in the California Current. That is the only other long-running count of deep-sea fish.

In an interview with Earth.com, Sutton said the fall itself is not the part that surprised him most. “The slow recovery is the most surprising finding, with the realization that this downward shift may be irreversible,” he said.

And the dense swarms that predators depend on nearly disappeared. Across 134 full-column tows in the whole series, only one catch after the decline held more fish than the leanest catch of 2011.

A crowd that shrinks fast can lose genetic variety, so the team sequenced three common lanternfish species collected between 2011 and 2023, the longest such record for any deep-sea animal.

Two of the three showed it. In one species, a standard measure of genetic variety fell about 11 percent between 2011 and 2016, then recovered partway by 2023. A second species followed the same path a few years later. The third showed no clear trend.

The same tows kept adding to the list of what lives down there. Sutton told Earth.com that the deep interior holds more kinds of animals than any other part of the Gulf of Mexico, coral reefs included.

His team has recorded almost 200 fish species there for the first time since the work began, he said. That is about one in every nine fish species now known from the Gulf.

“Our knowledge of what lives in the deep ocean is incredibly poor,” he said, “even in the best-studied systems in the world, like the Gulf.”

The authors checked their own methods first. The same net, the same crew and the same analysis ran across every year, so a change in gear can’t explain the drop.

Water temperature in the twilight zone from 650 to 2,000 feet (200 to 600 meters) barely moved from year to year, and the deep Gulf stayed well supplied with oxygen. The plankton these animals eat didn’t thin out either; in 2013, mid-decline, it was above average.

So the authors turned to the spill. The Deepwater Horizon blowout on April 20, 2010 released up to 4.9 million barrels of oil over 87 days.

Crews pumped 770,000 gallons (2.9 million liters) of chemical dispersant into the plume at the wellhead, 4,900 feet down.

Oil residues turned up in the eggs of deep-sea fish and the tissues of squid at least six years later, at concentrations known to kill or weaken fish.

The paper does not test oil on these animals directly. It argues from the sequence of events and from what oil did elsewhere. For example, herring in Prince William Sound collapsed four years after the Exxon Valdez spill and have still not recovered.

The Gulf’s deep-feeding whales eat these animals, and their numbers have been falling too. Long-term counts show Gervais’ beaked whales down 83.4 percent since the spill, and sperm whales down 31 percent. This is more than the spill’s own mortality models predicted.

Tagged sperm whales are now roaming the Gulf instead of feeding in their usual predictable spots.

Endangered Rice’s whales have been recorded feeding near the bottom, often without success. In addition, researchers at sea report seeing thin whales, while stranded ones are often described as emaciated.

Sutton said 27 of the 28 whale and dolphin species known from the Gulf live in the open ocean, and nearly all of them eat the animals his team counted. Less prey means fewer marine mammals, he said, “and those that are there may be less fit.”

Bluefin and yellowfin tuna, swordfish, marlin, sailfish and sharks feed on the same animals, he said. So do seabirds that hunt lanternfish at night, including some endangered species.

These animals also run what scientists call the biological pump, the sinking of carbon from the surface into the deep ocean. “That function affects every person on the planet.”

One obvious objection is that the 2011 baseline was a single, nine-month campaign, run just after the spill. The team’s answer is that counts from the 1980s and 1990s at one eastern Gulf station look like 2011, not like anything since.

The authors wrote that the deep Gulf is now in “a sustained, low-abundance state” for which the recovery time, “if even possible, remains unknown.”

Asked by Earth.com what a recovery would take, Sutton used the researchers’ name for that dark, open water, the deep-pelagic ocean.

“We do not have the capacity to restore the deep-pelagic ocean directly, so the best we can do is give the system time and not make it worse with more pollution,” he said.

Whether the deep Gulf is coming back at all is the open question, and the same grid of stations is where an answer would first show up.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6369. The 9 Best Portable Tire Inflators for Peace of Mind on Your Next Road Trip

These earned top spots after hands-on testing with real flats.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

There’s no polite way to say this. It stinks to get a flat tire and stinks even more when your spare is also flat. As a veteran road warrior who drives 4,000 miles round trip each year between the northern border of Oregon and the tip of Baja in search of waves, wind, and warm weather, I know firsthand that flats happen. I’ve experienced everything from a full-on blowout at highway speed to the inevitable nail-in-the-tire slow leak. I’ve also woken up to find that inexplicable flat tire which has a way of happening when the waves are pumping and I’m jonesing to get the beach—but thankfully I own a portable air pump.

For those times when you need to get air in your tire quickly and get back on the road, a portable tire inflator is ideal to have in your vehicle’s trunk and definitely a smart addition to any car emergency care kit.

A portable tire inflator is also handy to have when it’s not a worst-case scenario. I use one of these when I deflate my tires to drive my car on dirt and sand so I can access remote Baja beaches and then inflate the tires when back on pavement. I’ve owned several tire inflators over the years, everything from janky budgets jobs that take forever inflate a tire to my current favorite, the Viair 400P-RV.

There’s good reason why Milwaukee’s M18 Portable Tire Inflator earned inclusion in our prestigious 2025 Gear of the Year Awards and returns as the top choice among portable tire inflators: It’s the fastest to inflate a tire of any product that I tested. Its separate rechargeable 18-volt battery barely lost power while its detachable 36-inch inflator hose didn’t appreciably heat up like some of the others we tested.

Since it performs an automatic pressure check and shuts off once the target psi is reached, Wraight liked that he “could walk away without worrying about watching the inflation gauge.”

Also, it's the only one we tested that has four psi memory presets, an appreciated perk for Wraight, since he refills tires on various lifeguard vehicles at different pressures. The solid-brass screw-on Schrader chuck is another bonus (an inflation needle and nozzle and Presta chuck for bike tires are also included). Finally, at 5 years, the Milwaukee’s M18 Portable Tire Inflator has the longest warranty of any device tested.

This portable air inflator gets points for its simplicity. It has an LED display, physical + and - buttons to dial in a preset psi, and a toggle switch on one side to start inflation. It automatically stops after the preset pressure is reached.

Its 9.8-foot power cord was long enough to reach from the 12-volt outlet inside Wraight’s truck to all four tires while its 24.8-inch air inflator hose was adequate. While Wraight and I were impressed with this small, inexpensive device’s overall performance relative to its low price, thanks to its induction-magnet motor, it struggled with the truck’s large tires and took several minutes to go from 20 to 40 psi whereas the more powerful tire inflators we tested did this in under a minute. The hose and clamp-type Schrader chuck also got hotter than most other devices.

It also has an LED flashlight that turns on with the toggle switch and it comes with a Presta valve adapter for bicycle tires and an adaptor for sports balls and other inflatables. If you want ease of use and affordability, this is a solid option.

The Milwaukee M12 Compact Inflator filled the tires on Wraight’s truck almost as fast as its big brother and Best Overall and Gear of the Year pick, the Milwaukee M18.

The design of the M12 is smaller and lighter, weighing in at 3.45 pounds, than some of the other powerful devices we tested. It is intuitive to use with a digital gauge that shows the pressure reading, + and – buttons to set a target psi, a power button in between, and an inflation-start button underneath.

This device performs automatic pressure checks and shuts off once the target psi is reached and includes a brass Schrader chuck, Presta chuck, inflation needle, and two nozzles—like most of the other devices tested. But, like the Milwaukee’s M18 inflator, it requires buying a separate 18-volt battery and charger—and one that’s different from the one used with the Milwaukee M18 Compact Inflator—and this adds to its cost and weight.

For completists who want the best portable inflator not only for large vehicles but with all the trimmings, the Viair 400P-RV checks all the boxes.

In addition to the obligatory features such as preset psi and automatic shutoff. and standard accessories like a Presta valve adaptor, the Viair 400P-RV comes with an incredible list of accoutrements. These include a quick-connect Schrader chuck, a 45-degree extended-reach chuck designed for vehicles with rear-dually tires like many RVs, and an additional 30-foot inflator hose that attaches to the primary 30-foot hose, all of which fits in a heavy-duty storage bag. Whew!

This device has the same high 2.30-cubic-feet-per-minute (cfm) rating—and quick inflation—as the Milwaukee M18, but unlike that device, this one is powered by a car’s battery via a pair of heavy-duty alligator clamps at the end of an 8-foot cable, and doesn’t require a separate battery.

Of note: This inflator also has a feature not found on any of the other devices we tested—and one Wraight noticed immediately—a deflate button on the gas-station-style inflation gun that makes airing down tires a breeze.

The Etenwolf Vortex S6 is the inflator to get if you’re filling up larger tires and don’t want to worry about running out of juice. Its 19,200 mAh battery is massive, and Etenwolf says it can top off 18 F-150 tires (from 30 to 35 psi) on a single charge. That’s a claim that should put range anxiety to rest for anyone who regularly airs up after a day on dirt roads or at the beach.

A dual-cylinder motor and active cooling system give the S6 a true 100 percent duty cycle, so you don’t have to wait between tires for the unit to cool down. At 1.5 cfm, it fills a 31-inch tire in about a minute and maxes out at 160 psi. Seven preset modes and automatic shutoff at the target pressure make the Vortex S6 easy to use, and the gauge is accurate to within ±1 psi. The air chuck includes a built-in deflation valve for real-time pressure adjustments, so you can dial in the exact pressure.

Beyond tires, the S6 doubles as a power bank with USB-C and USB-A ports—the USB-C handles 45-watt fast charging in both directions—and has a 1,000-lumen LED with SOS and strobe modes. It comes with both high-pressure and high-volume hoses, the latter of which helps for inflating air mattresses, pool floats, and other low-pressure items. A Presta valve adapter, ball needle, and carry bag round out the kit. At about 7.9 pounds, it’s heavier than pocket-size inflators but lighter than you’d expect given the battery and motor inside.

Having tested the Battery Tender 800 AMP Jump Starter and Tire Inflator as part of a recent roundup of portable jump starters, and because I was so impressed with it, this became part of my family’s vehicle must-haves. Along with an emergency kit, something every motorist should carry, this is another trusted essential.

The jump starter can crank any 12-volt engine up to 6.0-liters gas and 3.0-liter diesel while the air compressor has an inflation pressure of up to 140 psi, and comes with adaptors for bikes and toys, a 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A outlet for charging devices such as phones, LED flashlight, and zippered soft-shell carrying case.

In addition to saving space by combining two devices into one small, lightweight package, I also like the Battery Tender 800’s intuitive interface. And I found that its built-in battery didn’t discharge as quickly as the Gooloo GT160 Dual that also uses a built-in rechargeable battery.

On the downside, this device has the shortest inflation cord of any units we tested and the inflation hose heated up, with the clamp-on chuck getting hot enough to burn Wraight’s finger when he disconnected it.

This device is small but mighty. It’s versatile, too, with preset modes for filling car, motorcycle, and bike tires as well as sports balls and other inflatables. There's a custom mode for anything else with a convenient auto shut off once a preset pressure is reached.

This inflator also has the only LED color display of any of the units tested, with 2000 nits of brightness, making it visible even in direct sunlight. A rotating indicator ring monitors tire pressure and tracks inflation in real-time. The device also has an LED flashlight and comes with adaptors like an inflation needle, Presta valve, and storage bag.

While its dual-chamber design and 160-psi rating quickly fill a tire, we noticed that going from 20 to 40 psi drained the built-in battery from 100 percent to 50 percent. That said, if you have more than one tire to fill, you’ll probably have to recharge the inflator using the supplied USB-A to USB-C adaptor. At just 20 inches, it also had the second-shortest inflation hose.

If you’re an off-roader, the Viair 88P is the perfect choice. It’s specifically designed for use with everything from large 4x4 trucks and other off-road vehicles like ATVs, side-by-sides, and dirt bikes, as well as average cars and SUVs, to balls, air mattresses, and inflatable SUPs. It is powered by a vehicle’s battery via alligator clips, so it is always ready if your vehicle has a good battery.

While priced slightly above some of the lower-cost inflators here, the Viair 88P doesn’t skimp on either quality or features. It comes with a heavy-duty gearless motor and brass twist-on Schrader chuck, and includes an LED flashlight, Presta-valve adaptor, and three other inflation tips. It also has 16-foot air hose, a 10-foot power cord, and comes with a carrying case.

The DeWalt 20V Max is the device to own if you frequently need to inflate items other than tires. It has both a high-pressure mode with automatic shutoff for inflating tires and a high-volume mode for inflating—and deflating—items like air mattresses.

It also has versatile power options using a supplied 12-volt cord that plugs into a car’s cigarette lighter outlet, a DeWalt rechargeable battery sold separately, or an available extra-cost 120-volt cord that plugs into a standard wall outlet. We also liked that the 12-volt power cord, at 13-feet long, still fit neatly into a side compartment.

In testing, we found that it was one of the fastest to inflate tires thanks to its larger battery. Like the Milwaukee M18, the DeWalt 20V Max’s rechargeable 20-volt battery lost little power, and its 36-inch inflator hose didn’t heat up appreciably. Another bonus: It's about 1.5 pounds lighter than the Milwaukee M18 and includes an LED flashlight for nighttime illumination.

I’ve been covering aftermarket automotive products as a journalist for more than three decades, and tested everything from radar detectors to dash cams to tire chains, not to mention more than a thousand new vehicles. I drive a 2015 Thor Majestic motorhome with six tires and tow a daily-driver 2007 Honda Element. Last season I hit a huge pothole at highway speeds and pulled the RV over to find a shredded back tire on the Element—and its temporary donut spare half inflated.

Fortunately, I had a portable tire inflator. I keep it on hand along with jumper cables, a portable jump starter, and an emergency kit. After inflating the spare, switching it out for the tattered tire and with daylight quickly fading on a deserted stretch of Mexico Highway 1, I limped 10 miles to a Pemex station where an attendant phoned his amigo to bring me a replacement tire.

Recently while I was in San Diego, I connected with my Baja surf buddy Adam Wraight, a lifeguard sergeant at Imperial Beach, California. Wraight helped me test these portable tire inflators since he and his crew regularly deflate and inflate the tires of their lifeguard vehicles to drive on the sand. He also shared valuable insights on each of the products I tested given his more than 25 years on duty at the beach and his daily deflate/inflate routine.

I met Adam on a weekday morning, and we ran the tire inflators through their paces by deflating the tires on his 2019 Chevrolet Colorado truck to 20 pounds per square inch (psi), and then inflating to 40 psi. Using the devices I brought with me for review, we evaluated how much time it took to inflate the tires, ease of use, useful features, and how hot the units and their inflation hoses and air chucks got. We also considered the length of each one’s power cables (where applicable) and inflation hoses, as these factors affected use.

In selecting the products to test, I considered how they would be used and who would use them. Consequently, I picked products that fit a range of applications and cover a variety of budgets—everything from the $30 Avid ACAP008 to the $365 Viair 400P-RV, and many in between. I also chose devices that use a variety of power sources with the idea that the average motorist only needs a relatively inexpensive device like the $75 Gooloo GT160 Dual with a built-in rechargeable battery.

Conversely, DIY Pop Mech Pro peeps who probably own portable power tools, and their separate rechargeable batteries, may lean toward the Milwaukee and DeWalt we tested. I also pored over online reviews to see what others had to say about portable tire inflators and read real users’ comments and reviews.

Portable tire inflators are simple devices, and there are two important interrelated, objective specs to be aware of—cfm and psi. Other subjective factors to think about are a portable air inflator’s power source and features like the air-valve connection, display type and memory settings. Here’s more detail below.

Cfm measures the volume of air that the compressor can deliver in one minute and indicates how much air a compressor can move. The higher the cfm spec, the faster a compressor can fill a tire; for portable inflators, a cfm of 1 works for most usage. However, if you are using the compressor often to fill all four tires or you drive a vehicle with large tires, then you might want a device with at least a 2 cfm spec.

Many people know the term psi from filling car and bike tires. It's a measure of the amount of pressure placed on one square inch of space. While cfm measures the amount of air a compressor can deliver in one minute, psi refers to the maximum amount of air it can deliver to an inflatable such as a tire or SUP.

While not a perfect analogy, think of cfm as relative to horsepower produced by a vehicle engine that determines the maximum amount of power it can deliver, while psi is analogous to the top speed the engine can deliver—and cfm and psi work hand in hand.

For most motorists, a portable tire inflator with a maximum capability of 120 psi is plenty. If you drive a bigger rig like my RV, you may want to consider a device with a psi of up to 150.

While cfm and psi are straightforward and easy to compare, how a portable tire inflator gets power depends on your needs, how often you’ll use the device, and if you have other portable devices that use compatible rechargeable batteries.

The portable tire inflators tested here rely on one of four power sources: a built-in rechargeable battery, 12 volts by plugging into a car’s cigarette lighter, 12.6-14.7 volts by connecting to a car’s battery via jumper cables, or 18 volts from a portable battery that’s the same used to power portable tools such as drills, saws, and sanders.

For the occasional roadside emergency, a low-cost portable tire inflator with a built-in rechargeable battery, or one that plugs into your car’s 12-volt cigarette lighter outlet, is adequate. The two Viair devices we tested that connect to a car’s battery both supplied impressive inflation power, but if you frequently air up tires—or are a gear guy or gal who owns a set of portable power tools—you may want to consider the higher power provided by a portable battery.

Keep in mind: With portable tire inflators that plug into a car’s cigarette lighter or connect directly to a car’s battery for power, you won't have to worry about not having a portable battery available or making sure a device with a built-in rechargeable battery is topped off. That is, unless you are unlucky enough to also have a flat tire and a dead battery, in which case a combo device like the Battery Tender 800 AMP Jump Starter and Tire Inflator is ideal.

While portable tire inflators are uncomplicated devices with few features, pay particular attention to the length of the power cables and inflation hose. With devices that plug into a car’s 12-volt outlet or connect to the battery, make sure the power cord is long enough to reach the rear tires.

Similar, although less critical, is the length of the air inflation hose. It can make the difference between easily filling a tire and wishing for a longer hose when dealing with a flat tire. The units we tested have hoses ranging from as short as just over 15 inches to as long as 30 feet.

Portable tire inflators also come with two types of Schrader chucks, the name for the connection that fits on the valve that’s standard on most car tires. A clamp-type (or push-on) chuck connects to a tire valve with a quick-release sleeve, and is faster and easier to use than screw-on chucks but can be less airtight.

Screw-on chucks that twist onto a tire’s valve stem provide a more secure, airtight connection that’s less prone to leaks, but take a bit longer to attach and remove. The Viair 400P-RV was an exception, with a convenient quick-disconnect Schrader chuck.

Finally, every portable tire inflator tested for this roundup has a digital display and the ability to dial in the desired tire pressure so you can set and forget it while filling a tire. All the portable tire inflators tested here can also be set for kPa and bar air-pressure measurements. In addition to a Schrader chuck, they all come with a Presta valve to fill a bike tire, an inflation needle for sports balls, and various other attachments.

Which of these is the best power source: a separate battery, a rechargeable battery, a 12-volt outlet plug, or battery clamps?

It depends how you intend to use your portable tire inflator along with other factors. For example, if you already own portable power tools that use a rechargeable battery, like the Milwaukee and DeWalt devices tested here, and/or want the maximum inflation power and use the devices frequently, that’s the way to go.

On the other hand, devices that connect to a car’s battery or 12-volt outlet for power or have an internal rechargeable battery are less powerful but also less expensive since you don’t need an extra battery. Devices like the DeWalt 20V MAX that run off a separate battery and have a 12-volt cord that plugs into a car’s cigarette lighter are the most versatile.

Do I need a separate inflator for tires and one for accessories?

Not really, since one inflator can serve dual duty for inflating a tire and, say, an air mattress. All the devices tested in this article except the DeWalt 20V MAX are designed mainly for high-pressure inflation.

They can fill things like air mattress and inflatable SUPs that require a large amount of air volume to fill quickly, but use low pressure. If you want to best of both worlds, go for a combo high-pressure/high-volume inflator like the DeWalt 20V MAX.

What is the difference between an air compressor and a tire inflator?

They both push air and can be used to fill a tire and other items. Here is the difference: An air compressor is a more powerful and expensive tool designed for tasks such as inflating large truck tires or running air tools, and usually used by tradesmen and mechanics, while a tire inflator is a smaller, portable, and less expensive device.

It is specifically for inflating car tires such as bike tires, sports equipment, and air mattress. Portable tire inflators are convenient since they are often run off a car's 12-volt power outlet, battery, or a rechargeable battery.

Depending on the quality of the device, frequency of use, and maintenance, a portable tire inflator can last anywhere from 5 to 20 years. My top pick, the Milwaukee M18 Portable Tire Inflator 2848-20, has a five year warranty.

Where is the best place to store this in my car?

I keep mine with my tool kit and emergency road kit in the cargo area of my Honda Element or with similar gear in the Thor Majestic RV. It can also easily be stored in a trunk. Just make sure that if your tire inflator has a rechargeable battery that you check in on it often.

#6368. Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A century-old pollution trail leads scientists back to Montana mining

At the turn of the twentieth century, the Anaconda Smelter in Montana spewed arsenic into the air — those heavy metal particles that are now trapped in Arctic ice cores.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting company in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

Joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

In the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

The largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a big hint, McConnell says, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, says Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”

Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data showed, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell says, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”

These new findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”

#6367. Staying social may keep an older mind sharp, but not every kind of activity counts

Among social activities older adults join, volunteering and sports clubs were linked to better memory in 24 countries. Church groups were not.

Older adults who volunteer or belong to a sports club tend to do better on memory and thinking tests than people who join nothing. The gap grows with each extra kind of social activity they take on.

The benefit didn’t show up evenly, though. Volunteering and sports clubs were linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline in all five national surveys studied. Church groups and political groups were not consistently linked to any gain.

Behind the pattern are the records of nearly 58,000 people in 24 countries, followed for about six years. The authors describe it as the first analysis to pool five national aging surveys to understand the impact of social connection.

Jiahong Sun of Guangdong Medical University and Bo Xi of Shandong University led the work with first author Yuedong Wang. It’s an observational study, so it can show that joiners scored higher, not that joining caused the higher scores.

In an interview with Earth.com, Sun said the practical message is about variety and sticking with it. “A practical step would be to take part in a few sustainable activities, ideally including three or more types of social engagement,” he said.

Social activities, he suggested, might include volunteering, joining a sports club, attending a training course or spending meaningful time caring for children..

The findings of earlier studies on the effect of social engagement disagreed with each other.

The Rush Memory and Aging Project linked higher social engagement to a five-year delay in the onset of cognitive impairment. A Dutch study of about 2,000 people found no link.

The authors suspected small samples, under 3,000 people, and inconsistent ways of measuring social life.

So Wang’s team pooled five long-running surveys of people in middle age and beyond. Three of them are the Health and Retirement Study in the United States, the English Longitudinal Study of Aging, and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study.

The Mexican Health and Aging Study and the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe complete the set.

The European survey alone supplied almost half of the 57,793 participants. Median ages ran from 57 in the Chinese survey to 73 in the American one.

Each survey asked people whether they had taken part in social groups over the past month or the past year.

Memory was tested by having people recall a short list of words, right away and again later. Thinking was tested with tasks like counting backward from 100 by sevens or naming as many animals as possible in one minute.

Because the tests differed, the researchers converted every score onto one common scale, so a result from Mexico could be compared with one from England.

On that scale, people who took part in at least one social activity scored higher than people who took part in none, in all five surveys.

Each added kind of activity came with a higher score. People who kept up three or more scored more than twice as far above the inactive group as people with just one activity did.

The three-or-more group’s advantage also grew over time. Their scores improved a little faster each year than the inactive group’s did, and that extra yearly gain showed up on the memory test.

On the thinking tasks, the yearly difference was too small to separate from chance.

What the study measured was test scores, not dementia diagnoses. The authors described the trend as a dose-response pattern: more kinds of social contact, higher scores.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised him about which activities helped, Sun pointed to two that showed the same link everywhere and several that didn’t.

Volunteering and sports club membership were linked to better cognitive scores in all five surveys. Attending training courses and caring for children were linked to faster yearly gains.

Political groups, community groups, church groups, and religious groups showed no consistent link across the surveys.

“This does not mean that these activities are harmful or ineffective; their associations may depend on the social and cultural context in which they occur,” Sun said.

Why would an active social life protect thinking? The authors offered three possibilities. Activities that demand attention may keep brain connections in use. This idea is often summed up as “use it or lose it.”

Social contact may add to the mental reserve that education builds up over a lifetime. And meaningful activity may lower chronic stress, which harms the brain region that handles memory.

The association was not the same for everyone. Sun said it appeared stronger among women, adults aged 60 or older, people with at least a high school education, and people without depressive symptoms.

It was also stronger among people who lived alone, were of normal weight, or lived in rural areas.

Two more groups that made the list puzzled the authors: current smokers and people who drank alcohol.

One possibility they raised is that smokers and drinkers may do their socializing in organized groups, the kind that keep a mind busy. They called that reading speculative and the whole set of subgroup results exploratory.

For people over 60, the authors’ explanation is plainer. After retirement, people have more free time for groups.

People were asked about their social activities once, at the start. The analysis assumed those habits held for the next six years., but this was not checked.

The thinking tests also differed from country to country, so a score in China and a score in England don’t measure exactly the same skill.

And people who were already sharper may have been the ones who joined clubs in the first place, which would make the clubs look better than they are.

The analysis adjusted for age, education, depression, loneliness, and several other factors, but the authors wrote that other differences between joiners and non-joiners could still explain part of the gap.

Dementia is the stake behind all of this. In 2019, about 57 million people were living with it, and the authors cited projections of nearly 153 million by 2050.

With no effective treatment available, they wrote, finding risk factors that people can change is a public health priority.

The study counted how many kinds of activity a person did. It didn’t ask whether they enjoyed them, led them, or how often they went.

“Our next steps are to examine not only the number of social activities, but also their quality, purpose, level of personal involvement and emotional experience,” Sun told Earth.com.

He added that future research should also test whether programs that get older adults into sustained social activity actually improve their cognitive health.

Until a study like that runs, the evidence is a pattern across six years and 24 countries. Whether joining is what makes the difference, or whether sharper people are the ones joining, remains an unanswered question.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health.
