The powerful Euclid space telescope is making the largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos, and ESA has just shared the first enormous piece of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery."

Captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.

Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

In its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, said in the statement. "That day is finally here."

The "grand design" spiral galaxy M81, imaged by Euclid.

The Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

The ring galaxy NGC 1291, imaged close up at Euclid's highest resolution.

Among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid shows a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.

Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

The first piece of the Euclid Wide Survey, covering about 14% of the total sky area that the telescope plans to survey.

This image shows the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

With about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.

#6365. The 7 Best Car Battery Chargers for Roadside Emergencies

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Maintain your car battery—or bring a dead one back to life.

The 12-volt battery is one of the least complex components in modern vehicles but one of the most crucial. If it’s not in good condition, the engine won’t start, and none of the vehicle’s fancy systems will work. Car batteries have a limited lifecycle and deteriorate with time. This can happen for many reasons, including extended inactivity, extreme temperatures, or even something as simple as accidentally leaving the lights on after you turn off the engine.

That’s why it’s handy to have an external car battery charger so your engine is ready to go when you need it. A charger can also help extend your battery's life, for instance, in a vehicle you don't drive often—a weekend getaway camper or an old classic cruiser. Some chargers also have a jumpstart feature, eliminating the need for jumper cables (and the inconvenience of a required second vehicle).

You might be surprised to hear that electric vehicles use the same 12-volt car batteries as their internal combustion counterparts. Regardless, modern vehicles rely on this ancillary battery to power lights and onboard electronics when the ignition is off. Here, we’ve compiled the best chargers for cars and motorcycles, including everything from a solar-powered charger to a model that can revive several vehicles at once.

Noco’s Genius 10, the brand’s flagship single-vehicle charger, offers many cool features, including the ability to “force charge” a battery so dead it won't generate any voltage when you hook it up. (Most modern chargers won’t do this.) Maintenance and “desulfation” modes extend your battery's useful life while keeping it ready to go.

Unlike smaller, less ambitious chargers, the Genius 10 charges a vehicle battery to full power in the shortest safe time. It can even charge the new generation of lithium-ion car batteries, like the complex, expensive units fitted to many newer BMWs.

All the basic features are here at a very low price, including protection from reverse clamping and a “float mode” for fully charged batteries.

The included set of bolt-on leads lets you quickly connect and disconnect the charger. Operation couldn’t be simpler: a green light shows the Motopower is on, and a red light indicates charging status. With 1.5 amps of power, it charges slightly faster than most competitors in the low-price bracket.

Think of this 15-amp charger as a miniature version of the shop-grade Schumacher. It’s also the form and function that will be most familiar to older or experienced users. The included clamps are high-quality and should fit most cars. Just clamp on, plug in, and select one of three modes.

The 15-amp rapid charge is slightly more than the competition can manage, and a carrying handle makes it easy to place where you want it.

This charger is compact, light, easy to operate, and almost bombproof. It delivers a 3-amp charge, then automatically switches to float mode to maintain proper voltage and prevent overcharging.

A two-color LED indicates charging status, and if the battery voltage drops below a certain level, it resumes full charging output in adaptive mode. It’s compatible with most automotive batteries and can switch between 6- and 12-volt batteries with the push of a button. Its battery clamps are spark-proof, and the Battery Tender 3-Amp will automatically detect reverse polarity. It comes with a 5-year warranty and lifetime customer service.

Dealerships and race shops that used to scatter CTEK individual chargers throughout the building are now switching to the multi-vehicle Noco 2x4 model. It weighs just under 8 pounds, mounts to a wall, and can handle four vehicles at the same time, each in a different mode.

Want to float charge one car, recondition another, and bring two other dead batteries back to life in force-charge mode? Not a problem.

If you own a vehicle you only drive occasionally, an under-the-hood charger saves the hassle of disconnecting it from the battery and storing it each time you want to go for a cruise.

The compact Schumacher SC1300 mounts under the hood to supply up to 1.5 amps, while a built-in microprocessor automatically adjusts the charging rate to maintain an ideal charge state. Float mode delivers a small current when needed.

Reverse hook-up protection prevents the charger from working if the battery clamps are installed in reverse polarity, and the Schumacher automatically detects 6-volt or 12-volt batteries.

If an electrical outlet isn’t available or if you just want to use the sun to keep your battery topped off, the Sun Energize solar-powered charger is a reliable option. It trickle-charges a variety of automotive batteries, as well as some lithium batteries.

A built-in charge controller prevents overcharging; charging stops when a battery is topped off and automatically resumes when it drains.

An LED indicator shows charge and battery conditions. The 20.1 x 13.8 x 0.7-inch solar panel is larger than the other chargers here, but it’s built to handle high winds and heavy loads and is IP65 waterproof.

We tested some external battery chargers under varying weather conditions, while others were chosen based on feedback from car enthusiast friends. The selections represent a wide variety of chargers with different capabilities to match a broad range of use cases. We have years of experience traveling the country with these chargers and know their performance very well.

If you store a vehicle for long periods, you’ll want a charger to keep the battery from fully dying and turning into a paperweight. (It’s also nice to know it will start without jumper cables.) But a battery charger can make a difference in plenty of other situations.

If you regularly experience below-freezing temperatures at night, a charger with a maintenance function can significantly extend your battery's life. If you rarely drive more than a few miles at a time, a charger can prevent your battery from discharging too far—leaving you with a no-start condition. Last but not least, older vehicles often struggle to recharge slightly depleted batteries on the move, so starting the day with a fully charged battery can also extend the life of your alternator and charging system.

Charging power is traditionally measured in amps. Think of amps as the amount of juice that can be put back into the battery at any given time; for example, a 10-amp charger puts twice as much charge into the battery as a 5-amp one. A quick stroll through a listing of battery chargers can be confounding, though. Some have 40 amps, and some have 0.75 amps, and yet they do the same thing. In reality, the difference is easy to understand. The more power a charger has, the more quickly it can bring a dead battery back to life. The tradeoff is cost, size, and weight.

If you’re charging a small motorcycle battery or maintaining a good-condition battery in a cherished collector car, then a 0.75-amp charger will do just fine. If you’re worried that your pickup won’t start in the winter, 2 to 10 amps is a better bet. Any capability above that is mostly for mechanics who need to quickly charge or recondition batteries in the shop.

Every charger here can “maintain” a charged battery, keeping it from slowly discharging between uses. Most chargers can also bring a depleted battery back up to full power. A few chargers offer specialized modes like “desulfation,” which helps a battery regain its chemical balance through carefully timed charge-and-discharge cycles. A “quick charge” can very rapidly (but safely) prepare a battery for use. A few battery chargers also offer a “jump start mode” that can start a car or motorcycle with a dead battery, but this is rare, and most of the time you’ll need a separate jump starter for that task.

Most chargers in this roundup are designed for conventional lead-acid (flooded cell) or Absorbent Glass Mat (AGM) batteries, which you’ll find in newer vehicles. If you have a vehicle with a lithium-ion battery, like some new BMWs, or a customized car with ultra-compact batteries from manufacturers like Braille, you’ll need a charger with that capability—different battery chemistries require specific charging protocols.

If you are dealing with a cramped garage, or travel between storage spaces throughout the seasons, consider a “wall wart” or direct-mount charger. The former keeps all the charging mechanisms in a large plug that some people might compare to model-train transformer plugs. The latter bolts into your car and plugs directly into the wall.

Not anymore. Today's smart chargers, like the ones in our article, won't overcharge a battery or give it more than it can handle. And choosing a more powerful charger won't shorten your battery's lifespan; quite the opposite, in fact!

It's usually as simple as removing the bolt from both battery clamps, slipping the thin copper loops between the bolt and washer, and reinstalling. Then you can coil the quick-disconnect cord in a convenient place, like inside a motorcycle fairing or under a car hood. The cables can melt when exposed to serious heat, so don't let them touch an exhaust pipe.

Yes, if the batteries are in reasonably decent condition. Any charger rated at 2 Amps or more should be able to rotate between multiple vehicles. If you have more than three or four, consider buying multiple chargers.

#6364. A tourist’s vacation photo of a yellow flower helped botanists catalog a completely new species

A new yellow-flowered plant species discovered through an iNaturalist photo in Portugal's Algarve faces threats from invasive trees and habitat loss.

A yellow toadflax that grows almost only in the hills of Monchique, in Portugal’s Algarve region, has been described as a new species, Linaria alfercensis.

Botanists first noticed it in a photo that a visitor to the area posted on iNaturalist. The citizen science platform lets people share pictures of wild plants and animals.

João Farminhão of the University of Coimbra’s Centre for Functional Ecology (CFE) described the species in August 2026 with four colleagues from Portugal and Spain. Its flowers “did not match any described taxon in corolla colour pattern,” the team wrote.

The iNaturalist record came from Castelo de Alferce, in the municipality of Monchique. The plant clearly belonged to a group of toadflaxes called Linaria subsection Versicolores.

This observation prompted dedicated fieldwork in the Monchique Igneous Complex in 2024 and 2025.

On April 4, 2024, André Carapeto of the Portuguese Botanical Society collected the plant that became the holotype, the reference specimen for the species. He found it at an elevation of 1,027 feet (313 meters).

The holotype is kept in the herbarium of the University of Coimbra, with a duplicate at the Royal Botanical Garden in Madrid.

The plant had been collected before without being recognized. Herbarium specimens gathered in 1995 and 1996 near Picota and in the Odelouca valley belong to the new species.

The name honors the civil parish of Alferce, where the species was first recognized.

The flower is deep yellow, with two orange to brownish-red stripes along the throat that split at the tip. The palate, the bulge that closes the mouth of the flower, is orange and often spotted with brownish red.

Flowers usually measure 0.8 to 0.9 inch (21 to 24 millimeters) long, including the spur. The erect flowering stems usually reach 6.7 to 15 inches (17 to 38 centimeters).

The plant flowers and sets fruit from March to May. Its seeds are black to blackish gray and measure 0.02 to 0.03 inch (0.4 to 0.8 millimeter).

Its closest relatives are Linaria algarviana, which has violet-purple flowers, and Linaria bimaculata, whose throat stripes are rounded at the tip. Together, the three form a group of toadflaxes found only in the Algarve.

Its fruit capsules are longer than those of these two relatives, usually measuring 0.13 to 0.15 inch (3.4 to 3.8 millimeters).

Farminhão and Carapeto raised Linaria bimaculata to species rank in a 2024 study of Algarve toadflaxes, drawing on 78 iNaturalist records. Many of those records had first been uploaded under another species name.

The Iberian branch of Linaria subsection Versicolores includes at least ten species. Toadflaxes belong to the tribe Antirrhineae of the plantain family, Plantaginaceae.

The new species grows mostly on soils derived from nepheline syenite, an igneous rock that makes up most of the Monchique Igneous Complex.

It occurs on the southern slopes of Serra da Picota, along the Odelouca river basin and near Marmelete. It favors annual meadows on gravel and sandy soils in clearings and on the edges of rocky heathland, often among boulders.

The researchers combined DNA analysis, using a method called genotyping-by-sequencing, with a near-complete review of herbarium specimens. They also compared where these toadflaxes grow with geological maps.

Records from iNaturalist entered the analysis only if they were classified as reliable after a check of their photos. Most also had a location accurate to within about 490 feet (150 meters).

Sandstone, coarse sand, igneous rocks and windblown sand plains act as soil “islands” for these plants, while limestone, fine sands, shales and graywackes appear to work as barriers.

Together with shifts in flower color and shape, this pattern points to a role for geographic isolation and inferred soil specialization in the group’s diversification.

The authors propose a preliminary listing as Endangered under criterion B of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). The listing reflects the species’ small geographic range, declining habitat quality and few locations.

The species’ extent of occurrence covers about 34.6 square miles (89.6 square kilometers). It is known from four locations, and its area of occupancy is about 17 square miles (44 square kilometers).

Each locality holds fewer than 50 flowering plants, although the total population cannot be reliably estimated.

The main threat is believed to be the invasive silver wattle, Acacia dealbata, whose spread has intensified after recurrent wildfires. Native to southeastern Australia, it is legally listed as an invasive species in Portugal.

The species has also lost habitat to eucalyptus plantations in the past. Forestry work, including road widening and timber storage, threatens plants along road verges, as does tourist development on the Picota slopes near Covão da Águia.

The study was published in the journal Plant Ecology and Evolution.

#6363. A strange red speck captured by Webb looked like a candidate for the earliest galaxy ever seen, but now it seems to be moving like a brown dwarf

Capotauro, a candidate early galaxy, moved 0.13 arcseconds in 3.5 years. Astronomers now say it is a cold brown dwarf in the Milky Way.

In December 2022, the James Webb Space Telescope photographed a strip of sky for the CEERS survey and recorded a compact red point that, according to the latest analysis, is a brown dwarf inside the Milky Way.

Astronomers later named the point Capotauro and calculated that its light might have left a galaxy about 100 million years after the Big Bang.

Webb returned to the same field in June 2026, and the point was no longer in the same place.

A team led from the University of Edinburgh’s Institute for Astronomy (IFA) says that rules out a distant galaxy, although the object’s distance of roughly 2,400 light-years remains an estimate.

CEERS, the Cosmic Evolution Early Release Science survey, covered a field in a region called the Extended Groth Strip.

Giovanni Gandolfi and his colleagues picked out the object, catalogued as U-100588. They named it Capotauro after the old name of Corno alle Scale, a mountain in the Italian Apennines.

Capotauro appeared only in the reddest filters of Webb’s NIRCam camera and vanished at shorter wavelengths. Astronomers call such an object a dropout, because it drops out of the bluer images.

Distant galaxies can behave this way, since hydrogen in the early universe absorbs their shorter wavelengths. Among the extragalactic options, Gandolfi’s team favored a redshift of about 32.

Redshift is a measurement of how far its light has been stretched by cosmic expansion. The confirmed record at the time stood near redshift 14, held by a galaxy seen 280 million years after the Big Bang.

That team also listed a very cold brown dwarf or a free-floating planet as possibilities, and it said the observations could not settle the question. The doubt was raised early, and an impostor closer to home stayed on the table.

Two Webb programs, MINERVA and SPAM, covered the same field in mid-to-late June 2026. Their medium-band images gave the Edinburgh group, with first author Fengyuan Liu, a second epoch about 3.5 years after the discovery data.

Galaxies at such distances do not show measurable motion across the sky over a few years, while objects in the Milky Way can.

Liu’s team measured Capotauro’s position in four images, F410M and F444W from December 2022 and F430M and F460M from June 2026. It had moved by 132 milliarcseconds, give or take 20, which is about 0.13 arcseconds.

For scale, that angle equals the width of a US quarter seen from about 24 miles (38 kilometers). The detection reached more than 6 sigma, a statistical level that leaves very little room for chance.

A shift that small can be faked by misaligned images, so the team built a local reference frame. It used 68 isolated, compact sources within 3 arcminutes of Capotauro, most of them galaxies, and solved for the alignment of all four images together.

The team then tested the noise under the object. The researchers planted artificial moving sources at 75 blank positions near Capotauro, ran 1,200 trials, and checked how far the noise pushed each recovered position.

The paper states that the data “completely exclude” any extragalactic source. That covers a galaxy and a black hole-powered nucleus, and also a proposal by Ferrara and colleagues that the light came from a giant supernova at redshift 15.

The new images also showed no significant change in brightness over 3.5 years, which counts against a supernova. Liu’s group found one more problem in the record.

It reports that its own brightness values differ from the earlier ones by as much as 58 percent, and it suggests the earlier measurement may have been too high because its aperture was oversized.

The team compared the object’s brightness across filters with templates of known cold brown dwarfs. The best match was spectral type Y1, with a temperature near 350 Kelvin, or about 170 degrees Fahrenheit (77 degrees Celsius).

NASA describes Y dwarfs as the coldest class of brown dwarfs, objects that never gathered enough mass to shine as ordinary stars. Webb has found brown dwarfs only about twice the mass of Jupiter in a young star-forming cluster.

Most known Y dwarfs lie within 30 parsecs, about 98 light-years. One of the coldest, WISE 0855, sits just 7.5 light-years from the Sun.

Capotauro’s estimated distance is 730 parsecs, with an uncertainty of 110, or about 2,400 light-years. The authors call it “one of the most distant Y dwarfs found to date.”

Combined with its motion, that distance gives a sideways speed of about 82 miles (132 kilometers) per second. Such a speed may mark an old object from the Milky Way’s thick disk, the authors wrote.

Maruša Bradač and her colleagues found two candidates beyond redshift 30 near the Bullet cluster, and spectra and motion measurements pointed to cold brown dwarfs instead.

Kevin Hainline’s group had reached similar photometric fits for Capotauro in a study of cold dwarfs in deep Webb fields, placing it about 1,600 light-years away.

Liu’s team explains why the confusion lands at that redshift. Water, methane and ammonia in a Y dwarf’s atmosphere can erase almost all its light through the F356W filter.

The brightness then climbs sharply near 4 to 5 microns. Read as a hydrogen break in a galaxy, that rise gives a redshift of about 30 to 32.

The authors recommend that future searches include cold brown dwarf templates and compare images from different years.

The 2,400 light-year figure is not a direct geometric measurement. Webb’s images could not pin down Capotauro’s parallax, the small annual shift that reveals distance, and the team derived the figure by scaling template brightness.

The template library stops at type Y1. Capotauro could therefore be colder and closer than the estimate, which would also lower its calculated speed.

A third set of Webb images, timed for parallax, could fix the distance. The object is so faint that detailed spectroscopy would be “inherently impractical,” the authors wrote.

In the June 2026 images, Capotauro was still a red point, about 0.13 arcseconds from where Webb recorded it in December 2022.

The study has been accepted by the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society and posted online as an advance article, before copyediting and typesetting. A preprint is also on arXiv.

#6362. The 5 Best Gas Snowblowers Can Move Mountains (of Snow)

Too much snow to shovel? A snowblower offers the most power and the longest runtime.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Winter will be here before you know it, which means the best time to prepare for cold weather and potential snowstorms is now. While snowfall isn't as regular in many parts of the country as it used to be, storm systems can still dump big piles of snow at once. When it comes time to dig out, there are few tools as effective as a gas-powered snowblower.

Although electric snowblowers are certainly attractive—they are relatively lightweight, easy to use, and require little maintenance—they lack the raw power and long runtime you’ll need if a storm drops 18 inches of snow or more on your home, especially if you have a large driveway.

The best gas snowblowers can carve a path as wide as two feet—giving you plenty of room to walk through as much as 21 inches of snow on a single pass. And if you keep a spare tank handy, you should have more than enough runtime to clear your walks and driveway multiple times. If you’re in the market for a heavy-duty snow removal machine, we’ve researched and tested plenty. These are our top picks, plus a breakdown of everything you need to know to pick out the best gas snowblower for your home.

If you have a large driveway and get a lot of snow, this is the machine you want. This big Ariens has a 30-inch-wide clearing path and an ideal clearing depth of 18 inches. Its four-stroke gas engine means no fussing with mixed fuel, and the push-button electric start means you don't have to exhaust yourself with a recoil starter.

This is a stout machine that is made for working. Test Editor Brad Ford runs a similar machine on his property, which is extra demanding because he has a gravel driveway. Thankfully, this machine can handle gravel surfaces thanks to its adjustable skid shoes, which allow extra clearance between the base of the auger and the driveway.

This machine is not for everybody; smaller properties will be well-served by the smaller picks below. But for those with the capacity for this kind of snowblower, this Ariens is a solid choice.

This model from Champion Power Equipment lists at $899, which is a good price point considering many two-stage snowblowers are more than $1,000. But it’s not short on features. This model gives you push-button electric start, a self-propelled drive system, remote chute control, and an LED headlight for clearing snow at night. After all, the snow doesn’t always stop falling during work hours.

It also handles fairly deep snowfall with a 24-inch width and a 20.5-inch height. To help keep the blades safe on uneven terrain, you can adjust the height to handle that, or clear areas like gravel paths. Another feature we really like is the ability to turn the wheels 180 degrees to help make tighter turns. Features like that can’t always be found at this price point, which is why it’s our pick for a snowblower that packs a lot of value.

A medium-sized property that only gets a moderate amount of guaranteed snowfall each year doesn’t need a two-stage snowblower. A single-stage model is fully capable of clearing your driveway and sidewalks. This model from Toro has plenty of power to get that job done, with a 212-cc engine that should cut through even wet snow and throw it up to 35 feet away. This model is also self-propelled to help you do the pushing.

Some of the features we like on it are a trigger and slide that can change the direction of the discharge chute from the handle and a push-button electric start—both make operating it a little bit easier.

Like most single-stage snowblowers, its intake is lower than a two-stage, so you can only expect to clear snowfall up to 10 inches. If you commonly get much higher than that, you’ll want a more robust snowblower, but if you only have a few moderate snow events each winter, this Toro will get the job done.

The Toro SnowMaster 824 QXE stands apart from other single-stage gas snowblowers because of its intuitive controls and powerful engine. With a 252-cc engine, it chews rapidly through snow, carving a 24-inch path through banks up to 18 inches high.

With a lighter, more compact frame and automatic steering, the 824 QXE is easier to maneuver than its dual-stage counterparts. And, unlike most single-stage snowblowers, the auger is slightly elevated, so you can use it on gravel surfaces without having to worry about sucking rocks into it.

This machine also brings lots of special features to make the clearing process easier. Not only is it self-propelled, but it features a “personal pace system” that automatically adjusts the snowblower’s speed to match your walking pace, so you don’t have to fumble with speed controls. If you're familiar with Toro's self-propelled lawn mowers, this system should be familiar.

The snowblower also has a push-button starter and joystick-operated chute control, which makes it easy to adjust your snow output on the fly. If you’re looking for a snowblower to clear up to 18 inches of snow from a small to medium-sized driveway, the SnowMaster 824 QXE is a worthy choice.

This snowblower from Murray is another great example of a two-stage snowblower from a respected company that doesn’t cost more than $1,000. It doesn’t have some of the extra features like our best value pick—namely, a headlight and a 180-degree wheel rotation—but it otherwise matches it in size and power.

It also has all the primary features you would want, including an adjustable chute that lets you aim the snow where you want, push-button electric start, an auger that can propel snow up to 40 feet away, and a self-propel drive with six forward speeds and two reverse speeds.

Something unique to the model, however, is a set of 15-inch snow-terrain tires that handle icy and rocky conditions better than others. Wheels are something other brands can skimp on, but Murray hasn’t done that here. If you have gravel paths or older sidewalks that present a challenge, this model is likely up to the task.

Gas snowblowers are the best tools for heavy-duty snow removal jobs at home. They’re effective against snowbanks piled up to two feet high, and can clear out larger areas, including wide driveways and walking paths. If you live somewhere that gets hit by many large snowstorms each season, and you’ve got a considerable-sized area to clear, then this is what you need.

Not everyone needs a gas snowblower, though. For homes with smaller needs, they may feel like more trouble than they’re worth. Gas-powered machines require more maintenance. Plus, they’re usually quite heavy, which makes them hard to use on tiered walkways with steps. If heavy snow is a rare occurrence, we’d recommend going with an electric snowblower instead, which will be more nimble and won’t produce any fumes.

Most gas snowblowers feature either a single-stage or two-stage mechanism, depending on how the snowblower collects, processes, and expels snow.

Also known as “snow throwers,” they use an auger to pull in snow, break it up, and throw the snow out through the chute in a single action.

These also use an auger to pull in snow, but then mash it up with a spinning impeller before spitting it out through the chute. Separating the snow-pulling and snow-crushing/throwing mechanisms allows the two-stage snowblowers to move snow more quickly and throw it a longer distance, which can be helpful when clearing larger driveways. These robust machines also work better on gravel, since their augers are slightly elevated and won’t draw rocks into the tines.

With an extra component that requires a more powerful engine to operate properly, two-stage snowblowers are generally larger, making them more difficult to maneuver around tight spaces. If you have a small walkway or gardens with uneven ground to avoid, operating one may feel unwieldy. As you might expect, they also cost more than their single-stage counterparts.

As with deciding between electric and gas snowblowers, consider the size of the area you normally clear before picking a single- or two-stage model. Single-stage snowblowers work well for clearing walking paths and the average-sized two- to four-car paved driveway. Dual-stage models are ideal for clearing deep snow from long paved or gravel driveways.

A snowblower’s clearing width and intake height determine how much snow it can move with each pass. The larger the snowblower’s intake, the more quickly you can get the job done.

Most single-stage gas-powered snowblowers have intakes that range from 22 to 24 inches wide, while two-stage snowblowers can have intakes that are up to 32 inches wide. The height of the snowblower’s intake, which is sometimes referred to as “clearing depth,” indicates the maximum snow depth it can handle. The intake height for a gas snowblower ranges from 18 to 21 inches.

Purchasing the snowblower with the widest, tallest intake may seem like a no-brainer, but keep in mind that there’s a correlation between intake dimensions and the overall size of the snowblower. The largest gas snowblowers will have a harder time maneuvering through tight turns. Ultimately, you should choose the smallest option that can effectively clear the paths you need and the amount of snow you expect to see.

A snowblower's job is to take snow in front of you and move it somewhere out of the way. With a more powerful snowblower, you can send the snow farther away. That’s crucial when you’re clearing out a large space, and you need to pile it up dozens of feet from you. Single-stage gas snowblowers can launch snow up to 40 feet, while two-stage snowblowers have a snow-throwing range of 50 feet or more.

Some gas snowblowers come equipped with a throttle on the dashboard that allows you to adjust the throwing distance by changing the speed of the impeller, allowing you to target a specific snow-piling plot.

Beyond the basics, many gas snowblowers have additional features that make them easier to use. Since they weigh hundreds of pounds, many are self-propelled, so you don’t have to push them forward. Most also have electric starters that eliminate the need to pull a starter cord. Some even have built-in power steering that automatically slows one wheel for easy turning.

Other quality-of-life features abound: You may find dashboard controls that allow you to change the chute direction and snowblower speed with one hand, LED headlights for late-night (or early morning) jobs, and handlebars that heat up to keep your hands nice and toasty as you work.

We selected the best gas snowblowers based on recommendations from the Popular Mechanics test team, as well as research and personal testing experience. Some of our picks were recommended by Popular Mechanics test editor Brad Ford, who has logged hours and hours testing snowblowers over the years. The final lineup includes a mix of single-stage gas-powered models for small to moderate driveways that can house four to six cars, and larger two-stage models that can clear snow from the longer and larger driveways you usually find on rural properties.

There are a few things you need to do to make sure your gas snowblower runs smoothly through the season:

First, check the oil level between each use and top off as needed. You should change the oil once a year, even if you didn’t use your snowblower all winter.

Change the spark plug at the beginning of each season to ensure it starts smoothly. A dirty spark plug can make it difficult to get your snowblower going, especially in extreme cold.

Lastly, small gas engines require plenty of airflow to run smoothly, so check the air filter once a season and replace it if it's dirty.

Snowblowers use unleaded gasoline—the same thing you put in your car—which begins to degrade after about 60 days. Running a snowblower with old fuel can clog the carburetor and make the engine hard to start, so you should never store your snowblower with fuel left in the tank.

Before putting your snowblower to bed for the season, either run the fuel tank dry or add fuel stabilizer, which keeps gasoline fresh for up to 24 months, to the tank. If you use fuel stabilizer, run the snowblower for a minute or two after adding it to the tank to circulate it through the engine.

A snowblower should be able to handle the lion’s share of your snow removal duties, but you should definitely keep a snow shovel around to clean up whatever the snowblower leaves behind. You may also want to save the gas and dig out with a shovel after a light, soft snowfall.

#6361. Gut bacteria cannot see the sun so they use your meal times to control how your body absorbs nutrients

Gut bacteria in mice read mealtimes, not daylight, and tell the intestine when to absorb, helping underfed mice grow and overfed ones get fat.

The body clock is supposed to run on light. Sunrise wakes the brain, and the rest of the body falls in line. But the bacteria in the gut live in the dark.

In mice, a common microbe keeps time another way: it reads when food arrives and tells the cells of the intestine to start absorbing.

The signal is a small molecule the bacterium makes while it digests phytate, a compound in grains, nuts and seeds. The molecule switches on genes that pull amino acids and fats out of a meal.

Give it to undernourished young mice and they grow. Give it to mice on a high-fat diet and they get fatter.

Zheng Kuang, an associate professor of biological sciences at Carnegie Mellon University, led the work from his lab. Colleagues at the University of Pittsburgh, UT Southwestern Medical Center and the Quadram Institute in England took part.

All of it was done in mice and in human gut cells grown in a dish.

In an interview with Earth.com, Kuang said what struck him most was that the bacteria convert the timing of a meal into chemistry.

“Their absolute numbers did not need to change substantially across the day – their metabolic activity changed,” he said.

The bacterium is Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron, one of the most common residents of the human gut.

Kuang’s team raised mice with no gut microbes at all, then gave some of them this one species and nothing else. They sampled the lining of the small intestine around the clock.

Mice eat at night. In the hours after dark, the colonized mice carried more of the bacterial signal molecule in their gut lining than they did in the morning.

Germ-free mice showed no such rise, and neither did mice given a mutant strain missing the enzyme that breaks down phytate.

The bacteria themselves were no more numerous at night than in the morning, Kuang’s team found. What rose was the activity of that one enzyme.

“We are not claiming these bacteria have their own internal clock,” Kuang told Earth.com. “Rather, they respond to feeding cues and produce molecules called inositol phosphates, which activate a protein called HDAC3 in intestinal cells.”

That protein, HDAC3, works inside the cells lining the intestine and helps decide which genes are on.

The bacterial molecule makes it grip a partner protein more tightly, and the pair then turns on a set of transporter genes that carry nutrients across the gut wall.

In colonized mice, 14 amino acids and 14 fatty acids rose in the blood during the feeding hours, while in germ-free mice they stayed low.

Of 248 transporter genes the team tracked, 122 cycled more strongly with the bacterium present, and most of those handle amino acids, sugars or fats.

The body’s master clock genes kept their normal daily rhythm either way. The bacterium didn’t reset the clock; it strengthened the daily rise and fall of the metabolic genes that follow it.

The team then fed mice only during the day, which is their normal sleeping time. The signal molecule fell and the gut’s daily rhythm in gene activity flattened, though the animals ate no less than before.

Mice allowed to eat only at night looked like mice allowed to eat whenever they liked.

The feeding experiment is the result Kuang pointed to when asked what people should take from the work. “The key message is to align your feeding schedule with the natural day-night cycle – eating during your active, daytime hours,” he said.

Artificial light has pushed human eating into the night, he added, and the study suggests that misalignment disrupts the bacterial signals.

Kuang said there was likely a metabolic cost to that disruption. The feeding experiment itself tracked the signal and the gene rhythms, not the mice’s weight.

Young mice were weaned onto a diet with the usual calories but little protein or fat, a model for childhood malnutrition.

Those given the bacterium grew longer bodies and longer thigh bones than those given the mutant strain. They had heavier organs, more amino acids in their blood and better blood sugar control, and they ate the same amount.

The signal molecule on its own did the same, in mice with and without a normal gut community. In mice bred to lack HDAC3 in their gut cells, neither the bacterium nor the molecule helped, and a drug that blocks HDAC3 blunted the effect too.

In a public dataset of children’s stool samples, the bacterium was among 19 species more common in healthy children than in undernourished ones.

Adult mice fed a high-fat, high-sugar diet for 12 weeks gained more weight with the bacterium than with the mutant strain.

They carried more belly fat and liver fat and had higher blood fats and worse blood sugar handling. They absorbed more fat from food and passed less of it in their stool.

Again, the mice lacking HDAC3 in their gut cells showed none of this, and food intake didn’t differ.

Kuang said that double edge is the finding he most wants understood. “This illustrates why it is too simple to label a bacterium as inherently ‘good’ or ‘bad’ – its effects depend on diet and the metabolic state of the host,” he explained.

The team’s reading is evolutionary. A pathway that extracts the most from every meal was an advantage when food was scarce, and the same pathway can work against a body surrounded by high-fat diets.

Whether this bacterium even lives and works in the human small intestine is an open question. The team also could not prove that the signal molecule in the gut cells came from the bacteria rather than from the cells themselves, which make related molecules.

And phytate intake varies from one diet to another, so the signal’s strength probably does too, the authors wrote.

Whether the same signal shifts in people who eat on a jet-lagged or night-shift schedule is a question the study does not reach.

Asked how soon the bacteria could be tested against malnutrition, Kuang said it is too early to give a reliable timeline for human testing.

The next step, he said, is to look for the pathway in human intestinal samples and in children with undernutrition. Until then, the case that mealtimes talk to the gut through its bacteria rests on mice.

The full study was published online in a publication of the Carnegie Mellon University.

#6360. Science to restore speech is moving fast. Here’s what’s next

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Michigan woman uses a brain implant to speak with her neurosurgeon. Efforts to restore speech highlight what’s at stake when we lose opportunities to talk.

Scientists are racing to restore people’s ability to communicate. Powerful AI-based methods to decode speech signals and predict words, along with advances in technology, promise success.

This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me takes listeners through the breadth of scientific efforts to restore words, emotions and even gestures to people who can’t move or talk.

We’ll hear from Casey Harrell, a man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis who can no longer talk. A user of today’s technology, Harrell has a unique perspective on what he’d like to see improved for the technology of tomorrow.

And as season two wraps up, listeners will be left with a reminder of the power of a voice: a piece of comedy from Jules Rodriguez, performed with his voice clone in front of a live crowd.

“Being backstage and then seeing him come out, like, roll out his wheelchair, and everybody goes nuts because they’re like, ‘What is going on here? This doesn’t make sense,’” says Jules’ wife, Maria Aleandra Fernandez. “And every time I was like, ‘This is life. This is love. This is passion. What else is there?’ I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here.”

Laura Sanders: OK, I want to ask who your favorite comedians are and why. Who makes you all laugh?

Jules Rodriguez: Pete Holmes and Mike Birbiglia are some of my favorites.

[Audio] He was just like, I’m a bear, et cetera.

[Audio] The best part of sleep is falling asleep. That’s the only part you’re there for.Jules: Their styles are different, but I have always gravitated towards their authenticity.

Sanders: There’s another comedian who is extra meaningful for Jules: Conan O’Brien.

[Audio] Today is a bit of a different sort of episode. I’ll be talking to Jules and Maria.

Sanders: After MA had reached out, Conan invited the couple onto his podcast, where they connected about comedy. Conan still checks in on Jules every so often.

[Audio] It’s incredible to me that in our conversations, you’re very frank about the pain that you go through, and how intense it is. But you’re also always so positive and funny and, frankly, you give me a lot of [beep]. Which I find to be, well I hate it, by the way, first of all. Oh, get over it, Conan.

Jules: Conan is very special to me. Watching and listening to him helped me disconnect from the harsh reality of my life. And when I got to meet him and chat with him, it meant the world to me.

Maria Aleandra Fernandez: Having the most normal conversation with Conan O’Brien is something I will never get over.

[Audio] So he has a bunch of banked phrases. He’s going to play a few of our favorites. OK. I’m fine. I’m perfectly [beep] fine. [laughter] Come on man, are we doing this or not? Oh my God, oh my God. I’m destroying this marriage. MA: He really is so genuine and like, not only willing to talk to us, but really looks forward to talking. Like, I love talking to you guys. I’m not just doing it to be a nice person, which feels, you know, feels wonderful.

[Audio] You have my love, my respect and we’re thinking about you guys all the time.

Sanders: As you were talking earlier, it made me think about what it means to make somebody laugh and to entertain them, and like how actually very, very special that must be. Just kind of, at its heart, it’s, it is joy and humans connecting. And so, extra special.

MA: That’s the other thing I’ve learned mainly through Jules, about humor and comedy. And who were we watching yesterday? The NPR interview with Dave Chappelle. [Audio] Dave Chappelle says he is very clear about his role as a comedian.

MA: And Dave Chappelle said something that is so spot-on. He said that comedians are how people metabolize things.

[Audio] We’re like the nation’s kidney. We help everyone metabolize not just facts, but feelings around facts, or ideas. And jokes are just a shorthand for all of that.

MA: And I’m also a nerd and I’ve been reading some Greek tragedies and studying about how, you know, that’s also like the artists that help people metabolize feelings and emotions. And when he said that, I was like, that’s exactly it. And that’s what Jules has done.

It’s something that heals. And it’s not even like it’s self-deprecating. It’s not like, oh, let’s make fun. And the way he does it is so smart and genuine, but also not taking himself seriously. It just disarms everything. You’re just like, oh, OK. And that idea of metabolizing the really hard feelings that come around grief, mortality, losing a person, seeing how he’s trapped in his body, but he chooses not to be trapped in that really big way is so profound.

Sanders: Science is iterative. It builds. It may take a wrong turn or two, but overall, it’s moving toward a deeper understanding of our world and of ourselves.

By using their voices, by telling their stories, by telling their jokes, Jules and MA are helping me, and maybe you too, metabolize the pain – and the joy – of living. Welcome to The Deep End, Talk to Me.

[Voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi.

Sanders: I’m Laura Sanders and today, we’re going to look ahead to what’s coming next for the human voice and efforts to restore it.

Sanders: In some ways, this podcast is a story of progress, of figuring out, little by little, more about the brain, and more about technology and more about people. Today, Jules can type with his eyes, and his son can hear his dad’s voice say I love you. In earlier episodes, you heard from Casey Harrell. Casey can think about saying a word to his daughter, and boom, they’re off playing a game together.

Casey Harrell: So this has kept me still in touch with people and the world, and it is not hyperbole to frame it this way.

Sanders: Casey has ALS and can no longer speak. He volunteered for a clinical trial, and now he has a device implanted in his brain that detects neural patterns as he tries to say a word. This system has changed his life.

Casey: It is the ability to parent my daughter. It is the ability to connect with my wife. It is the ability to make a wry joke with my friends. Timing is everything, and that is why having nothing, this is completely revolutionary.

Sanders: But there aren’t many people like Casey. Leigh Hochberg is the director of the BrainGate clinical trials consortium, the trial that Casey is participating in. I asked him how many people might have participated in similar sorts of research projects. How many people have electrodes in their brain that can help them speak?

Leigh Hochberg: In terms of actually decoding attempted speech, I’m almost sure it’s still less than 10. It may be closer to five or six, so far, and that number undoubtedly is going to increase fairly quickly.

Sanders: So this is a small but growing number. Growing, because we now have a solid scientific understanding of the brain’s speech signals, and other signals too. And neurotech companies are very interested.

Hochberg: About 10 years ago or so, the academic research had de-risked this field sufficiently that it allowed for the entry of now likely a dozen or more companies that are actively pursuing their own version of an implantable brain-computer interface.

What I anticipate will happen, what I guess I hope will happen, is that the companies will continue to very carefully, thoughtfully and in a very focused manner, create their systems, and test them rigorously. And hopefully they’ll be demonstrated to be safe and effective. And at the same time, the academic groups have the opportunity to continue to demonstrate what’s possible, to push beyond that, and to show hopefully what those medical devices, once they’re actually available to market, might be able to do next.

Sanders: I talked with Vikash Gilja, a neural engineer who works at a company called Paradromics. He sees this momentum that Hochberg describes too.

Vikash Gilja: And, you know, we can see all the pieces coming together. These tools weren’t available even five years ago. And what we’re seeing is like, you know, month over month, there are new tools available. So we’re able to leverage those and move faster.

Sanders: Paradromics has developed its own brain-computer interface for communication. The device is about the size of a dime, and it sits on the motor cortex. That’s the part of the brain that creates speech signals. The chip then detects these signals as a person thinks about saying a word.

Matthew Willsey: So the cortical module has 421 tiny little sensors.

Sanders: That’s neurosurgeon and biomedical engineer Matthew Willsey, of the University of Michigan Health. He’s describing the device from Paradromics here.

Willsey: They’re about one and a half millimeters long. And you know, it’s smaller than your thumbnail, like kind of all the way around. It’s like a cylinder. And at the bottom of the cylinder are the electrodes, is what we call them. And we get them really close to the brain. And then when we deploy it, what it does is it pushes those electrodes down into the brain.

Sanders: Those tiny sensors are listening to the nearby neurons that control the muscles required for speech.

Willsey: The principle is to try and get these things as small as possible to disrupt the least amount of tissue as possible, and then to get them really, really close to the individual cells, the neurons themselves that have the information we’re trying to record.

Sanders: The goal here is to restore a person’s ability to talk.

Willsey: So in the ideal situation, the electrodes would sit, you know, right next to those neurons. This type of technology that’s very intuitive, that can record activity from the brain in kind of a high-throughput way, can put the words up at a good speed and a good accuracy, allows them to kind of regain the ability to communicate with others close to how they maybe were before they had the illness. So that truly is very powerful.

Sanders: You might remember that Casey’s implant, called the BrainGate 2 system, requires ports on his head that are connected to external wires.

Casey: What is annoying about this device is really easy to answer. It is not portable, and it is not implanted only inside my head.

Sanders: Unlike Casey’s implant, the Paradromics device is fully implantable. That means it’s wireless. This summer, Willsey implanted Paradromic’s device in a volunteer’s brain. The brain belonged to a 68-year-old woman who lives in Michigan. She has primary lateral sclerosis, a disease that has taken away most of her ability to talk. So far, the Paradromics system is up and running, and the volunteer is testing her abilities out.

Here she is talking with Willsey and other researchers in a video provided by Paradromics. You’ll hear her natural voice, which is hard to understand, and then a digital voice speaking the words her brain implant decoded.

[Audio] I love the change of seasons in Michigan. And my favorite one is the fall. I love the change of seasons in Michigan. And my favorite one is the fall. Yeah, it’s good.

Sanders: This volunteer has used the device to talk to her grandkids on the phone. But this is just the very beginning for this research project. There’s so much more to test.Casey is still working on his system, too — particularly, streamlining the process. When Casey uses his brain-computer interface, it decodes speech signals from his brain, then puts words on a screen. Casey then selects a button, using his eye movements or his brain-computer interface, to say these words out loud with a digital voice. Here’s Casey.

Casey: It is not fast enough to provide enough instant conversation with other people that need to slow down to talk to me.

Sanders: But scientists want to skip this middle part — the words written on a screen. They want instead to go straight to speech, and perhaps make conversations faster. Casey says this goal to go directly from brain signals to a speaking digital voice would be his top priority.

Casey: That one is the holy grail of what this will become in terms of speech. It will allow you to have a seamless conversation. I am talking about, yes, I will intend to talk, and then it will just translate that automatically into speech, like we do, and you are doing right now.

Sanders: In an earlier episode, we talked about attempts to do just this with Casey’s system, to push it to do what they call brain-to-voice. Early attempts were hard to decipher. But it has already improved, by a lot. In the latest tests, this brain-to-voice process produces words that are understandable – reaching about 95 percent accuracy for listeners. Here’s Casey speaking test sentences. It comes from a preprint manuscript posted on the website bioRxiv.

[Audio] The day is not over yet. Please come in with me.

Sanders: Scientists have another thing on their to-do list. And this one goes beyond the words themselves. Here’s Gilja, from Paradromics.

Gilja: Let’s say I identify whether a sentence is a statement or a question. Well, now you can pass that information on to speech synthesis, so that you get these two different versions.

Sanders: The same words could be a statement or a question. You see what he means. You see what he means? And that information can be pulled out from a person’s brain activity.

Gilja: If I’m decoding prosodic information, if I’m decoding speed, when a word is meant to appear, that can also be passed on to modern speech synthesis systems, so that you’re more accurately capturing the prosody that somebody intends. Same thing with loudness, right? So you can see how as that information becomes available from the neural channels, it can be provided to the AI speech synthesis to get closer to the intended voice in the moment that the individual wants to generate.

Sanders: All of these signals can be collected and used to build a more accurate voice — one that says things exactly how a person intends to say them, like a Minnesotan’s ooftah or a slow southern hey y’all. Stavisky: We definitely have our work cut out for us on the singing and melody side of things.

Sanders: All sorts of voice signals could be pulled from brain activity.

Stavisky: Ultimately, we want people to be in full control of what they’re communicating. This should come from their intent. So, yeah, we are trying to decode all of the aspects of his voice, whether it’s the pitch, the timbre, the loudness, the intonation, which word he’s stressing. All of that, ideally, we would decode from brain activity, including kind of all of that emotional nuance.

Sanders: Voice clones can speak with various emotions. You heard my voice clone do just that in earlier episodes. But the difference here is that a person wouldn’t have to type in the instructions. They would come straight from their brain, seamlessly. Other nonverbal signals can be pulled from the brain, too.

Samantha Brosler: In the past five years or so, there have been a lot of advancements in the field of BCIs for restoring individual functions to people with paralysis.

Sanders: That’s Samantha Brosler, a bioengineer at the University of California, San Francisco. Some brain-computer interfaces can pick up movements. We haven’t talked much about them, but these implants have their own very successful research history. They’ve allowed people to control a robotic arm, for instance.

Brosler: Most of these devices so far have been designed to restore one function at a time, whereas in reality, frequently people who are paralyzed are missing both the ability to speak and perform body movements. And so in this study, we asked whether a single brain implant could be used to decode both speech and movement at the same time.

Sanders: It turns out, it could. She and her colleagues were able to decode gestures for communication — things like thumbs up, or a head nodding yes — and words. This combo approach is a more natural way of getting a point across.

Brosler: We naturally use gestures alongside our speech. Sanders: My kids know that a slow maybe with a skeptical eyebrow raise is much closer to a no than my fast upbeat maybe with a little head nod. There is so much subtext in our body language.

Brosler: So I think of, you know, gestures and body movements as an additional communication channel that can work together with speech to add expressivity to what we’re trying to say.

Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

Casey: What does my voice mean to me? It means so much. I think it is the most important thing that I have lost in this whole disease.

Sanders: So now we are here, in this moment, as Jules would say, right here, right now. And right now, the human voice is shifting and changing, expanding in ways that were completely unthinkable even just a few years ago. The future of the human voice and its many replicas is anybody’s guess.

Sanders: In one of Jules’ comedy sets, the one he did in November of 2024, he wheels out onto the stage as the song “Walking on Sunshine” plays.

As the crowd settles and finishes their clapping and woo-ing, Jules pauses. You can’t see this, but he wiggles his eyebrows — a lot. The crowd goes crazy every time. He hasn’t said a single word yet. After another pause, he deadpans with his voice clone: “That is all the time I have. My Make-A-Wish covered only a few minutes. Goodnight, everybody.”

And with that, Jules takes control and he’s off on a tear, ripping through stories of a weatherman who seems too happy about standing out in hurricanes, the exquisite guilt trips lovingly crafted by his Cuban parents, and the indignities of having body parts shaved with his sister right there in the room. Jules has the audience laughing so hard. It’s magnificent.

MA: And being backstage and then seeing him come out, like roll out in his wheelchair and everybody go nuts because they’re like, what is going on here? Like, this doesn’t make sense. And every time I was like, this is like life. This is love. This is passion. This is like, what else is there? Like, I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here and what I can help him do.

Sanders: I get what MA meant when she said that comedy is something that heals. When his set actually does come to a close, he tells the audience. [Audio] Now you have to watch me slowly get off this stage. Goodnight, everybody.

Sanders: It’s hilarious. It’s happy. It’s sad. It’s perfect.
