Mitochondria can become compromised in a number of medical conditions. What if they could be replaced like batteries?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A newborn baby's heart is roughly the size of a walnut — which makes open-heart surgery challenging.

Each year, about 10,000 babies in the United States are born with critical heart defects that may require surgery to fix, often fairly soon after birth. In these infants, the two major arteries of the heart could have swapped positions or the left side of the heart may be far too small to pump properly.

Even if their surgeries go well, these babies face perilous recoveries. A complication can arise when blood flows back into the repaired heart, triggering what's known as an ischemia-reperfusion injury. This can stun the organ, triggering extensive damage that requires doctors to place the baby on a life-support machine that pumps and infuses oxygen into blood to sub in for the hampered heart and lungs. Only about 40% of newborns make it off the machine, because often, their tiny hearts don't recover.

Doctors and scientists at Boston Children's Hospital have been working to improve those odds using a creative idea: replacing the fuel source in damaged heart cells to help them bounce back from injury. That fuel source is mitochondria, the "batteries" found in most cells in the body. In this case, the mitochondria are isolated from an abdominal muscle and then injected directly into the heart.

As of April, 17 babies have undergone this procedure, and 80% made it off ECMO. It's too soon to say if the treatment improves overall survival rates, but the early data hints that it might. A clinical trial is currently underway.

James McCully (left) and his colleague Dr. Sitaram Emani of Boston Children's Hospital have developed a technique to transplant mitochondria into the hearts of children recovering from surgery.

"The first one or two for me were pretty nerve-wracking," said James McCully, a research associate at Boston Children's Hospital and associate professor of surgery at Harvard Medical School whose pioneering work paved the way for these procedures. His team isolates and purifies the mitochondria that a surgical team then transplants into patients.

"But you know, the heart comes back — you can actually almost see it coming back" in real time, he told Live Science. A heart deprived of energy looks pallid, while a freshly rejuvenated heart blushes a healthy pink.

Baby heart infusions are just one example of the promise of "mitochondrial transplantation." Following McCully's lead, other scientists have started investigating whether infusions of mitochondria could revitalize donated organs destined for transplantation, help stroke patients recover, and treat kids with devastating diseases. This work is still highly experimental, and its route to regulatory approval remains unclear.

But at its core is a straightforward idea: When a battery dies, you replace it.

The human body contains tens of trillions of cells, most of which contain hundreds to thousands of mitochondria. Following some back-of-the-envelope math, that means the total potential energy in each person "is the equivalent of a lightning bolt," Douglas Wallace, director of the Center for Mitochondrial and Epigenomic Medicine at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, told attendees last year at a symposium on mitochondrial medicine.

Mitochondria, in a word, are powerful. They produce most of the chemical energy used by complex cells by churning out a molecule called adenosine triphosphate (ATP). The idea of transferring these fuel factories from one cell to another as a medical treatment emerged less than two decades ago — but cells have been doing such swaps on their own for eons.

A leading theory posits that mitochondria evolved from simple microbes. And today, they still retain distinctly microbial features.

Dr. Jon Brestoff, an associate professor of pathology and immunology and director of the Immunometabolism Initiative at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, describes this ability to move from cell to cell as a relic of mitochondria's bacterial past. "It is hypothesized that mitochondria transfer has likely been retained throughout evolution of eukaryotic life," the huge domain of life that includes all plants, fungi, protists and animals, Brestoff told Live Science.

Mitochondria are the powerhouses of nearly all complex cells on Earth, and there are a few theories as to how they adopted that ubiquitous role. A leading idea posits that, some 1.5 billion to 2 billion years ago, one simple cell engulfed another. The bacterial cell that got swallowed carried a circular loop of DNA inside its membrane, and that captured cell later became what we now know as the mitochondrion. The new organelle enabled cells to take advantage of the abundance of oxygen on our planet by converting it into usable fuel.

Mitochondria retained bacteria-like features, such as having their own DNA and membranes. But in 2006, researchers reported that mitochondria can also exit their "host" and survive the journey into a totally different cell — a phenomenon known as mitochondrial transfer.

"That was a complete revolution in thinking," said Dr. Lance Becker, professor and Chair of the Department of Emergency Medicine at Northwell Health and the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research. "With that notion that mitochondria might be mobile, that they might cross boundaries, that they might go from one cell to another cell, came the possibility that maybe that was something we could use to help people."

The 2006 study showed that cells that had been depleted of their own mitochondrial DNA could obtain healthy mitochondria from neighboring cells. After receiving other cells' powerhouses, the once-depleted cells were able to conduct energetically costly processes, such as cell division.

This research provided the first evidence that one cell can "donate" metabolic properties to its neighbor by sending over a fresh batch of mitochondria. Scientists once thought cells had to make all of their own mitochondria, but now, "I think cells have the ability to 'put their hand up' when they need mitochondria," Becker told Live Science.

Jon Brestoff is studying the use of mitochondrial transplantation for genetic diseases that impair the function of these cellular powerhouses.

Because those first experiments were done in lab dishes, initially, "it was unclear whether or not it was really biologically meaningful or relevant," Brestoff said. But within the past five to six years, improved tools and techniques have enabled scientists to watch mitochondrial transfer unfold within living organisms, he noted. It's been shown that cells of the same type can exchange mitochondria, as can cells of different types.

As scientists' fundamental understanding of mitochondrial transfer grew, the notion of doing the same thing therapeutically gained more traction.

"That procedure," Brestoff said, "is rooted in the biology of mitochondria transfer."

Just two years after the landmark 2006 paper, McCully's research group released data that hinted at the medicinal potential of mitochondrial transplantation.

Since then, these complementary lines of research — the foundational biology and the preclinical investigation — have continued in parallel. McCully's preclinical work helped to inspire other labs to explore the use of mitochondrial transplantation for a range of medical applications, including organ transplants and treatments for stroke and genetic disease.

McCully is "the pioneer — the guru of the field," said Dr. Giuseppe Orlando, a professor of surgery and regenerative medicine at Wake Forest University School of Medicine who is exploring mitochondrial transplantation as a way to maintain the integrity of transplant organs.

McCully's road to mitochondrial transplantation started in the 1980s. As a molecular biologist, he wanted to uncover mechanisms that protect the heart from damage, particularly when the organ's oxygen supply is compromised — such as during ischemia, or low blood flow. With an eye on older adults, he wanted to spare patients' heart tissue from the damage and cell death that can occur before and during heart surgery.

It changed color, went back to a pink hue, and just kept on going.

McCully and his collaborators initially "didn't care about the mitochondria one iota," he said. They were more focused on the nucleus, the control center that houses most of a cell's DNA, and its influence on cellular pathways that might boost the heart's resilience to ischemia. But "what we found was that everything we did started coming back to the mitochondria," he said.

They found that ischemia triggers damage and dysfunction in mitochondria that persists even after the heart's oxygen supply is restored; this dysfunction ultimately kills cells. The damaged mitochondria swell up, leak their innards, and set off a chain reaction that causes a cell to self-destruct.

McCully and colleagues observed that biological pathways that seemed to reduce this cell death often centered on the mitochondria. "We were looking around at either pathways upstream of the mitochondria or downstream of the mitochondria," he said.

So, logically, they started looking directly at mitochondria, studying what the organelle looks like before, during and after ischemia. One day, while isolating mitochondria from a laboratory pig, the animal developed fibrillation, meaning its heart began beating very quickly, with an uncoordinated and rapid rhythm. The team tried to reset the heart's rhythm with electric shocks and medications, to no avail. But McCully had an idea.

"At that point in time, the heart's kind of [got a] gray pallor, and it looks dead," he said. "And I said, 'Go upstairs; grab some of those mitochondria that we've isolated from the non-ischemic type. Just bring them down.'" They'd previously gathered some healthy mitochondria from the same pig, in hopes of generating a "before-and-after" picture of ischemia. Instead, McCully suspended those healthy mitochondria in a solution and then injected them directly into the pig's fibrillating heart.

"And the heart came back — started beating normally. It changed color, went back to a pink hue, and just kept on going," he said.

Surgeons sample a small piece of muscle from the patient. That muscle will serve as the source of healthy mitochondria.

After mitochondria have been isolated from the muscle sample, they are prepared in a syringe and injected into the heart tissue.

That serendipitous experiment led to a formal test of the technique in rabbit hearts, the results of which were published in 2008. In the study, they introduced healthy mitochondria to the rabbits' hearts during ischemia, just before reperfusion — when blood is reintroduced into the oxygen-starved tissue. They found that the mitochondria improved the organs' recovery and reduced tissue death. Further research in animals suggested that mitochondria that originated from one type of tissue, like liver tissue or skeletal muscle, could be introduced to other tissue types, such as cardiac muscle.

After seeing McCully's results in various animal experiments, including more with pigs, Dr. Pedro del Nido, chair of cardiac surgery at Boston Children's and a professor of child surgery at Harvard Medical School, approached him about testing the technique in human patients — namely, in babies on a life-support machine known as ECMO.

"He saw it in the animals; he saw what was going on," McCully said. "And he deemed it as being a possible intervention to save these kids."

They sought permission from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to test the procedure and cleared the required regulatory hurdles. The process was made slightly easier because the mitochondria were coming from the patients' own bodies, not from a donor, McCully noted. Once given the go-ahead, they set forth with the help of Dr. Sitaram Emani, a heart surgeon at Boston Children's. The first procedure took place in 2014.

During each procedure, Emani and the surgical team collect a small sample of skeletal muscle from the patient, and McCully then isolates whole mitochondria from the tissue and prepares them in a syringe. He refined the isolation technique so the time from collecting the muscle sample to injecting mitochondria is only 30 minutes. Lately, the team has been developing a technique they can perform in the operating room, rather than in a lab, which could cut the time to 20 minutes. Emani uses various tests, including echocardiography, to see which areas of the heart tissue move the least, and injects mitochondria straight into those areas.

"It's great to be able to see something you've done and worked on for so many years actually provide a benefit," McCully said.

Dr. Giuseppe Orlando thinks that mitochondrial transplantation could serve as a potential method for fortifying donated organs that are intended for transplant patients.

While McCully is trying to protect infant hearts, other scientists want to do the same for other organs — including those destined for transplant surgeries.

To Orlando, mitochondria represent a potential way to make donated kidneys work better. "In transplant medicine, one of the major issues is making sure that the organs that are procured are well stored and kept viable until implantation," said Orlando, who is also president of the Cell Transplant and Regenerative Medicine Society.

Maintaining an organ's viability means preserving mitochondrial function as much as possible, but the transplantation process is tough on the organelles. "That energy plant is damaged. So it's pretty obvious that you should start thinking about a way to replace the damaged mitochondria," Orlando said.

Donated organs suffer some damage when they're unplugged from the donors' bloodstream, in part because this cuts off mitochondria's crucial oxygen supply. And then, paradoxically, the donor organs also get damaged when they're plugged into the recipient's bloodstream. That's because the fast flow of blood triggers the production of free radicals — unstable molecules that damage tissues.

While healthy organs normally produce some free radicals, reperfusion unleashes a flood. "It's more than the organ can bear and sustain," Orlando explained. This damage contributes to a phenomenon called delayed graft function, in which a transplanted kidney doesn't work right away so the patient ends up needing dialysis in the first week after surgery.

"You want to make sure that the kidney wakes up faster," Orlando said. That's where mitochondria come in.

Orlando was introduced to the idea of mitochondrial transplantation around 2019 through a collaboration with Dr. Benedetta Bussolati, a nephrologist and full professor of laboratory medicine at the University of Turin in Italy. Her lab had been studying mitochondrial transplantation in isolated kidney cells in lab experiments, and they reached out to Orlando about extending that work to lab animals.

In pigs, the researchers ran experiments in which the animals' kidneys were collected and stored in the same way human kidneys commonly would be prior to being transplanted. One set of kidneys received a placebo treatment, while another got an infusion of mitochondria from the donor pigs' muscle tissue. Upon being reperfused, the treated kidneys produced fewer free radicals and accrued less damage than the untreated kidneys did, the team reported in 2023.

They backed up this finding by analyzing RNA, a molecule that reflects which genes are active in cells. Compared with the untreated kidneys, the treated kidneys showed greater activity in genes involved in mitochondrial metabolism and lower activity in genes involved in repairing injuries.

Orlando thinks that mitochondrial transplanations could help organs "wake up" faster after being transferred from an organ donor to a recipient.

Some groups are exploring mitochondrial transplantation in other donor organs, like the lungs — specifically, lungs treated with "ex vivo perfusion" (EVP), an emerging approach that helps retain the viability of transplant organs. Rather than placing a donor organ in a cooler of ice, as is generally standard, EVP flushes an organ with nutrient- and oxygen-rich fluid, helping to maintain its function until the transplant surgery. In lab experiments with pig and human lungs, scientists found that introducing fresh mitochondria during EVP further improved the organs' function while reducing inflammation and free radicals.

Across different organ transplants, Orlando sees mitochondria as a potential means to improve patient outcomes and expand the pool of available organs. There are scenarios in which would-be organ donors die unexpectedly of cardiac arrest and their organs are damaged in the process; mitochondrial transplants may help make such organs fit for patients, Orlando has said.

In the near term, Orlando and his colleagues are continuing to study the basic science of mitochondrial transplantation for this clinical purpose; they've also been cleared to run a clinical trial with donor kidneys but need more funds to proceed.

Looking to the more distant future, he and other experts in the field envision a world where transplant organs can be bioengineered and stored in banks, ready and waiting for the patients who need them, Orlando said. If that vision materializes, he suggested, mitochondrial transplants might be useful for preparing banked organs for transplantation "by giving them kind of an energy boost."

If infusions of fresh mitochondria could help the heart, kidney and lungs, what about the brain? That's the question Dr. Melanie Walker and colleagues at the University of Washington School of Medicine (UW Medicine) want to answer.

Walker, a clinical professor of neurological surgery, treats patients who have had ischemic strokes, which are caused by blood clots blocking blood flow to the brain. The immediate aim of post-stroke treatment is to clear out the blocked "pipe" and restore circulation to the brain as quickly as possible, she said. But no matter how quickly this is done, some brain cells are damaged. And once the blood clot is removed, the brain may then suffer a reperfusion injury.

Standard treatments can dissolve the clot but don't protect the brain, Walker said. "What about all those cells that are maybe not quite dead — they're on the verge of maybe dying? What can we do to support those guys?" she asked.

The UW Medicine team had heard about McCully's work in Boston and wondered if something similar could be applied in stroke patients. But while heart surgery exposes the tissue in need of new mitochondria, accessing the brain is trickier. "You don't do a craniotomy to give an IV medicine," Walker told Live Science.

But Walker realized that a harmful downstream effect of stroke might provide an opportunity for treatment. Immediately after a stroke, the brain's protective shield — known as the blood-brain barrier — becomes more permeable than usual, allowing more substances to pass from the bloodstream into brain tissue. That might open a door for mitochondrial transplantation.

One method of treating ischemic strokes is to physically remove the clot using a procedure called a thrombectomy, which a surgeon is preparing for in the photo above. Dr. Melanie Walker and colleagues tried combining this approach with mitochondrial transplantation.

A 2023 mouse study spearheaded by University of Virginia researchers and co-authored by Walker backed this idea, finding that mitochondria entered the brain after stroke and integrated into brain cells. These mitochondria had been gathered from muscle tissue, as in McCully's studies, and introduced to the brain via an artery. The treatment increased ATP production while reducing cell death caused by the stroke, compared with untreated mice's brains.

This work paved the way to the first trial using mitochondrial transplant in the human brain. The small safety trial included adult patients who'd had ischemic strokes and underwent thrombectomies ‪—‬ surgeries to remove the clots from their blood vessels. Four received mitochondrial transplants during their procedures and 12 did not. Mitochondria were injected near the site of each patient's stroke, into the closest branch of one of the brain's major arteries.

No negative side effects were tied to the transplants, hinting that the procedure is safe in humans. "But the next question is, how do we understand if it helps? And those are harder trials to design," Walker said. That's partly because the transplants are tacked onto the clot-removal procedure, so it's difficult to separate their effects from those of the clot removal itself, she noted.

Future trials will also need to explore exactly where the transplanted mitochondria end up in the human brain, how well they function once inside brain cells, and how the dose and timing of the transplant affect patients' outcomes, the trial runners wrote in their report. For the moment, Walker said her team is focused on exploring the safety aspects of the approach and have no further trials planned at this time.

Beyond heart defects, transplant organs and stroke, researchers are looking to mitochondrial transplantation as a solution for genetic conditions that harm mitochondria directly. Brestoff and colleagues are investigating the therapy's potential for treating Leigh syndrome, a rare neurological condition caused by genetic mutations that disrupt the fuel-producing machinery in mitochondria.

"Those kids have a terrible prognosis," Brestoff said. Most children with the most common form of the syndrome, whose symptoms show up by age 2, die by age 3. There is no cure for the syndrome, and treatments to relieve its symptoms are limited. So if it works, mitochondrial transplantation could fill a big gap.

So far, the approach shows promise in lab mice with a severe form of Leigh syndrome, improving the rodents' function and extending their median lifespan by 19% to 24%, the researchers demonstrated in 2024. They're now studying the approach in cells derived from patients with the disease.

I can get the mitochondria from you and put them into me, me into you — doesn't really matter.

Some companies, such as Israel-headquartered Minovia Therapeutics, are already running clinical trials with patients with other types of mitochondrial disease. Minovia is running one with children with Pearson syndrome, in which missing mitochondrial DNA hinders the function of bone marrow, which normally makes blood and immune cells.

While patients with a heart or brain problem may be able to pluck mitochondria from healthy muscles, people with mitochondrial disease don't necessarily have healthy mitochondria to spare. Especially for these patients, getting mitochondria from other people ‪—‬ known as heterologous transplantation ‪—‬ likely makes the most sense. What's more, for transplantation to be used widely for any purpose, there would need to be an "off-the-shelf" mitochondrial product available, Brestoff said.

Such a product could eliminate the step in Boston Children's heart procedure where mitochondria have to be isolated from a patient while they're waiting, open on an operating table. "Getting them from the recipient can sometimes be problematic, because the recipients are sick. All the organs, all the tissue is quite distressed," McCully noted. A standardized and safety-tested mitochondrial product would therefore be a boon for the field.

Brestoff is on the scientific advisory board of LUCA Science, a company developing mitochondria as therapeutic agents, and a consultant for Cellergy Therapeutics, which is making mitochondrial products to combat conditions from muscle degeneration and aging. These companies exemplify the effort to come up with ready-made products that could someday bring the therapy to more patients.

A shift to heterologous transplantation does raise concerns about immune reactions. "You have some variations in the proteins that are present in your mitochondria that I don't have," Brestoff noted. "So it is possible that our immune systems recognize heterologous mitochondria as non-self."

But McCully doesn't expect immune reactions to be a big problem, based on his research in animals. "I can get the mitochondria from you and put them into me, me into you — doesn't really matter," he said. Early trial results from Minovia and others suggest heterologous transplantations come with minimal side effects, at least at doses tested so far.

Another roadblock is that the FDA has not approved any organelles as therapies yet, so the standards and regulatory framework for the field are still being established, Brestoff said.

Despite that hurdle, the field has advanced significantly since its start as a niche, theoretical interest and then a highly experimental procedure for the sickest newborns. Scientists are now exploring the treatment as a solution to many common conditions, from rheumatoid arthritis to chronic pain.

Becker compared the state of the field to the early days of organ transplantation.

"It just turned out that it was revolutionary, when all of a sudden you could just give a person a kidney transplant," he said. "I think it's going to be kind of similar with mitochondria."

#6358. Nov. 11, 1875: The birth of V.M. Slipher

Vesto Melvin Slipher was born on a farm in Mulberry, Indiana, on Nov. 11, 1875. He graduated from high school, taught briefly at a country school, and then enrolled at Indiana University in Bloomington. In 1901, one of Slipher’s professors, Wilbur Cogshall, persuaded the founder of the fledgling Lowell Observatory to bring the young astronomer on staff. Percival Lowell was reluctant; as far as he was concerned, the association would be temporary. In the end, however, Slipher would stay at the observatory for 53 years. In 1915, he became assistant director, and when Lowell died the following year, Slipher became acting director and then director by 1926. He served as the observatory’s chief until retiring in 1954 at age 79.

In the fall of 1912, Slipher recorded a plate of the “Andromeda Nebula” that he felt was sufficiently good to obtain its radial velocity. No radial velocities of nebulae were known at that time. He recorded better plates in November and December 1912, and measured the plates over the first half of January, finding that the nebula was moving three times faster than any previously known object in the universe. On Feb. 3, 1913, he wrote to Lowell that the Andromeda Nebula was approaching Earth at the unheard-of velocity of 186 miles per second (300 kilometers per second), still an accurate value. “It looks as if you had made a great discovery,” wrote Lowell. “Try some other spiral nebulae for confirmation.”

By the 1914 American Astronomical Society meeting, Slipher was able to announce results for 15 spirals. Nearly all were receding at high velocities. Three years later, Dutch astronomer Willem de Sitter theorized that the universe is expanding. It was Slipher’s observations of the so-called spiral nebulae that established this fact. And then in 1923 came Hubble’s discovery of the nature of galaxies. By 1929, Hubble derived his crucial velocity-distance relationship for galaxies, using, as Hubble wrote Slipher, “your velocities and my distances.” Slipher and Hubble had together uncovered the expanding universe, the nature of galaxies, and a way to measure extragalactic distances.

David J. Eicher is editor emeritus of Astronomy magazine.

#6357. City squirrels seem to be thriving, but their genes tell a different story

Berlin’s red squirrels show subtle genetic differences across nearby green spaces, raising questions about how freely they move through the city.

Eurasian red squirrels are a familiar sight in the parks and gardens of Berlin, where they often appear to be perfectly at home.

Yet the roads and buildings lying between these green spaces may be making it harder for the animals to mix.

In a study of squirrels at three sites across the city, small genetic differences were found between groups living only a few miles apart. Survival, on the other hand, was much the same in all three places.

The findings reveal subtle genetic differences between groups, even though researchers detected no clear differences in survival.

The work was led by Sinah Drenske of the Leibniz Institute for Zoo and Wildlife Research (Leibniz-IZW), and wild squirrels were followed for close to four years.

“We do not see any highly isolated populations,” said Drenske. “But we are already detecting subtle genetic differences that suggest that squirrels cannot move completely freely through the city.”

All three sites have plenty of trees, but they differ in how built-up they are and how many people visit.

The quietest was a woodland area of about 94 acres (38 hectares) on the city’s outskirts, part of a much larger forest.

A cemetery of about 25 acres (10 hectares), surrounded by homes, parks and other cemeteries, fell in the middle.

At the other extreme was a city park of about 237 acres (96 hectares), crossed and bordered by major roads.

How crowded was each site? Walkers, dogs, bicycles and other activity along the paths were counted by observers in half-hour blocks. By this measure, the park was roughly 16 times as busy as the woodland.

Live traps baited with walnuts were set from autumn 2021 to spring 2025, over eight spring and autumn trapping periods of about six weeks each.

Each new squirrel was fitted with a small tag under the skin of its shoulder (so that it could be recognized later).

A tiny sample of ear tissue was also taken for DNA testing before the animal was let go.

Altogether, 141 squirrels were caught, one of them on 19 separate occasions.

The amount of variety in a population’s genes is known as its genetic diversity. It’s the raw material a population needs in order to adapt to change.

For 135 of the squirrels, genetic profiles were built from 16 stretches of DNA that commonly vary from one animal to the next.

Levels of diversity were broadly similar at all three sites. In fact, they were higher than the values reported for several squirrel populations in France, Great Britain and the island of Jersey.

There was, therefore, no sign that life in the city had sharply reduced the genetic variety of the squirrels (and inbreeding levels were low as well).

A closer look did turn up small differences, however. Individual squirrels in the busy park carried less genetic variety, on average, than those living in the woodland.

Such differences were read by the researchers as an early stage of genetic separation rather than a sign of serious isolation.

In the Japanese city of Obihiro, a 2024 study had found lower genetic diversity in city red squirrels than in rural ones. Compared with that result, the effects in Berlin were described by the authors as considerably weaker.

Three genetic groups had been expected, one for each site. Instead, only two were found by a computer analysis that sorts animals according to how genetically similar they are.

Most of the squirrels in the cemetery belonged to one of these groups, while most of those in the park belonged to the other. Yet the two sites are less than 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) apart.

In the woodland, about 12 miles (20 kilometers) from the cemetery, the squirrels carried a mix of both genetic backgrounds.

“If one considered only the geographical location, one would have expected the populations in the city park and the cemetery – which are just a few kilometers apart – to be genetically similar, whilst the forest population, which is significantly further away, would stand out more,” Drenske said.

Because close relatives can make a population look more divided than it really is, 35 closely related squirrels (21 of them from the park) were taken out of the data.

When the analysis was run again, two groups still appeared, although the split between them was weaker.

Earlier work on hedgehogs in Berlin had a different outcome, as an apparent genetic split vanished there once relatives had been taken into account.

Researchers believe squirrels from the woodland may have moved into the two city areas. Over time, limited movement between these places could have increased their genetic differences.

Berlin’s wide roads, railways, and waterways may make it harder for squirrels to travel between green spaces.

An earlier computer model suggested that the park could connect the woodland and cemetery. However, it only showed possible routes, not whether squirrels actually used them.

The findings suggest that even when paths exist, squirrels may struggle to move freely through the city.

Survival was estimated from the trapping records, which were used to work out the chance of a squirrel still being around six months later.

The chance of surviving six months came to 75% in the woodland, 74% in the cemetery and 69% in the park.

The figure for the park was the lowest of the three. However, the uncertainty around the estimates meant researchers could not establish a clear difference between the sites.

Were more inbred squirrels less likely to survive? If anything, they showed a weak tendency to survive slightly better (the opposite of what had been predicted), though the trend wasn’t statistically significant.

In addition, these survival estimates cannot distinguish between a squirrel that died and one that permanently left the study area.

There were also no measurements of food supply, predators or disease.

Stephanie Kramer-Schadt, who heads the Department of Ecological Dynamics at Leibniz-IZW, supervised the research. She is also a professor at the Technische Universität Berlin (TU Berlin).

The term connectivity is used by scientists for how easily animals can move between patches of habitat.

“The results show that Berlin’s squirrels exhibit a high level of genetic diversity and that there is currently no evidence of significant inbreeding or advanced isolation,” said Kramer-Schadt.

“Should connectivity between urban habitats continue to decline in future, this could also lead to a further reduction in genetic exchange.”

Over many years, even small differences in survival could add up, the authors noted. It isn’t yet known whether that will happen here.

Studies that follow Berlin’s squirrels for longer (and across more of the city) could show whether the genetic split ever affects how long the animals live.

The full study was published in the journal Ecology and Evolution.

#6356. The 7 Best 3D Printers for New Makers, No Matter What You’re Making

Whether you’re printing parts, toys, tools, or making art, a 3D Printer is an incredible tool for crafting and creating.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s an example of why I love 3D printers. Over the holidays, the drain in my bathroom sink broke. Part of the pop-up assembly snapped, and the stopper was stuck in the down position. I didn’t have time to run to the hardware store, so I searched for an at-home solution. I checked online and found that someone had created a 3D-printable version of the exact part I needed. And 30 minutes later, part in hand, I repaired my sink.

3D printers can replicate virtually any part or product through a process called additive manufacturing, which assembles physical objects by layering a pliable filament or building material. Most consumer 3D printers work with various plastics, but there are printers that work with a wide range of materials including metals, ceramics, composites, wood, and more.

In the decade since 3D printers first exploded onto the consumer tech scene, these tools have become much easier to use. It used to be that you’d spend more time fiddling with the printer than using the product that you just printed. While they are still hobby-grade (read: expensive) tools, modern printers make it easy to set up a print, and you don’t have to babysit your project to make sure everything comes out okay.

Buying a 3D printer today isn’t too different from buying a table saw—you’ll need to do some research to find one that fits your space and can print what you want to print. Once you have it, you can focus on designing and printing everything from toys to tools to tech.

I’ve taken the time to test some of the most highly rated and popular 3D printers to highlight the best for new users. These are some of the easiest printers to use, and should allow technically minded newcomers to get up and printing as quickly as possible.

I’ve been a maker and tinkerer for decades, and have used 3D printers both professionally and as a hobby, printing everything from board game pieces to replacement parts for appliances. I’ve seen first-hand how diverse the 3D printing community is, and that we have a wide range of needs.

A tabletop gamer needs a different type of printer than a print farm operator, or an artist, or a maker. On top of that, there are a ton of nuances to consider when comparing 3D printers from size and speed to print quality and affordability. For this guide, I specifically prioritized printers that are easy to use. I imagine that, if you’ve come to Popular Mechanics for advice, rather than a deep message board or 3D printing influencer, there’s a good chance that you’re just starting out and haven’t put down roots in the community. That’s okay! Welcome! I’m here to help you get started.

Nearly all of these printers are new models, released in the last year. There’s one exception, the Creality Ender 3 V3 SE, which is our “Easiest to Use” pick. It was tested, though, by contributor Sascha Brodsky to see how well it holds up against newer models.

I tested each of the printers we recommend by printing all kinds of things, from detailed busts and decorative lithopanes to peg board organizers, table saw rails, and shop vacuum accessories. I sent a core group of models through all the printers, and pushed the boundaries of individual printers with a range of sizes, styles, and filament types. All told, I stacked up more than 100 hours of print time per printer.

I focused on printing with common filaments that a new user would most likely use, such as polylactide (PLA), polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG), and thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). During testing I used the manufacturer’s slicer and – when possible – their branded filament as well. I printed models taken off the manufacturer’s online services, as well as third-party sites. I selected a variety of models, from functional to decorative, and from large to miniature. I tried to push all the printers in terms of consistency, performance, and precision.

I also recorded how long it took to set up each printer, from opening the box to producing a completed 3DBenchy benchmark model. (Or “box to Benchy” time, as I like to call it.) I also had more subjective measurements, such as how intuitive the printer interface and slicer are. I made note of anything I found confusing in their UI, and I tracked whether they needed babysitting to complete a print. I also tracked any failed prints, to see if the printer had an error detection system, or if it continued to run through the failed print.

And through it all, I identified which printers made the process easiest, from set up to printing and troubleshooting. Once I got them through all that, I was able to see which ones stood out from the rest in terms of price, performance, and features.

Released in the U.S. last November, the Bambu P2S is Bambu’s mid-line printer, falling between the entry-level A1 and their premium H-Series models. This is hands-down the most user-friendly 3D printer I’ve ever operated. From setup and basic operations to remote printing, it’s so easy to use it almost feels like running on autopilot.

In the last few years, Bambu has revolutionized the 3D printer industry by bringing more intuitive, beginner-friendly features to the market. Their business is based on creating a full ecosystem for users to explore. Bambu provides their own filament with RFID chips on the spools, so the printer can change its settings to match that specific filament’s needs. And their Maker World website is full of models and tools, including one-click projects (such as RC cars), that start a 3D print and simultaneously ship out any hardware or electronics needed to complete it.

Bambu encourages—some critics would argue “pressures”—users to use all of these integrated services. The situation is not unlike the “walled garden” of Apple’s iOS App Store, which curates a library of beautifully designed products that are accessible and easy to use, at the expense of some creative freedom for both users and developers.

Regardless of how you feel about this kind of manufacturer ecosystem, though, the P2S is an impressive machine. It’s an intuitive system that’s easy to use, and works right out of the box. Of all the printers I tested, the Bambu P2S was the only one that never gave me a single connection issue, and any failed prints were identified and paused to allow me to address the issue.

That ease of use even extends to the Bambu mobile app. Most 3D printers have a mobile app that allows you to track progress or view your print progress in real time through a camera, but Bambu’s Handy app is on another level: It connects directly Bambu’s Maker World, allowing you to set up prints remotely from your phone, automatically handling slicing. To be honest, I didn’t think I’d use the app, but I quickly found myself breaking out my phone while watching TV and sending a quick print to the P2S. It was so easy to use, it just became second nature.

For new users, I loved Bambu’s tutorial library, including tutorials in both text and video. This is even true for the “experimental” services in their Creator’s Maker Lab, where users can create their own models using a range of manual and AI tools. I tried a few of these with moderate success. (It struggled with photos of people wearing glasses, and it tended to generate disturbing results, including a 3D model that combined two of my dogs into a single nightmare creature that would be at home in a Cronenberg film.)

No printer is perfect, of course. The P2S uses a single nozzle to print multiple colors, which means the machine needs to reset, purging the old color and cutting some filament for the change, before resuming the print. Doing that once isn't a big deal, but complex prints may have hundreds or even thousands of color changes.

This takes its toll on both efficiency and print time: In a couple of complicated prints, I found that the printer discards three to four times as much filament as it used for the actual print. Likewise, I printed a single-color mask piece in 2 hours and 4 minutes, but a 3-color version of the design took an astronomical 19 hours and 30 minutes.

One other minor issue: it struggled with any filament that wasn’t well-wound. I buy a fair amount of this stuff, and some manufacturers ship filament that’s loosely wound. I can get away with using it on a single-color printer or even a multi-toolhead machine. But with filament changing designs like the P2S, the filament gets bound up. I never had this issue with Bambu filament, or with well-wound 3rd party filament.

The Bambu P2S exemplifies how 3D printers have improved over the past few years. While other printers may have a specific task where they perform better, but the P2S is so incredibly easy to use, which makes it a great all-around option for beginners who may or may not know what they plan to print most. It’s the closest thing to a “set it and forget it” experience that you can get with a 3D printer.

The Centauri Carbon is fast, affordable, and fun to use. It’s also a rare find for entry-level printers looking to enter the hobby with a low investment, with print quality and features that are typically seen in more expensive models. It doesn’t have many of the bells and whistles that I love from my other picks, but it delivers great value for its price, and it’s a perfect starting point for general use printing.

It has a strong sense of fun in its design. For example, the included waste-bin model that clips to the back of the printer isn’t just a bland box, it’s a tiny model of the Centauri Carbon. I felt the slightly playful nature of the design reflected a desire to make things enjoyable for the user, something that included keeping setup simple, with a box to Benchy time of one hour, 11 minutes, the fastest time I’ve found to date.

Elegoo seems to want to balance a streamlined UI with robust options. Their custom version of the Orca slicer tucks away some features in the name of streamlining, but they’re still there if you go digging. (That may be a good thing or bad thing, depending on how much you like to tinker with settings.) A recent software update added an integration for Nexprint, Elegoo’s 3D model site, which makes it much easier to download projects straight into the slicer.

One simple UI choice that I appreciated is that the mobile app has a clear pause button, so if something looks wrong, you can stop the print before it completely goes off the rails. It’s a weird bit of psychology, but just being able to clearly see it made me more comfortable during long print jobs.

The Centauri Carbon was noisier during operation than the other printers I tested, but silent at rest. (It has relatively hard feet, which seemed to cause more vibration in the bench than other printers.) That left me more inclined to leave it on, which opened the door for me to queue up projects more spontaneously.

One issue worth noting: When the Centauri Carbon debuted, Elegoo announced that it would have a multi-color option sometime in 2025. Now, finally, a multifilament printing option is slated for Fall 2026 availability with the $55 Canvas upgrade.

Out now is the full-blown second iteration of the Centauri, the Centauri Carbon 2 Combo (which comes with the Canvas upgrade) and will run you $450, while the original Carbon costs about $415—$360 for the printer, plus $55 for the Canvas upgrade.

Read the Full Review of the Elegoo Centauri Carbon 3D Printer Here

The QIDI Q2 can print with more durable materials that can withstand abuse from high heat and prolonged sun exposure. It lacks some of the added conveniences found on Bambu’s P2S or Snapmaker’s U1, but it’s priced accordingly. That makes it a standout if you’re looking for a fully enclosed, single-color printer that can print more robust materials.

There are two specific areas where the Q2 excels: First, it’s a great choice if you want to print materials that require a higher nozzle temperature and/or could produce a higher volume of fumes. Second, it keeps most of the customization options readily apparent, making it a good printer if you know you like to tinker with settings and dial-in custom quality and performance.

The Q2 was easy to unpack and to set up, with a box to Benchy time of 1 hour and 20 minutes. (The unit I tested did not include the QIDI Box multi-color kit, which meant I only had to set up a single filament feed.) That said, setup may pose a couple challenges for first-timers: The quick-start guide was light on details, and occasionally skipped steps. For example, there’s no mention of the cover in the setup instructions. It’s not a dealbreaker—chances are that you’ll realize you can put the cover on top—but I found myself wondering more than once if I’d accidentally missed something. Once the Q2 takes over the process and begins to calibrate, though, setup is a breeze.

I found almost everything about the Q2 worked right out of the gate. If you find that you need to make tweaks, though, there is a library of helpful tuning tutorials with photos. (I wish someone handed me these back when I started 3D printing).

It has single-band, 2.4 Ghz WiFi, which allows you to send files directly to the printer, and an interior camera so you can monitor prints remotely. The Q2 is relatively smooth and quiet while printing, though it keeps a fan running even when idle, ironically making it both among the quietest and loudest printers I tested.

It has an AI error detection that can potentially spot the “spaghetti” strands of filament caused by a failed print. Mine went off twice, alerting me in time so I could make adjustments before the print went off the rails.

I did run into an issue with a clogged nozzle after about 60 hours of printing. When I took off the cover, I pressed on the nozzle fan and found it had snapped its support struts. I’m not sure if the fan went bad and caused the clog, or if I damaged the fan when I pressed on it. Regardless, QIDI sent a replacement fan and hot end, and I was up and running with relative ease.

While my tests focused on basic filaments such as PLA, PETG, and TPU, the QIDI Q2 has a higher-temperature nozzle (370 degrees Celsius) and an interior box temperature of up to 65 degrees Celsius. This allows it to print with more robust materials, like polycarbonate (PC) and acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS). It also ships with a hardened steel nozzle, allowing it to print materials like carbon fiber (CF) or glow-in-the-dark filaments, which would damage softer brass nozzles. If your long-term printing goals include using your printer to make automotive parts, or other, more durable items that need to withstand high temperatures and forces, I think the Q2 can help you learn the ropes, and get where you want to go once you know what you’re doing.

I have a lot of affection for the Creality Ender-3 V3 SE. My colleague Sascha Brodsky recommended it as our “easiest to use” pick when it launched in 2023, and for good reason. It was one of the first 3D printers to come mostly assembled, with clear instructions and enough user support to get you up and running, as well as features like automatic bed leveling that made the printer far easier to use than other models available at the time.

Today, the V3 SE is older than most of my recommendations, but it’s still an attractive (and very affordable) option. In its heyday, it was an outstanding selection for those new to 3D printing, and helped bring features like auto-leveling and partial assembly to market at an affordable price. Three years later, it still compares favorably with newer models in terms of setup time, with about an hour and a half from box to Benchy, putting it only a little behind the single-color enclosed printers on our list.

It's worth noting that even a few years in, I use this printer fairly regularly, especially when printing TPU or other flexible filaments. Softer plastics are generally susceptible to print issues, especially in enclosed printers that tend to run hot. If you’re not careful, you can end up with a sticky, stringy mess of a print, or even a clogged nozzle. Luckily, the Ender-3 V3 SE’s open frame and durability manages heat well, and gets the job done with ease. I’ve never had a problem, and that's what keeps me coming back.

That said, the design has started to show its age. It doesn’t have WiFi, so you’ll either have to set up a controller (such as a Raspberry Pi) or shuttle an SD card back and forth. With a max toolhead speed of 250 millimeters per second, it’s far slower than modern printers like the QIDI Q2 which can run at up to 600 mm/s. It also has a smaller print bed, no camera for remote monitoring, and no error detection.

The Ender-3 V3 SE is capable of producing attractive prints, but the quality you’ll get is dependent on your ability to dial in the settings. It doesn’t automate settings or provide a seamless integration with online models. It also doesn’t have advanced calibration features like input shaping, which updates the printer’s settings to account for environmental vibration. Instead, you’ll need to hand-calibrate all those settings. On the plus side, it’s wide open to tweaking and adjustments, making it a great choice if you like to tinker and optimize performance.

The Ender-3 V3 SE is a venerable printer, and still has a lot to offer. Its user-friendly design was ahead of its time and, while it’s no longer our pick for Easiest to Use, the V3 SE remains a great choice for users who want to use flexible filament or are working with a tighter budget. It’s often available on sale, bringing its cost below $200, and if you’re willing to be patient, Creality sells factory-refurbished models for even less.

The Snapmaker U1 set crowdfunding records when it launched on Kickstarter, thanks to its clever multi-head system that keeps four nozzles preheated and loaded with filament. It can change tool heads on the fly, rather than changing filament fed through a single nozzle. With no need to purge older filament, the U1’s design cuts print time and dramatically reduces waste. Seeing this printer go head-to-head with a filament changer, the choice is clear: I'll take the Snapmaker every time.

The U1’s setup kit is top-notch. It has an extensive, step-by-step assembly document, with full color images of each step, and a QR code that links to a video walkthrough. I loved that it shipped with extra parts, so a broken part doesn’t bring you to a complete standstill until you order a replacement.

Assembly and calibration took longer than other printers, because with four print heads, there’s essentially four times the work. It had a box to Benchy time of 2 hours and 49 minutes, more than double single-color printers like the QIDI 2 or Elegoo Centauri Carbon. (For an apples-to-apples comparison, I printed an actual Benchy model; the full-color test model that comes with the U1 adds a few hours of time, though the result is an adorable baby dragon, which immediately scored me points when I gifted it to my wife.) Even with the longer setup time, it never felt onerous.

I was pleasantly surprised to see that the U1 comes with a generous amount of starter filament. It ships with four colors, each with 500 grams of filament, compared to most printers which ship with only a few grams, just enough to print a test Benchy. Snapmaker filament rolls also have RFID, so that you don’t need to manually enter the filament details.

Unfortunately, it does not ship with a lid for the enclosure, or any kind of filter in the case. This can become a problem when you print with materials that require higher nozzle temperatures. Snapmaker doessell a lid, along with a HEPA/activated carbon air filter, for $150. With the lid attached, the internal chamber can reach up to 50 °C, allowing the U1 to print higher-temperature materials like ABS and PC. Obviously, though, it’s annoying to pay extra for a feature that you might see as a core component of the printer. (If you’re open to a DIY solution, though, the U1 forums have a discussion thread where users are sharing their own custom tops. This is why I love the 3D printing community!)

Overall, printing was a breeze, whether using Snapmaker or third-party filament. The U1’s AI error detection worked well, pausing prints if any debris was detected, and allowing me to fix it or cancel the job without wasting more filament. In fact, I had no problems with the U1's hardware at any point during testing. Where I did run into headaches was with the software. As it stands, Snapmaker's version of Orca is sluggish to load, and I had to reconnect the slicer to the printer every time I opened the software. The software is still in beta, and I expect this will be improved before release. Hardware this polished deserves a quality app to go with it.

Testing the Elegoo Mars 5 Ultra was an exercise in both delight and frustration. There’s no disputing its print quality, especially when I produced beautifully detailed game miniatures. But I ran into regular obstacles on the path to those beautiful prints, in the form of poor or even confusing documentation. In a review focusing on ease of use, those pain points really stood out.

Resin printers like the Mars 5 Ultra are especially popular with gamers, who print miniatures for tabletop games. These small figures tend to be packed with details, and printers like the Mars 5 Ultra can generate layers as thin as 0.01 mm, 10 to 20 times thinner than a typical FDM printer. If you want sharp visual details, resin printing is the way to go. The Mars 5 Ultra is an especially good way to learn about printing with resin, thanks to a pair of features that make it more user-friendly than its peers.

First and foremost, it has a tilt-release resin vat that reduces the suction forces between the build plate and the vat. When the build plate bed lifts up after each layer is complete, the vat tilts, creating an angle that makes it easier to separate. (Think of it like pulling off a sticker or a bandage -- it takes far less force if you start on one corner.) Since the tilt-release makes separation easier, your settings don't have to be dialed in quite so precisely in order to get a clean separation from the vat, and support points can be slightly smaller. As a result, you spend less time adjusting settings or removing support marks, and more time enjoying your finished prints.

It also has a very helpful error detection feature, which is great for new printers. If the Mars 5 Ultra detects foreign objects in the vat—usually chunks of supports or models that have fallen off the print plate—it will pause operation and send a notification. That can minimize damage to the model you’re printing, and prevents debris from getting trapped, which could also crack the vat itself. (In general, I think any feature that keeps toxic resin where it belongs is a big value-add.) Both the vat and error detection save time and reduce the frustration of a failed print. They’re also more commonly found on printers that cost twice as much as the Mars 5 Ultra.

Unfortunately, the standout design is somewhat undercut by Elegoo’s confusing and contradictory support documentation. The instructions told me to install Chitubox (an industry-standard slicer) from the included USB stick. But the only slicer on the USB was Elegoo’s SatelLite slicer. Now, I actually like SatelLite, but it’s not what they told me to expect. What’s especially frustrating is that Elegoo actually has a fantastic unboxing video with a clear, easy to follow walkthrough. But there’s no mention of it in the manual and no QR code linking to it on the packaging. So I only saw it when I stumbled across it online.

Setup aside, this is an excellent printer. It’s well designed and easy to use, and produces quality prints with minimal fuss. (Or at least minimal fuss for resin.) The touchscreen is easy to read and well laid out, with an easy to understand user interface. It is a little small, but it’s sensitive enough that I didn’t need to tap twice, even while wearing gloves.

I also love Elegoo’s optional in-box heater. I picked one up when the temperatures plummeted. Since I’d set up the printer in my garage, I thought I’d fall behind on testing. But the heater installed easily and worked spectacularly well. Before I knew it, I was churning out prints even though the weather was well below freezing. But that heater was the reason I was able to get a full test run on the printer, even during a polar vortex.

The Bambu X2D costs about $100 more than the P2S, and for that additional cost it delivers active heating, better venting, and a dual-nozzle design, letting you print more demanding materials faster and with less waste.

Most enclosed printers depend on passive heating, maintaining the internal temperature simply with the captured heat from the nozzle and print bed. By contrast, the X2D has a built-in heater allowing the internal chamber to reach temperatures up to 149 degrees Fahrenheit (65 degrees Celsius). The X2D’s active heating also allows this temperature to be consistent, making it much easier to reliably print materials like Nylon and ABS (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene).

If you want to print material that can withstand the heat of an engine bay or exposure to the elements, the X2D is a fantastic choice. In addition to the active heating, it has an external carbon and HEPA filter to reduce fumes and airborne particles. It also has a dual-nozzle design that reduces waste when printing two-color models, and allows for easy support printing and removal.

The downside to the X2D is that I found it’s surprisingly prone to minor issues and inconveniences. I ran into a weird error when printing the Benchy model that shipped on the internal memory, and had to do additional tweaking to align models and the prime tower on the print bed. None of these would be unusual from another manufacturer, but Bambu has made a name for themselves by delivering the smoothest possible user experience. The X2D doesn’t quite live up to that standard.

It’s a very good printer for both standard and high-temperature filaments. And for the relatively small step up in price, it compares favorably to the P2S if you want to move beyond decorative items and start creating durable objects that can withstand a real-world environment.

There are two types of 3D printer built with home users in mind: FDM and resin. (While other types of 3D printers are available, they’re intended for industrial use, with a learning curve and price tag to match.) As a rule of thumb, FDM printers are faster and produce more rugged prints than resin, while resin printers excel at fine detail.

Fused deposition modeling printers (FDM) are like a hot glue gun for plastic. They feed a strand of plastic filament through a heated metal nozzle, laying out the print onto a heated metal bed. They’re cleaner and easier to use than resin, and require less safety precautions. They tend to have larger print volumes, but they don’t produce prints that are as highly detailed as resin.

Resin printers, on the other hand, create layers of material by dipping a flat bed into a vat of liquid resin, then curing a layer of material with UV light. (It’s similar to the process of making candles, where you dip a wick into wax repeatedly.) They are typically more complicated to use, as the models have to be washed and cured after printing is complete. Printer resins are toxic until cured, and using resin printers requires significant safety precautions. Resin printers produce highly detailed prints, prized by users ranging from tabletop gamers making miniatures to the dental offices, creating surgical implants and guides.

Both types of printing have their pros and cons, depending on your space, your style, and what items you want to print. Generally speaking, FMD printers are good for larger items, items that need to be more durable, or when you need to turn around prints quickly. They are also a good choice if you’ll be printing in areas with less ventilation or if you’ll have children or pets around while printing. Resin printers are a better choice if you want outstanding detail, and have room to set up a cleaning station for your prints.

FDM printers are usually described by the head movement (either CoreXY or bed-slinger) and whether or not it’s enclosed or open frame. CoreXY printers move the head left to right, and front to back. On a bed-slinger, the head moves left to right, but front to back adjustments are made by moving (“slinging”) the bed itself.

Enclosed printers are just that–enclosed on all sides. These are typically CoreXY printers, and allow for higher temperatures and provide filtered vents for filaments that produce more fumes. They also usually cost more than open-bed printers.

To start printing, you’ll need some 3D models and software (called a slicer) to send them to your printer. Luckily, some of the best options are free.

Every 3D Printer uses some type of slicer software, which allows your printer to analyze objects and create a blueprint for making a 3D printed copy. True to its name, it creates a digital model and “slices” it into anywhere from one to a few thousand printable layers, creating the building blocks of a 3D print design. The result is a detailed set of instructions for printing, called G-code. When you load a design, your printer follows the G-code to assemble the design, layer by pre-sliced layer.

Printer manufacturers provide a proprietary slicer or an open-source slicer customized for their specific machines. For testing purposes, I used the slicer provided by the manufacturer. Honestly, once you get used to one slicer, they’ll all feel pretty similar.

Creating your own print designs isn’t necessary, though, if you don’t feel compelled. There’s no shortage of sites with free or paid 3D print designs that you can download and print. Once you have a little bit of experience printing, there’s a whole world of printable tools and products to explore within the 3D printing community.

When a plastic part breaks, there’s a good chance someone else has run into the same issue and created a 3D version of that part to download and print. Many printer manufacturers support some kind of community site, where users can upload, remix, and review 3D models.

Yes, when used properly. Both FDM and resin printers pose safety risks during operation. FDM printer risks include the hot end of an FDM nozzle and fumes from melted plastic. Resin printers pose more risks, as resin itself is toxic, and should not be allowed to touch unprotected skin, and should only be used in an area where the fumes can be safely vented outdoors. Resin printers also use UV light to cure the prints, which can damage your eyes if not properly filtered.

FDM safety precautions are fairly straightforward. First, don’t stick your hand in the print area while the printer is running. This may sound obvious, but it’s surprisingly tempting to do, since sooner or later you’ll spot a bit of loose filament or some other bit of debris laying on the bed in the middle of a print. It’s very easy to reach in and grab that debris without pausing the print -- but the print head moves very fast and without warning. That nozzle is probably around 300 degrees celsius / 580 Fahrenheit, and having it slam into your knuckle can leave a puncture and a burn.

Second, make sure the room where you operate the printer is well ventilated. Proper ventilation is especially important when using high VOC filaments. These include acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) and acrylonitrile styrene acrylate (ASA), but the fumes will vary by manufacturer, so err on the side of caution.

Resin requires more extensive safety precautions. You’ll need to invest in PPE such as nitrile gloves, a respirator (use filters rated for VOCs and not just dust debris), and possibly UV safety glasses. When resin printing, venting is even more important. In most cases it’s easy to safely vent your 3D printer, but if you’re concerned, consider getting an air quality monitor to ensure that you’re working in a safe environment.

Your primary expense using a 3D printer is your printing material, which will be plastic filament for these printers, but could be other materials with more advanced models. You can buy a one-kilogram reel of PLA filament for about $12 to $19. If you need a specialty filament, you’ll likely pay double that amount, and prices can go much higher for premium materials.

Then there’s the hit to your electric bill. FDM printers typically use about 50 to 100 watts to operate, depending on what material you’re printing and the ambient temperature. If your electricity is 20 cents per kilowatt-hour, your printers will likely cost less than 2 cents per hour to operate.

Lastly, there will be other costs over time: You may need replacement bed plates for FDM printers, or post-processing supplies for resin printers. Other parts may break and need replacing, as well.

Once you have a print and some compatible printing material, all you need to do is figure out what and how to print. I recommend new printer users pick up some calipers ($30 or so, but you can get away with a $10 set). You can actually 3D print most of the other tools you’ll use. In fact, printing storage bins and organizers for your printing tools is a great way to learn the ropes while making useful prints.

The Sun’s partial phases march down to the horizon, where totality lasted about 73 seconds — the site’s first total eclipse since 1539. The photographer composited frames shot with a Sony mirrorless camera and a 35mm lens; the foreground is a 1/30-second exposure at f/2 and ISO 160.

#6354. Why do we feel colder as we age? Scientists are tracing the signals

A mouse study suggests immune signals slow brown fat’s response to cold with age, offering clues to why older bodies struggle to stay warm.

An older person can feel chilly in a room that feels comfortable to someone younger. Some of the explanation may lie in brown fat, which burns sugar and fat to supply the body with heat.

In a new mouse study, this fat took much longer to respond to cold in old animals than in young ones. The researchers followed that difference back to a substance released by nearby immune cells.

Older brown fat had more of this substance, which helps hold down heat production. A separate drug experiment showed that the mice could recover some of their lost warmth.

Anying Song and Qiong A. Wang led the work. Wang, an associate professor at City of Hope, is a corresponding author.

In young mice at room temperature, 28.8% of brown fat cells were in a state that produces lots of heat. The share more than doubled to 61.7% after a day in the cold, reaching 89.7% by the third day.

Mice aged about 74 weeks started far lower, at 0.31%. Three days later, the figure was 50.9%, still short of the younger animals’ level on day one.

The older mice got colder while their fat was making this slow adjustment. Within two days, 25% had died.

The laboratory’s 2020 work had shown that the cells differed in their supply of a protein called UCP1. A brown fat cell uses this protein to make heat.

There was plenty of UCP1 in some cells and hardly any in others. Those with little of it were doing less of the heating.

In these less active cells, another protein called H6PD was more abundant. H6PD helps the cells maintain a supply of active stress hormone.

Cortisol is the main stress hormone in humans, while corticosterone plays that role in mice.

With this hormone acting inside them, the fat cells respond less strongly to nerve signals that call for more heat.

At 75°F (24°C), the mouse tissue contained about as many cells in one group as in the other. Only a few cells had both proteins.

For the human part of the study, the researchers used tissue from five patients who had thyroid surgery in Ancona, Italy.

Colleagues at Marche Polytechnic University helped examine the fat, which came from above the collarbone.

The human cells divided into two nearly equal groups as well. These patients were between 18 and 48 years old, leaving the researchers without samples from older adults.

The young mice spent a week in a room at 43°F (6°C). By the end, the cells making plenty of heat accounted for 85.6%, up from 31.1% before their stay in the cold.

Once the animals were warm again, the change went into reverse.

To check the part played by nerves, the team cut their connection to brown fat on one side of young mice. In cold conditions, 85.6% of cells on the side with working nerves became highly active, compared with 29.1% on the side without them.

That second side looked pale, too, as brown fat does when it makes little heat. It was in the same cold surroundings as the other side, but couldn’t receive the nerve messages.

The nerves release noradrenaline, so the researchers tried adding that chemical to fat cells in a dish. H6PD levels stayed as they were.

The next clue involved two types of immune cells found in the fat, neutrophils and macrophages. Some of them made IL-1 beta, a substance involved in inflammation.

After a week in the cold, the team measured 53% less IL-1 beta in brown fat. Moving mice into a warm room raised its level 3.3-fold.

IL-1 beta was produced by 10% of neutrophils and 1% of macrophages in the tissue. Under the microscope, less active fat cells lay closer to these immune cells, while cells making more heat lay farther away.

This arrangement suggested that the immune cells could have an effect on their nearest neighbors. The team also worked out how IL-1 beta kept those fat cells from making much heat.

It kept H6PD from breaking down, so the amount of this protein rose 3.5-fold. With its supply maintained, the active stress hormone could keep heat production low.

When the researchers blocked IL-1 beta inside brown fat, the balance of more active cells to less active ones doubled at room temperature. Blood levels of the signal didn’t change along with it.

Older brown fat contained six times as much IL-1 beta and 1.8 times as much active stress hormone, although blood hormone levels weren’t higher.

It also had 2.3 times as much of the protein supporting that hormone and 40% less of the protein used to make heat.

Extra weight didn’t produce the same pattern. All the young mice that became obese on a high-fat diet survived a week in the cold, and their brown fat appeared more active.

The researchers tried mifepristone, a drug that blocks the receptor through which the stress hormone acts. They gave it to 72-week-old mice for a week.

Without treatment, only 0.5% of cells were in the active group at room temperature; with the drug, 8.3% were. After a cold day, those figures were 10.6% and 32.8%.

The treated animals stayed warmer, and their brown fat contained smaller fat droplets. They burned more energy and used more oxygen through day and night, although they neither ate more nor moved more.

Removing the hormone receptor from active fat cells in another experiment also kept heat production going.

It continued for days after the mice returned to warmth, using extra fuel even though the animals’ food intake hadn’t changed.

Mifepristone isn’t a treatment for feeling cold. Because it acts in many tissues, the experiment couldn’t pin all the improvements on brown fat.

All the mice were male, and the human samples included no older adults.

“Learning how the body controls this process may offer insights into obesity, type 2 diabetes and other metabolic disorders,” said Wang.

“That possibility matters for more than staying warm. Thermogenic fat also burns glucose and fat, and its activity tends to decline with age.”

For the older mice, at least, some capacity to make heat remained. The experiments showed that changing the signals reaching their fat cells could bring some of it back.

The study is published in the journal Nature.

#6353. Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.

Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of New York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.

Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani says gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.

To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”
